nytimes.com.title: Over 100 Migrants Are Dead After Boat Capsizes Near Djibouti
nytimes.com.text:
At least 139 people have died, including 15 children, after a boat carrying hundreds of migrants capsized while traveling from the Horn of Africa to Yemen, the International Organization for Migration said on Sunday. An additional 84 are still missing, the United Nations body said in a statement, stoking fears that the death toll could climb.
The shipwreck is among the deadliest ever recorded on the route, one of the most dangerous crossings in the world. More than 80 people survived, all of them Ethiopian nationals.
The boat was carrying 305 people when it overturned between Thursday night and Friday morning, near Guhere, north of Obock, a small Djiboutian port town, the migration agency said. The migrants were traveling from Djibouti to Yemen across the Bab el-Mandab Strait, the agency said. Last year, more than 900 people died or went missing while making the journey, according to an agency tally.
The bodies of nine girls and six boys were among the 139 recovered as of Sunday, the U.N. migration agency said. The cause of the disaster was not immediately clear.
Tens of thousands of men and women from Ethiopia and other East African countries make the desperate sea crossing from the Horn of Africa to Yemen every year, seeking jobs and security in Saudi Arabia and other Persian Gulf states. The boat trip is only the first part of a route fraught with danger. In Yemen, which has been torn apart by civil war since 2014, migrants risk violence, thirst and hunger as they traverse the country toward the Saudi border, frequently on foot.

cnn.com.title: Buried bodies, cleared rubble, Israel’s yellow line: How war is hampering the search for Gaza’s missing
cnn.com.text: Dusk had fallen in the northern Gaza neighborhood of Jabalya when an Israeli quadcopter broke the evening lull on November 1, 2024. That evening, Mohammad Yousef Shalayel had settled into his in-laws’ home with his wife and children – after visiting 16 relatives displaced at his parents’ house nearby. He didn’t know that would be the last time they saw each other. An “enormous explosion” rocked the area, “completely collapsing” the Shalayel house. When Shalayel returned to the site of the attack the next morning, “all four floors had fallen on top of one another, on the people who were inside,” he said. Among them were his elderly mother, his two brothers and his sister, and their children and in-laws, too. “I will never forget… I found dismembered remains of children and women,” he told CNN in late September. “I broke down, but I tried to hold myself together so that I could gather the pieces of flesh that were scattered around.” Nearly two years later, Shalayel has been unable to return because the Israeli military has since occupied more than half of the shattered territory. He says almost all his family members remain unaccounted for. Amid the ruins of Gaza, Palestinians say they are trying to survive a conflict with no clear end in sight. Three years after Hamas and other militant groups killed around 1,200 people in Israel on October 7, 2023 – and a year after a US-brokered ceasefire was supposed to end the ensuing war in Gaza – Israeli strikes remain a near daily occurrence. According to the Palestinian Ministry of Health, more than 74,000 people have been killed in the coastal enclave during the Israeli offensive. And the number may still rise significantly. Some 8,000 people are reported missing, according to Gaza’s Civil Defense, most of whom are likely buried beneath what the United Nations estimated last year to be 61 million tonnes of rubble. And with each day that passes, the chances of identifying the dead grow slimmer as “crucial evidence” is lost, said Pat Griffiths, a spokesman for the International Committee of the Red Cross in Jerusalem. Under international humanitarian law, the parties to an armed conflict “have an obligation to conduct search and recovery work” for the remains of those killed, missing or injured, and to collect, preserve and transfer that information to the other side, Griffiths told CNN. Access blocked Under the October 2025 ceasefire plan, Israeli forces were instructed to withdraw to the “yellow line,” which demarcated occupied areas. That shifting demarcation zone has blocked Palestinians from accessing swathes of land where their loved ones could be buried under the rubble, residents and aid workers say. Several people in Jabalya told CNN they witnessed the Israeli military demolishing mosques, homes and buildings or clearing rubble near the yellow line. “Where are the bones of our loved ones?” asked one resident, Yahya Odeh. “Where are their bodies? There are entire families beyond the yellow line who have been separated from their relatives.” In September, the UN human rights chief, Volker Türk, warned against the clearance of rubble in areas under Israeli military control “by bulldozers with no respect for the dead,” after Euro-Med Human Rights Monitor, a Geneva-based NGO, reported that such activity could erase evidence of war crimes. Türk said the recovery of “what appears to be entire families” from under the rubble in areas accessible to Palestinians highlights the need for evidence of possible war crimes to be preserved, and called for international investigators to be given access to all of Gaza. Meanwhile, Israel’s restrictions on heavy machinery entering Gaza have prolonged recovery efforts in parts of the enclave where Israeli troops are not currently present, Palestinian officials say. In August, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu rejected a 15-point plan laying out a pathway to long-term stability in Gaza, insisting Israel’s forces would not withdraw “until Hamas is genuinely disarmed.” The militant group in turn demanded that the Israeli military stop striking Gaza and pull back to the yellow line, as set out in the ceasefire plan. Last year, an independent UN inquiry found Israel has committed genocide in Gaza, a finding rejected by the Israeli government. Gaza City’s sole excavator In parts of Gaza accessible to Palestinians, Civil Defense members scour bombed-out homes for the remains of missing people. Since last October, field crews have recovered around 1,000 bodies from the rubble, according to Mahmoud Basal, the Civil Defense spokesperson. But only one excavator is available in Gaza City, with another in central Gaza, said Basal, adding that operations could be “completed” if Israeli authorities were to provide the 10 excavators, 10 bulldozers and 30 trucks requested by Palestinian officials. The Israeli aid agency tasked with facilitating the entry of aid into Gaza, COGAT, said Israel has allowed in “essential equipment” including engine oil, medical supplies and tents. However, COGAT insisted authorities would withhold heavy machinery and reconstruction materials until Hamas disarmed, according to Reuters. Recovery efforts are made more dangerous by the presence of unexploded ordnance, said Griffiths. Many rescue workers are “literally scraping away, a few centimeters at a time,” he added. When they do find buried Palestinians, some show signs of having been eaten by rodents or stray dogs, said Basal. Shalayel told CNN how he wrapped a blanket around his brother’s arm, which protruded from the rubble of their parents’ house, to try to protect it from an “enormous number” of roaming dogs. “It was a horrific sight,” he said. “In the end, the family tries to comfort itself by believing that all of its relatives have been recovered from beneath the rubble,” Basal said. “But we cannot state (that) with certainty.” Dr. Ahmad Dheir is one of only three remaining specialist forensic doctors in the enclave, he said. Even before the war, doctors had no access to DNA testing facilities, Dheir said, after a years-long blockade imposed by Israel and Egypt limited the entry of medical supplies. The slow eradication of Gaza’s medical infrastructure – following repeated Israeli strikes on health centers – has made medical workers even more reliant on elementary identification techniques, said Griffiths. When rescue teams deliver unidentified bodies to hospitals, the lack of freezer storage, fuel shortages and frequent power cuts hasten the deterioration of samples, said Dheir. With no DNA testing available, health workers have resorted to inconclusive blood typing and laboratory tests, condemning many relatives to a perpetual state of uncertainty, he said. ‘Deep human need for truth’ Suha al-Sharif’s son, Jihad, was supposed to care for his mother in old age. Instead, his absence is her only companion. “When Jihad left, I realized that he was the one carrying me. He was my strength,” the 55-year-old told CNN. Jihad, 33, was shot and killed on November 9, 2023 – when the family was displaced from Gaza City, Al-Sharif said. His body was taken to Al-Shifa Hospital, in the north, but Israel’s intensifying attacks meant health staffers could not bury people. Again, the family were forced to flee, journeying south. Nearly three years later, Al-Sharif has not been able to find him. “The hardest thing is that I couldn’t bury him; I don’t know where his body is,” she said. “At night, when I put my head on my pillow, memories come back,” she added. “There is nothing left to cry for. My life feels over.” Her sense of dispossession reflects that of many survivors in Gaza. Palestinians whose relatives are still missing have been presenting signs of “ambiguous loss” – a situational disorder where people feel lost, unable to concentrate, anxious, depressive or guilty, two aid workers told CNN. Some people pray, preserve photographs or loved ones’ belongings to “keep their memory alive,” according to Israa Alqahwaji, the mental health program coordinator in Gaza for the UK-based NGO Medical Aid for Palestinians. Wanting to find a person’s body “reflects a very deep human need for truth,” Alqahwaji said. “Continuing to live does not mean abandoning or forgetting the person they have lost,” she added. The cemetery of the missing In Deir al-Balah a cemetery of the missing, as locals call it, has become a totem for the unknown fate of hundreds of Palestinians. About 1,000 unidentified people have been buried there, according to Gaza’s Civil Defense. Authorities have been working with international aid agencies to build a digital information sharing system, ascribing serial numbers to unnamed graves so that if DNA testing becomes possible, loved ones may be able to identify their relatives in years to come. “We believe these people and their families have a right, as a matter of human dignity, to find their loved ones,” said Dheir. Shalayel hopes that one day he will find his family and lay them to rest with dignity. “For us, the people of Gaza, there is a well-known saying: Honoring the dead means burying them. Our religion, customs and traditions teach us that when someone dies, they should be buried, and their burial place should be known.”

cnn.com.title: Russia deal, execution plans and deportations tell a defining tale about Trump and power
cnn.com.text: Donald Trump is trying to make America more like him. But voters will soon get to deliver a verdict on the president’s efforts to redefine how the government he leads wields power at home and abroad. Three flashpoints illustrate how his coercive and transactional instincts are changing the character of the country and how the rest of the world sees us. Ever since World War II, America has nurtured democracy. But by allowing Russia to supply markets with diesel, Trump will reward a ruthless authoritarian, President Vladimir Putin, who is killing scores of Ukrainian civilians as he aims to crush their independence. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s plan to livestream the death by firing squad of the Fort Hood mass shooter meanwhile risks putting the United States in the category of Iran, the Taliban and Hamas in carrying out public executions. And the shooting by federal agents in New York last week of a citizen of the Dominican Republic while a 5-year-old was in the car was the government’s latest flex of violent force in public in an intensifying deportation crackdown. Each event sparked a political backlash, and each raises questions about the unconstrained use of presidential authority and how eroded legal and behavioral standards will ultimately sit with the national conscience. But each also directly flows from the personality of a president who made no secret of his intentions when he was twice chosen by voters in democratic elections and who represents the views of tens of millions of citizens. The midterm elections are being dominated by high prices for food and housing, a backlash against AI data centers, and public fury over the Iran war. But the election also marks 10 years since Trump first won power, and it will serve indirectly as an accounting of his attempts to define 21st century national greatness through a prism of his truculent and idiosyncratic values. Growing concerns about the Russia diesel deal, a potentially livestreamed execution and Immigration and Customs Enforcement activity may hint at Trump’s eroded political clout nearly halfway through his second term. And the shift of the electoral calendar to a presidential cycle in a few weeks will begin a debate on whether Trump’s redefinition of American exceptionalism is an aberration or whether it will linger in his image when he’s left office. A startling deal with Russia Trump’s deal with Putin to send diesel onto international markets is a blunt demonstration of “America First” in action and the US president’s tendency to use foreign policy to promote his political goals. The move shatters the international sanctions regime that battered Russia’s economy after the invasion of Ukraine; delivers a huge propaganda victory to Putin; and reflects the US president’s pattern of accommodating the Kremlin strongman. It deals a new blow to the morale of Ukrainian civilians, who are under escalating Russian attacks, including at least 33 who died when two public buses were targeted. It opens a huge rift with NATO allies at a moment when Moscow is accused of a campaign of sabotage, harassment and airspace violations in Europe. The Dutch defense minister last week branded Russia “our enemy.” And Trump’s demand Saturday for Ukraine to replace President Volodymyr Zelensky — a key Moscow condition — will renew fears that he’s siding with Kremlin war aims. Those fears were also recently exacerbated by Trump’s failure to license Kyiv to produce Patriot missiles. But there is a logical explanation for Trump’s decision. He’s in a political and economic bind because the cost of diesel has hit record levels, hammering US agriculture and raising food prices. Most of this is because of his war in Iran, and it is unclear whether the deal will lower prices quickly. But he had a burning domestic political imperative to do more, whatever the expense. “It’s another example of our president thinking out of the box,” House Majority Whip Tom Emmer told ABC News’ “This Week” on Sunday. Emmer added: “Our president is trying to find every answer possible to help the American people.” But former Vice President Mike Pence balked at easing the economic vise on Russia. “America should not be throwing a lifeline to Putin’s war machine. Now is the time to stand strong against Russian aggression as we did during the first Trump administration,” Pence wrote in a post on X. Trump rejects the kind of hawkish, traditional Republicanism that Pence represents. The president has a narrower definition of national and personal interest: On the same day he delivered a huge win for Putin, an accused war criminal, and again warned he may destroy Iran, Trump slammed his latest Nobel Peace Prize snub as “an embarrassment” and “disgraceful.” What Hegseth thinks people ‘need to understand’ Nidal Hasan is a US Army major convicted of 13 counts of premeditated murder for targeting soldiers headed to Afghanistan. The question is not whether his victims deserve justice following a judicial process. It’s whether staging a public execution would infringe constitutional protections; whether it is consistent with America’s modern values; and if it would hand Hasan the martyrdom he sought. Hegseth explained last week that the execution would be public because “people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things.” The defense secretary favors the performative use of force and is contemptuous toward those who fear it violates American principles. He has, for example, defended US strikes on alleged drug-trafficking boats in the Caribbean and the Pacific that have killed at least 221 people and that critics call unconstitutional extrajudicial assassinations. A backlash could still scupper the livestream execution plan. Trump said over the weekend that he will decide whether it will happen. But opponents worry that going ahead will stain America’s moral reputation and reward extremist groups with a propaganda triumph. “What is he mimicking, ISIS executions?” Connecticut Sen. Chris Murphy told CNN’s Erin Burnett on Thursday. “I understand that in this country we have the death penalty, but public executions is medieval.” Some Republicans are also concerned. “I absolutely support the sentence of death, but livestreaming executions is what jihadists do. America is better than that,” said Georgia Rep. Austin Scott. And Utah Sen. John Curtis warned on X, “A civilization erodes when it cultivates an appetite for executions as a form of entertainment.” ‘He was a thug’ The public use of military-style force in law enforcement and a narrative of governmental toughness also underpins the deportation crackdown. It has come with grave consequences, including the deaths of protesters Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minnesota. In the latest controversy, Oscar Belgal, 28, from the Dominican Republic, suffered a superficial wound to the neck when he was shot by immigration agents in the Bronx last week. His child was not physically injured. Federal authorities said officers believed that their lives were in danger. The injured man had previously pleaded guilty to fourth-degree grand larceny and received five years of probation, according to court records. Critics see such confrontations as unacceptable examples of untamed federal government power. New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said the officers involved were not wearing uniforms and that ICE agents are “making the city terrified.” But Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told CNN’s Jake Tapper on “State of the Union” on Sunday that Belgal was to blame. “The truth is this guy was an awful human being. He was a thug. He was a gangbanger,” Mullin said. He placed the blame on Belgal for putting his child at risk: “The last thing I would have done is put my son or one of my kids in danger.” Mullin’s comments are consistent with the views of many Americans who favor stronger immigration enforcement and who responded to Trump’s searing promises to launch law and order crackdowns in his campaigns. Yet while a majority wanted more action on the border after the Biden administration’s neglect, there are signs the aggressive tactics are a political liability. In a Pew Research poll in May, 52% said the administration was doing “too much” on deportations. Still, only 19% of Republicans thought so, underscoring that confrontations might please GOP midterm base voters. An existential question voters must answer American history is scarred by violence and stifled justice: lynchings; the crushing of civil rights protests; internments in wartime; and foreign wars that killed thousands of innocent civilians. So Trump’s muscularity is far from the first time that government power has challenged traditional perceptions of US values. Yet few modern presidents have been as willing to test American ideas about limited government power, the restrained use of force, international alliances and American global leadership. Ultimately, citizens must decide at the ballot box if this is what they want.

cnn.com.title: Takeaways from the South Carolina Senate debate
cnn.com.text: South Carolina has emerged as perhaps the most surprising Senate race to be competitive late in the 2026 midterm elections. And on Sunday night, appointed GOP Sen. Darline Graham, Democrat Annie Andrews and Libertarian nominee Kasie Whitener took part in the only debate currently scheduled in the race. The debate was often contentious, with both Graham and Andrews taking aim at each other. Andrews focused on the idea that Graham — the late former Sen. Lindsey Graham’s sister, whom President Donald Trump plucked from obscurity to succeed him — is the choice of political insiders and not running a serious campaign. She at one point alluded to an embarrassing moment at a primary runoff debate in which Graham said, “National security is not my thing.” “If your surgeon said that appendectomies aren’t really his thing, would you still hand him a scalpel? No,” Andrews said. “So why would we hand Darline Graham a full term in the US Senate? She is unserious and unqualified.” Graham also hit Andrews early and often, seeking to tie her to the political left. And she repeatedly took offense to the attacks that Andrews lodged, accusing Andrews of going after her family. Below are some takeaways from the debate. Graham avoided another major flub Job No. 1 for Graham was avoiding a moment like the one on national security. And she cleared that bar. At that GOP debate against Rep. Ralph Norman, she was asked a relatively basic — at least for a senator — question about US foreign policy interests in Taiwan and the South China Sea. Seemingly not knowing where to go with it, she just admitted that she didn’t know much about the issue. At the same debate, she also mistakenly cited 50 million people living in South Carolina, when the actual number is less than 6 million. That doesn’t mean Sunday was smooth sailing. Graham paused awkwardly at times. She struggled to make some of her attack lines, such as on transgender rights, land. Some of her claims — like that Iran nearly had a nuclear weapon before the US and Israel launched the war earlier this year — don’t actually appear true. But for a Republican running in a pretty red state, she came across as more capable than before. Graham came out swinging That being said, Graham seemed to confirm that her campaign is quite concerned about Andrews, judging by how much time she spent attacking the Democrat. It started almost instantly, with Graham calling Andrews “most radical liberal that’s ever run for state office in South Carolina” in her first answer. She accused Andrews of supporting government-run healthcare, which Andrews denied. She pointed to Andrews’ past work on gun control issues. She attacked Andrews for opposing President Donald Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill” and for having the support of Jane Fonda’s political action committee. And after Andrews mentioned her primary runoff debate moment, Graham accused her of lying about her liberal positions. “Let’s talk about what’s not your thing. Your thing, apparently, is not being honest with the people of South Carolina. At least I’m honest. If I don’t know something, I am glad to say it, and I’ll say it again tonight,” she said. “But you are deceiving the people of South Carolina. You have flip-flopped on everything. There’s so many social media posts out there to prove different. Shame on you.” The attacks confirmed the competitiveness of the race. The national GOP recently turned heads by spending $5 million to shore up Graham’s campaign. Andrews distanced herself from the Democratic Party and the left But Andrews had a pretty memorable answer for much of it. “She’s been told to come out here and call me Bernie Ocasio Mamdani; that’s what’s in her script,” Andrews said, referring to a trio of democratic socialist lawmakers. “But the truth is: My name is Annie Andrews, and there shouldn’t be any confusion about that because, unlike my opponent, I haven’t changed my name recently.” Graham opted not to use her married name — Darline Graham Nordone — when she was appointed as a senator. “My legal name is Graham and has always been Graham,” she said. “And you know why it’s Graham? Because I lost my parents when I was a little girl, and I kept the name Graham so that I felt connected to them.” At another point in the debate, Andrews said that “both parties have failed on immigration” and that “Democrats have failed on the border.” Andrews added: “And the truth is, I support the Second Amendment. I believe we need a secure border, and we need to deport illegal immigrants who break the law, and yes, I want to lower taxes on the middle class.” Graham tries to make transgender attacks land Few attacks have been as central to the race as the GOP’s efforts to focus on transgender issues. Just in the last week, Trump posted on social media using an anti-transgender slur for Andrews, and Andrews launched a direct-to-camera ad defending herself on the issue. But if you blinked, you might have missed it Sunday night. Graham brought it up twice, but only briefly. And she did so both times at the end of an answer, right before the debate quickly moved on. That included at the very end of the debate. “But let’s talk about a couple of other concerns I have — that she’s deceiving the people of South Carolina with these transgender issues,” Graham said in the final words of the night. The debate moderator quickly signaled the debate had to end there, and it was over. That was a win for Andrews, in that she didn’t really have to answer for the issue — or explain her 2022 comments on social media calling a state law banning transgender athletes from playing on girls’ and women’s sports teams at public schools “shameful.” Graham defended the Iran war Andrews repeatedly pointed to Graham declining to vote with Democrats and a few Republicans to bringing the Iran war to an end, noting Graham has had three chances to do so. Graham responded by claiming that Iran nearly had a nuclear weapon — which is not backed up by known US intelligence. But unlike some GOP Senate candidates who have said the war needs to end, she went a little further in defending the need to give Trump more time. She argued Iran is being strangled financially. “Why in the world would we stop now when they are still dangerous and we are close to ending the war?” Graham said. “Again, I think the president wants to end the war. I know he does. We all want the war to end. But I support a strong military. I believe in peace through strength.” Few mentions of Trump Few things loomed as large over the debate as Trump; his unpopularity is a major reason South Carolina and other deep-red states are as competitive this fall. But he wasn’t a major focus. There was the occasional mention of something Trump has done, but he wasn’t really a focal point for anybody. In fact, the word “Trump” was only uttered a handful of times. Graham mentioned the president just a few times, praising him for creating an AI task force and waiving restrictions on red-dye diesel. Even when Andrews was arguing Graham was the pick of insiders, she didn’t actually cite the one insider above all who elevated Graham: Trump. And when talking about the war, she generally didn’t attach it to the president. That perhaps shouldn’t be too surprising from the Democrat. While Trump is broadly unpopular nationwide, this is still a state he won by 18 points in 2024.

cnn.com.title: US threatens to suspend intel sharing, weapons purchases if Ukraine continues Russia energy strikes, sources say
cnn.com.text: The Trump administration has warned Ukraine and allies in Europe that the US could suspend intelligence sharing and European purchases of US weapons for Ukraine if Kyiv does not halt its deep strikes on Russian energy facilities, two European officials told CNN. The warnings from the State Department and the Pentagon were sent over the weekend to officials in Ukraine and Europe, including communications from the US military directly to Ukrainian commanders. Another source familiar with the matter said the US threatened to cut intelligence sharing. The Financial Times was the first to report the threats to end intel sharing and weapons purchases. CNN has reached out to the Department of Defense, the State Department and the White House for comment. The threats come as President Donald Trump has been fuming at Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky over attacks on Russian refineries, CNN previously reported. Trump has long blamed the rise in global diesel prices on the Ukraine-Russia war and demanded that both sides halt attacks on energy facilities. Those high prices have also been exacerbated by the US’ war with Iran. Earlier Sunday, Trump announced that Russia and Ukraine agreed to what he described as an “energy ceasefire,” a development that a source close to Zelensky said was a surprise. “Ukraine supports the ceasefire, and it is important that Russia support it as well. We are awaiting details from the American side,” Zelensky wrote on X after the announcement. A European official told CNN that intelligence sharing and weapons purchases are “vital” to Ukraine, describing the threat as a “sad day” for Kyiv and its allies. If acted upon, the suspension would have an immediate impact on Ukraine’s defenses. Intelligence provided by the US helps Ukraine to defend against Russian ballistic missile attacks, by providing the locations of missile launchers and data on where the strikes are heading, and when. Suspending weapons purchases — which take place via the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List, or PURL, mechanism — would have the most damaging effect on shipments of Patriot interceptor missiles, which Ukraine is already desperately short of as Russia has expanded its missile and drone attacks across the country. NATO had not yet seen a change to the PURL program over the weekend, another European official told CNN. The Trump administration previously suspended intelligence sharing with Ukraine in March 2025 following a contentious meeting in the Oval Office between Zelensky and Trump. The US later restored intelligence sharing after Ukraine accepted a proposed US ceasefire following talks in Saudi Arabia. The threats are sure to further complicate the tenuous relationship between Trump and Zelensky. The pair have sparred in recent days over a US deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to supply markets with Russian diesel. Ukraine’s continued refinery attacks were part of what led Trump to strike the deal, a US official previously told CNN. Trump on Saturday suggested Ukraine should get a new leader and replace Zelensky.

cnn.com.title: Boat disaster off Djibouti leaves at least 139 dead, with toll feared to rise
cnn.com.text: At least 139 people, including children, have died after a boat carrying more than 300 migrants capsized off the coast of Djibouti in east Africa, the International Organization for Migration said Sunday. That number only includes those buried by authorities in Djibouti. Others have been buried by the migrants themselves but they won’t be added to the official count until authorities can verify the bodies, Alexandre Coissac, IOM Chief of Mission in Djibouti, told the AP via the phone. “What is terrible is that they were buried with no names, in a common grave, like in a war situation,” Coissac said. “They all have a mother, a father, and we may never learn what happened.” Coissac said the migrants boarded the ship in the evening of Oct. 8 and that it sank very soon after, close to the shore, “mainly because it was overcrowded.” “The local authorities did their best,” Coissac said, “but they were overwhelmed with all the bodies that kept coming at once towards the shore.” He said authorities were bringing the surviving migrants to the IOM rescue center in Obock where they receive medical assistance after swallowing sea water, and psychological support. “They’re all in a state of shock,” Coissac, who visited the area of the shipwreck Saturday, said. “I tried to talk to some of them but it’s very difficult.” Some of the migrants in the IOM center are already aware that their family members died during the shipwreck. Others were given access to phones to call loved ones back home to notify them they are alive. At least 84 people remained missing in one of the deadliest shipwrecks yet on the popular but perilous crossing from the Horn of Africa to the Arabian Peninsula, where many migrants seek work in rich Gulf nations. The boat was traveling from Djibouti to Yemen when it capsized on Thursday night or Friday morning, according to the IOM. More than 80 people survived, all of them Ethiopian nationals, it said. The Geneva-based UN migration agency said the vessel had 305 people on board and warned that the death toll could still rise. Personal items likely belonging to the migrants, including shoes, were seen on a beach in a video shared by IOM. Rescue work continued as fears grew for the missing. Tens of thousands of migrants from the Horn of Africa travel every year through Djibouti and across the Bab el-Mandeb Strait towards Gulf countries in search of safety and economic opportunities, the IOM said in its statement. That movement has continued despite newly escalating fighting in Yemen, on the other side of the strait. “This is a devastating loss of life,” said Coissac. “This tragedy is a stark reminder of the dangers faced by migrants along this migration corridor as they seek economic opportunities.” In recent weeks, at least 2,000 Yemenis have received aid in Djibouti as the fighting has escalated in Yemen between the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized government and Iranian-backed Houthi rebels. That’s the opposite direction from the movement of the migrants who died in the shipwreck and the typical migration patterns of recent years: The tens of thousands who cross from eastern Africa toward Yemen each year have typically been looking for work in places like Saudi Arabia. Over 900 migrants died or went missing along the route last year, according to IOM’s Missing Migrants Project. “No one gets into a boat like that unless they believe there is no other safe way,” IOM Director-General Amy Pope said. “We cannot keep treating these deaths as normal. Safe and legal pathways save lives. I am asking governments and donors to act before the next boat goes down.”

cnn.com.title: Trump considering firing Kimberly Guilfoyle after reports of misconduct, source says
cnn.com.text: President Donald Trump is weighing whether to dismiss Kimberly Guilfoyle from her position as US ambassador to Greece after a string of reports about misconduct, a person familiar with the matter said Sunday. Trump has been monitoring reports claiming Guilfoyle, who was engaged to Trump’s eldest son Donald Trump Jr. for four years, accepted lavish gifts as ambassador and sought money in exchange for providing access to administration figures before she was confirmed. The reports have irked senior administration officials, particularly since they emerged when Secretary of State Marco Rubio was visiting Athens for a high-profile speech on Western democracy delivered from the Acropolis. Trump is expected to decide soon whether to fire Guilfoyle, the person said. The president offered no defense of Guilfoyle when questioned by CNN about the allegations Friday. “I just heard about it. Too bad. I mean, I don’t know,” Trump said. “I just heard a little bit about it. I don’t know too much, but she was always very nice.” CNN has reached out to the White House for comment. Eric Deters, a former Trump donor, said Guilfoyle asked him in a text message to wire her $100,000 to pay off an American Express card in the days before her Senate confirmation. Deters ultimately did not wire Guilfoyle the money, saying he didn’t have the liquid assets at the time. A lawyer for the ambassador told the Wall Street Journal, which first reported the messages, that Guilfoyle disputed the authenticity of the messages. Guilfoyle denied to administration officials last week that she sent the messages, the person familiar said. Guilfoyle has remained close to the Trump family. After her breakup with Donald Trump Jr., she received the plum assignment in Greece. Allies of the president and his son told CNN they felt the episode is embarrassing, though it’s not clear whether there will be consequences for Guilfoyle. Trump has repeatedly made clear he is not happy when allies profit off of their relationship with him. Vice President JD Vance on Friday withheld judgment on whether there should be consequences for Guilfoyle, saying he refused to “try people in the court of public opinion.” But the vice president said, in general, he was uncomfortable with access-for-pay schemes. “Of course I don’t like anybody selling access to another government official, certainly a high-level government official,” he said. “Let’s see what the truth is. And obviously, if there was something bad that happened, then people have to suffer consequences for it,” he said.

cnn.com.title: Hurricane Simon skirts Mexico’s Pacific coast as beachside communities and tourist areas prepare for impacts
cnn.com.text: Hurricane Simon threatened coastal communities and popular tourist destinations along Mexico’s Pacific Coast on Sunday, as authorities urged residents to take shelter. The international airport in Puerto Vallarta, a resort city on the shore of Bahía de Banderas, suspended operations as the powerful storm moved north-northwest offshore, along the coast of Mexico. Initial models projected Simon would make landfall as a Category 4 storm Sunday, but its path has shifted and is getting harder to predict. The storm weakened to a Category 3 Sunday night and is now expected to remain offshore through Monday though models are split on whether it will move inland or stay entirely offshore. The hurricane is moving at a speed of 5 mph with maximum winds of 120 mph, according to the 11 p.m. ET report issued Sunday by the US National Hurricane Center (NHC). “Simon moving slowly just offshore of west-central Mexico… threat of destructive winds and flooding rains continues along the coast,” the NHC report said. The national coordinator of Mexico’s Civil Protection Agency (CNPC), Laura Velázquez Alzúa, told reporters that despite the hurricane not yet making landfall, it is still “very close to the Mexican coast.” But authorities are urging residents to take shelter, as the storm’s path is still somewhat uncertain. “We ask that you remain vigilant,” Velázquez said. The coordinator said that the effects of Simon — which include “strong winds, high waves, and storm surge,” particularly along the northern coast of Jalisco state — will continue through Monday. The storm’s current projected path indicates that it has several “probable impacts” on certain states, which is why “Simon concerns us greatly,” Dr. Jorge Zavala, a climate scientist at the National Autonomous University of Mexico, told CNN. Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum urged residents of Jalisco, Colima, Michoacán, and Nayarit to remain in shelter “until an official announcement that the danger has passed” after the CNPC warned of “exceptional rainfall” and “intense winds” in those states. “The wind and rain will suddenly and deceptively subside, creating an apparent calm that does not mean the danger has passed,” the agency warned in a statement. Nonessential activities have been suspended, and precautionary evacuations are continuing, Sheinbaum said on Sunday. Along the boardwalk in Puerto Vallarta, police reminded tourists that the area was closed and urged them to take shelter as the storm approaches, the Associated Press reported. “We don’t know the extent of the danger yet,” visitor Brenda Villareal told the AP. “We’re just starting to see what’s going on.” Mexico’s Navy deployed more than 4,600 personnel to help with the response to the incoming storm, along with excavation equipment, heavy machinery, and other emergency resources. As Simon moves closer to the coast, its heavy rain has already caused damage. Federal authorities are working to restore power in some areas, including Acapulco, a coastal city in Mexico’s Guerrero state that was devastated three years ago by Hurricane Otis. In Manzanillo, the Navy helped remove water from some houses that were flooded by the storm. Manzanillo resident Cecilia Palomar told Reuters that the water started rising in her home at dawn. “It had risen before, but not like this,” Palomar said. “Beds, refrigerators, heaters, all the furniture got wet, the whole house is flooded.” The Pacific Airport Group (GAP) reported that the Puerto Vallarta airport will remain closed until 10 a.m. ET on Monday. Flights at the airport in Manzanillo were also suspended for the day. Laura Sharman and Uriel Blanco contributed to this report.

cnn.com.title: ‘I had the flu’: Talarico returns to campaign trail and dismisses theories about absence
cnn.com.text: Texas Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico on Sunday denounced the wide-ranging speculation about his whereabouts in recent days as Republicans seized on his absence from the campaign trail. “I had the flu. This is the craziest thing I’ve ever heard. It’s wild that someone can just post something on the internet and then the media just runs with it,” Talarico told MS NOW. The state representative, who is locked in a tight contest with Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, said he had been working from home as he recovered and meeting with his team via Zoom. Talarico returned to public events over the weekend, seen speaking to attendees at the Austin City Limits music festival on Friday and in the front row of a Kacey Musgraves concert in Dallas on Saturday. Paxton and his allies, however, have zeroed in on the Democrat’s absence during the final stretch of a race that could be critical to determining control of the Senate. At a rally in San Antonio on Wednesday, the GOP Senate nominee started a “Where is James Talarico” chant in the crowd. Paxton’s campaign also published a flurry of social media posts claiming Talarico is “nowhere to be seen.” President Donald Trump has also chimed in, describing Talarico as “MISSING IN ACTION” in a Truth Social post. A claim also circulated in conservative circles online that Talarico was receiving treatment for a stress-induced episode. “That’s not true. I just had the flu and feel much better. But it’s a good reminder that you can’t believe everything you read on the internet,” Talarico told NBC 5 Dallas-Fort Worth on Sunday. Talarico revealed he had been diagnosed with the flu on September 30 during a virtual appearance at the United States Hispanic Business Council, an event he was supposed to attend in person. He said he had started to feel under the weather and visited urgent care in Dallas. Before his reemergence this weekend, his last in-person campaign appearances took place on September 26, when he held a press conference in Texas and then on September 28, when a Talarico campaign source said the candidate attended a private fundraiser in New York City featuring actor Robert DeNiro. In his interview with MS NOW on Sunday, he dismissed the speculation that there was another reason for his absence as “silly season in our politics” before turning the focus to Paxton, who has yet to agree to a debate. “I’ve heard credible reports that Ken Paxton has a serious medical condition that causes clinical levels of cowardice,” Talarico joked. “He has asked for proof of life from me, I’m asking for proof of spine from him.” Even after Talarico’s return to public events, Paxton continued to cast suspicion on his absence. “I don’t know whether to believe him about the flu or not, I just know that … almost everything that he says has been false since the beginning of this campaign,” Paxton told Fox News on Sunday evening. Talarico’s return to the campaign trail comes ahead of a town hall on Wednesday evening hosted by CNN and Jubilee Media and moderated by Erin Burnett, live in Fort Worth, Texas. The media outlets have also extended a town hall invitation to Paxton. This story has been updated with additional details.

cnn.com.title: Trump’s US-Russia diesel deal draws bipartisan criticism
cnn.com.text: President Donald Trump’s diesel deal with Russian leader Vladimir Putin is facing bipartisan blowback in the US as lawmakers warn that the Trump administration is defying a federal law meant to crackdown on Russia after the invasion of Ukraine. Seven senators, among them four Republicans, released a statement on Sunday asking the Trump administration to “immediately reverse course” on its plan to supply markets with Russian diesel fuel. The bipartisan group points out that Congress passed a ban on energy imports from Russia in 2022 to “prevent American dollars from financing Putin’s brutal war against Ukraine.” “President Trump’s decision to allow Russian diesel imports to the U.S. runs directly counter to that law,” the senators said, adding that the administration did not consult with Congress or submit a justification for the decision as the law requires. “The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians. The Administration must immediately reverse course,” they urged. Trump announced in a social media post on Friday that Putin agreed in a call to “immediately supply” more than 300,000 tons of diesel to global energy markets, with another 500,000 tons promised in November. The White House has scrambled to find ways to decrease skyrocketing fuel prices ahead of this fall’s pivotal midterm elections, though former US officials have said it is unclear whether Putin even has the amount of diesel that Trump cited to sell. Energy market analysts say the amount promised by Trump is unlikely to make much of a difference in global diesel prices. Sen. Thom Tillis, one of the Republican signatories, along with Sens. Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski and John Curtis, predicted the choice to enter into a deal with Russia would have “deadly consequences” by “giving Vladimir Putin any sense that we’re going to put our foot on the brakes versus put on our foot on the accelerator to ending this war and ensuring peace in Europe.” The North Carolina Republican, who is retiring after this term, said in an interview Sunday on NBC’s “Meet the Press” that he thinks Trump’s agreement with Russia is “tarnishing Lindsey Graham’s efforts,” echoing a sentiment made by former vice president Mike Pence on Saturday. Congress passed a bipartisan bill last month spearheaded by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham to place heavy sanctions on countries that import Russian oil and gas. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent contended that the administration is working within both its legal authorities and political mandate to purchase the diesel. “Look, President Trump they came into office with a with a mandate to work for the American people, and this is good for the American people,” he said in an interview on “Fox News Sunday,” also slamming European critics of the deal as “hypocritical” because they “cannot wean themselves off Russian energy.” Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso also downplayed the contradictions between Trump’s actions and the broadly popular support for Russia sanctions, arguing that Graham’s law was meant to give the president another “point of leverage” against Putin. “The high diesel prices that are impacting everyone. The president is balancing and has to make tough decisions,” he told CBS on Sunday. Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, who’s facing a tough reelection race in a Pennsylvania district that Kamala Harris carried in 2024, announced over the weekend that he’ll try to force a House vote on bipartisan legislation to block “any and all purchases of Russian oil.” The Republican said he plans to introduce the “Ronald Reagan Peace Through Strength Act” and collect the at least 218 signatures needed to bring a bill to the floor under a procedural maneuver known as a discharge petition.

cnn.com.title: Judge orders Trump to halt taxpayer-funded ads with hours left in administration’s push
cnn.com.text: A federal judge on Sunday evening ordered the Trump administration to cancel any further airings of the controversial taxpayer-funded ads that promote President Donald Trump’s agenda. Judge Jennifer Rochon granted a temporary restraining order requested by a coalition led by the nonprofit government watchdog group Common Cause, which had challenged the ad buys in a New York federal court. The Justice Department told Rochon, an appointee of Joe Biden, late Saturday that the ad push was set to end Sunday night. But Rochon said that timing didn’t render the lawsuit moot and ordered the government to halt any further airings as of 6:45 p.m. ET. Earlier, the government said in a filing to the court that it has already spent $19 million in taxpayer money on the ads. The administration allocated $20 million for the ads, which were classified as “public service announcements,” from US Customs and Border Protection, CNN previously reported. An advertising company, LMD Agency Inc., “purchased media buys under the terms of the Order through Sunday, October 11, 2026, at an approximate cost of $19,000,000,” senior Department of Homeland Security official Holly Mehringer said in a sworn declaration in the case. The Department of Homeland Security, which includes CBP, directed LMD “to not make any additional media buys past October 11,” she added. Mehringer noted there are “no plans” to purchase any additional ads. Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle expressed concerns about the unprecedented ad campaign when it began late last month. On October 5, Trump acknowledged the backlash and said “I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc.,” his super PAC. But six days later, the taxpayer-funded ads were still airing. The Trump administration created at least 13 campaign-style ads, some of which have aired on TV networks including CBS, CNN, MS NOW, Fox News and Fox. Watchdog groups, including the nonprofit, nonpartisan Common Cause, said the ads mark a clear violation of appropriations law restricting the use of federal funding for propaganda or partisan communications. Common Cause and the Democratic National Committee separately sued the Trump administration over the ads. In a response to the Common Cause lawsuit, the Justice Department said in a filing late Saturday that an effort to halt the spending should be denied because the ads “will not continue past tomorrow.” The judge’s order Sunday would block any further ad buys for two weeks, so if the administration does consider resuming the ad campaign at taxpayer expense, DOJ lawyers would need to get the court order lifted. The coalition that brought the suit praised the judge’s order, writing, “We are pleased the court acted swiftly to prevent more taxpayer dollars from being used for such blatantly unlawful political propaganda.” CNN previously reported that Trump has personally driven the video ads, including helping select the imagery and videos used, according to a source familiar with the matter. Two Trump advisers familiar with the ads said they were being created in-house by the White House video team — which is part of the communications team, responsible for the administration’s public messaging — though at least one of them was produced by a pro-Trump meme group. Mehringer, in the court filing, described the ads as “depicting the President of the United States and his administration’s various efforts related to protecting America’s borders, including enhancements of border security by combating drug trafficking,” though that is not the exact substance of many of the ads obtained by CNN. And while the Justice Department conceded the ads “(attack) a generic list of ‘villains,’” it emphasized they did not “address any specific race, electoral candidate, or party.” A White House spokesperson said Monday that Trump did not plan to reimburse the government for the money already spent on the ad buys, and Mehringer and other officials did not indicate any plans for a refund. The White House Office of Management and Budget last month allocated $20 million in taxpayer money from CBP for what it called “OBBBA commemorative events.” (OBBBA is an abbreviation for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which Trump signed into law in 2025.) Mehringer emphasized in her declaration that that money “did not fund the creation or production of any videos or media” and “only funded the airing of preexisting media.” Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin was pressed during an appearance Sunday on CBS News’ “Face the Nation” on whether the taxpayer dollars would be refunded. “Anytime we can do a public service announcement and brag about America, I’m all about it,” Mullin said, taking aim at negative coverage of the Trump administration as he pointed to success in securing the border and lowering fentanyl-related deaths. “We should be bragging about what’s happening inside America,” he said, adding, “I commend the opportunity of President Trump to give us the opportunity to brag about America.” This story and headline have been updated with additional developments.

cnn.com.title: Trump’s diesel deal with Putin drives a wedge through the Western alliance
cnn.com.text: By agreeing to open Russia’s taps and release hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel into a starving global market, the Kremlin has achieved something that raw military might on the battlefields of eastern Ukraine could never deliver. The deal, which involves suspending fuel export sanctions on Russia for six months to allow for diesel sales at market prices, will be a welcome boon for a Russian economy that is creaking under the strain of a war in Ukraine that has dragged on far longer than anticipated. But for Vladimir Putin, Russia’s strongman president, the real benefit isn’t the billions of dollars in fresh revenue. It is the wedge this deal, and the rhetoric around it, drives right through the heart of the Western alliance, which has aimed to isolate Moscow over its war in Ukraine. US President Donald Trump spelled out the new and extraordinary reality in stark terms as he mocked the angry reaction of Ukraine’s wartime leader, Volodymyr Zelensky, who derided the deal as a “weak decision by a strong partner” that provides “extra money for this war.” “We said you can do whatever you want to Russia. Don’t hit the refineries because that’s a world problem that’s caused and he wants to make problems for the world. He wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers,” Trump said before calling for a new Ukrainian leader, essentially blaming high global fuel prices, especially acute in the United States, on Ukraine. Canada’s Prime Minister Mark Carney sided with Zelensky as the two leaders spoke on Sunday, saying that the agreement stands “in direct opposition to the efforts of Ukraine, Canada, and our allies to create peace and stability in Europe.” In recent months, relentless Ukrainian drone strikes, flying deep into Russian territory with terrifying precision, have systematically crippled oil refineries that serve as both the economic engine and the fuel tank for Russia’s military. Amid domestic fuel shortages and severe production cuts, the Kremlin suspended all diesel exports this month so that it had enough for its own needs — a stunning setback for a country that used to be the second-biggest diesel exporter in the world before the Ukraine war. Whether Russia can actually provide the promised diesel or not, by framing the Ukrainian drone strikes on refineries as an assault on American interests, Washington is effectively aligning its economic priorities with Moscow’s survival — even as analysts have suggested the deal is unlikely to dramatically move the needle on diesel prices. The US has powerful levers it can pull to get Ukraine to play ball. Washington no longer provides money and weapons to Kyiv. But vital American intelligence sharing — the digital backbone of Ukrainian defense — risks being cut off if Ukraine now continues to strike at the Russian infrastructure Trump wants left untouched. The threat is real — the US did just that in the wake of the notorious Oval Office blowup last year. Mindful of the risk , Zelensky has indicated he is willing to cooperate, but only if Russia does the same. “Ukraine will be ready to stop striking Russian oil refineries if Russia stops striking our energy infrastructure,” Zelensky said in a recent statement. For Ukraine, this entire episode may seem like yet another bitter, existential betrayal by an American leader who has at times acknowledged a begrudging respect for Kyiv’s bold military tactics. Now, its most effective asymmetric weapon — relentless drone strikes on oil refineries — is being undermined and may be neutralized, not by Russian anti-air batteries, but by American diplomatic pressure along with Trump’s irrepressible urge to do a deal with the Kremlin. In Moscow, on the other hand, the mood is upbeat. “The Russian side confirmed its willingness to supply oil and petroleum products to the US market and global markets at large,” Putin said in an official statement after a prearranged telephone call with Trump on Friday night. “I am convinced this will have a positive impact on the entire global economy,” he added. Privately, the Kremlin leader must be rubbing his hands with glee. Both he and Trump want Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian refineries to immediately stop. Both want Ukraine’s president to be replaced with someone who will agree a quick deal. And just a few weeks after Trump signed a bill into law, sponsored by the late US Senator Lindsey Graham, allowing for punishing sanctions to be imposed on any country that bought Russian oil, Washington has now become a customer itself. All at once, it seems, a battered but relatively unified Western front that has stood against resource-rich Moscow for more than four years looks like it is being dealt another powerful blow.

Republican Sen. Roger Marshall settled his debts this weekend with a bakery in Kansas after a bill for hundreds of treats his campaign ordered for a 2020 event sat unpaid for six years.
“This isn’t about political parties or policy disagreements. It’s about my personal experience as a small business owner and the importance of honoring financial commitments,” Thomas said. “That experience is why Roger Marshall will never get my vote.”
Thomas said she reached out several times but never heard back, noting that the lack of payment came as her business was just beginning and at the height of the coronavirus pandemic. “Six years later, I haven’t forgotten,” she said.
“We have absolutely no idea how this happened, but rest assured as soon as it became known to us, we immediately attempted to contact the business in order to apologize, and we have repaid the bill from 2020, double,” Marshall said on social media.
Thomas confirmed a few hours later that she can “finally mark the invoice paid.”
The Republican senator is facing a competitive reelection race this fall, with voters’ strong disapproval of President Donald Trump and widespread economic anxiety raising the possibility that Kansas could send a Democrat to the Senate for the first time in nearly a century. A recent poll by The New York Times and Siena University showed Marshall tied with Hamilton at 45% among likely voters.
The repayment of the bakery bill come as Marshall, a former obstetrician-gynecologist, has faced criticism over a report last month that he sued hundreds of patients over unpaid medical debt.
The New York Times found that he had filed lawsuits against more than 700 patients with outstanding bills and at least 81 of those individuals were arrested for missing court dates. Democrats have leaned on the story in ads, accusing Marshall of disregarding people’s concerns about healthcare costs.
A spokesperson for Marshall told the Times that the longtime doctor spent many years treating patients regardless of their ability to pay.
“Judges issue warrants when people repeatedly miss court dates, not doctors,” spokesperson Payton Fuller said in a statement to the outlet.

cnn.com.title: Early voting figures suggest Democratic gains in Ohio’s most Trump-friendly counties
cnn.com.text: After the first days of early voting in Ohio, a state that could help determine control of the Senate, there are clear signs Democrats are more enthusiastic to vote. So far, affiliated Democrats make up larger shares of pre-election voters than they did two years ago, even in the most Republican parts of the state. At this point in 2024, Republicans had a 30-percentage point lead over Democrats in counties that voted for President Donald Trump by 20 points or more, according to data from the Ohio Secretary of State. This year, that’s shrunk to just five points. Voters in other counties have also shifted, including in the counties that voted most strongly for former Vice President Kamala Harris, where they’re about 25 points more Democratic. That’s based on the latest available set of statewide data, from after early voting on Thursday. There’s evidence from the counties for which later data is available that Friday was slightly better for Republicans. The data is just the latest sign of a positive midterm environment for Democrats, as former Sen. Sherrod Brown looks to defeat Republican Sen. Jon Husted, and it comes as a CNN poll finds Brown leading by six points. In the governor’s race, Democrat Amy Acton leads Republican Vivek Ramaswamy by eight points. The overall electorate so far is about 27 points more Democratic than it was at the same point in 2024. It’s important to note that while these signs align with other data that have shown Democrats more enthusiastic to vote this year than Republicans, it’s far from determinative. Even party registration data doesn’t reveal who voters marked their ballots for, and these trends could change, as Republicans in recent years have much been much more likely to vote early in person or on Election Day. Plus, it’s still very early. Ohio is at about 11% of its total early voting turnout from 2022. That’s happening at the same time that the state’s most Democratic places are also turning out more quickly than the most Republican places. Those counties that went most strongly for Harris were at 74% of their turnout from the same point in 2024, while the strongest Trump counties were at 67%. That gap is similar to the one we’ve seen in Virginia, where there’s also a 7-point difference, according to data from Catalist, a company that provides data, analytics and other services to Democrats, academics and nonprofit advocacy groups, including insights into who is voting before November. That gap is smaller than it was earlier this month. A Garden State shift This partisan difference is also apparent in other states. Voters in Ohio don’t select a party when they register, but the state reports party affiliation based on which primary a voter participates in. That’s not the case in New Jersey, where voters do register with a party. Democrats had an unusually weak election in the Garden State in 2024. Former Vice President Kamala Harris beat Trump there by less than 6 points, the narrowest margin for a Democrat since 1992. The counties that were strongest for Trump have seen the biggest partisan shifts towards Democrats in pre-election voting so far, according to Catalist’s data. The breakdown of voters who have returned ballots so far in the state’s three counties that voted for Trump by 20 points or more has shifted nearly 11 points toward Democrats compared to this point in 2024. Turnout is also more Democratic in the strongest Harris counties, but by less than two points. In-person early voting hasn’t started in New Jersey yet, so these shifts could also reflect Republicans continuing to shift away from voting by mail. A shift in method Ohio’s data also reveals a shift in the way people are voting. Since pre-election voting started, there have been indications that 2026 would continue the trend of Americans moving away from voting by mail after the Covid-19 pandemic. It’s early in Ohio, but while early in-person voting is at 72% of what it was at this point in 2024, mail voting is at just 25%.

cnn.com.title: After oil increasingly left the Gulf, Iran is trying to regain its stranglehold on shipping
cnn.com.text: Iran is stepping up attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and Persian Gulf in an effort to restore its leverage over the critical waterway. There have been more than a dozen strikes on shipping since the end of September, reducing the volume of oil transiting the strait and keeping crude prices above $100 a barrel. US President Donald Trump announced Thursday that he has no plans to strike Iran before the midterm elections, where rising energy costs could play a part in his Republican Party losing the House of Representatives, the Senate – or both. “We will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections to be held in the United States on November 3rd,” Trump declared on Truth Social, adding that the administration is “having productive discussions” with Tehran and that his main goal is to ensure the country does not obtain a nuclear weapon. Tehran, however, is focused on Hormuz as a “strategic red line” and is broadening its range of targets in the Gulf. Leverage over Hormuz is non-negotiable for Tehran as it weathers US pressure despite a sinking economy. But Washington has said that the principle of free navigation in international waters is inviolable, a stance echoed by Gulf states that rely on the strait for much of their trade. In one of the latest incidents, the National Guard of the United Arab Emirates said Saturday it had rescued 22 people following an oil tanker fire. Those rescued were Indian citizens – India is one of the largest suppliers of seafarers. The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) – which tracks shipping incidents – has reported several other attacks in recent days. It said the master of an outbound tanker reported it was struck Saturday by an unknown projectile in the Strait of Hormuz, causing a fire on board. UKMTO reported another attack in the same area on Sunday, resulting in damage to the vessel. All crew members were reported safe. The navy of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) claimed on Saturday that a supertanker carrying crude oil suffered a massive explosion after striking a naval mine while attempting to leave the Strait of Hormuz through a route Tehran hadn’t authorized. “No extra-regional power has the right to threaten, maintain a domineering presence, or interfere in it. The Strait of Hormuz is Iran’s strategic red line,” said the head of the IRGC, Ahmed Vahidi, in a post on X. UKMTO said Sunday it had also received a report from several ships in UAE waters that they had been directed via VHF radio messages to move from their anchorages. Iran has avoided targeting the UAE recently. Shipping analysts Ambrey said the IRGC Navy had issued a warning to six vessels anchored around 16 miles (25 kilometers) from the port of Ras al Khaimah in the UAE. “The vessels were advised to heave up anchor, exit the area immediately, and transit to Dubai anchorage,” Ambrey noted. Analysts say the rise in Iranian attacks and threats is in response to higher volumes of oil and petroleum products through the strait. They averaged about 13.1 million barrels per day at the end of September, according to Kpler, a marine data tracking service. That’s just under 80% of the 17.1 million barrels that had traveled through the strait each day before the war broke out. But flows appear to have slowed this month. Just seven tankers transited the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday, less than half the seven-day average and the lowest number since July 23, data from Kpler showed. However, figures are at times revised higher after ships have moved through the strait, as many switch off their identification systems to try to avoid detection. The US military continues to enforce a blockade on Iranian ports, as part of a strategy of maintaining economic pressure on Iran. On Saturday it had disabled a cargo vessel in the Gulf of ⁠Oman after the ship’s crew ignored warnings and ⁠attempted to run the ongoing naval blockade against Iran. “A U.S. military ‌fighter ⁠jet struck the stern of Panama-flagged M/V Ocean Molica (also known as the “Arika Sun”) with a precision ‌munition, fully disabling the ship’s propulsion without harming ⁠the crew,” US Central Command posted on X. The US blockade has been highly effective, according to analysts. September was the first month that Iran loaded no crude onto tankers since maritime data tracking service Kpler began monitoring Iranian exports in 2013. Last week, Mohsen Rezaei, Secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, described the current economic situation as one of the most difficult periods the country has faced. Tehran has insisted that if it can’t export its oil, its neighbors won’t be able to either. It believes it holds the initiative, given US shortages of air defense interceptors, and says its military posture has moved towards the offensive. “Both the Americans and other countries should know: As we have said before, in a region where we cannot sell oil, no one else will be able to sell oil either. And if our security is not guaranteed, no infrastructure will be safe,” Iran’s chief negotiator Mohammed Bagher Ghalibaf, said late in September. It now seems intent on turning that threat into reality.

cnn.com.title: Trump really wants to make ‘super intelligence’ happen. Is it going to happen?
cnn.com.text: Unable to convince Americans to embrace the AI data centers they hate, President Donald Trump is instead exercising the one power he believes is absolute in the presidency: a rebrand. But unlike Lake America, the Gulf of America, military bases or a mountain, this change is about altering public opinion rather than scoring political points. Trump first told fellow world leaders at the United Nations last month that “use of the word artificial makes intelligence fake, it makes it sound fake.” It’s not fake, Trump says; it’s amazing After Trump signed an executive order in late September, the US government has been changing official documents and websites. Cabinet secretaries and other aides immediately used the new term. Elon Musk said on X that he would change the name of his company from SpaceXAI to SpaceXSI, although that particular change has not yet occurred. Trump has refused to answer questions that use the old term. He told supporters at a campaign rally in Nebraska that he would henceforth repurpose “artificial” — an “ugly” word, he said — for the news media. AI is for ‘THE ENEMY’ On Thursday, the president said on social media that anyone who uses the term artificial intelligence instead of super intelligence will be viewed by his White House as “THE ENEMY!” All of this might feel very much like Trump’s “weave” — the mental meanderings of Trump’s public statements — but it has also been fascinating to watch the infrastructure of the federal government respond to what many Americans might write off as a semantic distinction. Renaming things is within Trump’s power There are things that are out of Trump’s power — passing spending bills, renaming the Kennedy Center, ending his war against Iran — but he has shown that presidents have power to change names. It’s also evidence he knows the unpopularity of data centers and concerns about AI in general at a time when he is a major booster of AI. Will a rebrand be effective? Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has long pushed to view AI as superintelligence. In August, he published a 6,000-word treatise about how Meta would approach AI. In rose assessments of the future, he referred to the promise of superintelligence. When he referred to AI, it was usually in reference to what he argued were unfounded worries. Zuckerberg said Meta will be committed to an open source model that provides for superintelligent agents working on behalf of every individuals. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman told Politico’s “Decoded” podcast there are no plans to change the name of his company to OpenSI. But he did say that people in the industry have been using the term superintelligence for a while. It might be a better term, ultimately, than artificial intelligence, but “still sort of understates the magnitude of what I think is happening,” Altman said. Altman predicted people would still use the term AI and questioned whether Trump’s rebrand would accomplish its goal of changing people’s opinions of AI. “Does superintelligence sound obviously less scary to people than artificial intelligence?” Altman wondered. Time will tell. Superintelligence is a separate concept What is definitely true is that the concept of superintelligence, while it sounds better in Trump’s view, is arguably distinct from AI and should be no less intimidating to Americans. The term artificial intelligence has its roots in the 1950s, when a group of Dartmouth professors held a summertime conference “on the basis of the conjecture that every aspect of learning or any other feature of intelligence can in principle be so precisely described that a machine can be made to simulate it.” Superintelligence, at least academically, seems more like the next step of artificial intelligence, or artificial generative intelligence. That happens when the machines learn. The Oxford philosopher Nick Bostrom has written extensively about superintelligence, including in the 2014 book “Superintelligence: Paths, Dangers, Strategies.” Here’s how Bostrum first defined superintelligence in a 1997 essay: Asked how he views Trump’s rebrand, Bostrum said that from a technical perspective AI has traditionally “been this wide umbrella term that refers to every form of intelligent information processing in machines.” We’re talking everything from the Google searches and email spam filters, the current crop of AIs and “hypothetical future more powerful ones.” “If the idea is to use the new word superintelligence to cover all of that, it’s a little bit of a stretch, maybe, to call my spam filter a superintelligence,” Bostrum told CNN. In the theoretical evolution of AI, what comes next, he said is AGI, or artificial general intelligence, which refers to a system that has the same kind of learning and reasoning as humans, something Atman says might already have occurred. “Superintelligence was reserved for this sort of hypothetical future form of artificial intelligence that not only matched but radically exceeded humans across all cognitive domain,” according to Bostrum. That is exactly the thing that frightens the AI “doomers.” But it is incomprehensible to Trump that the machines could outwit him. Trump moves to control the narrative “The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!” Trump wrote in September, arguing against any sort of AI regulation. Bostrum has written both about potential pitfalls of superintelligence as well as the enormous potential to improve and extend human life. But by changing the name, Trump seems to just want to control the narrative. Bostrum doesn’t necessarily think it’s a bad idea. “It’s not up to me to decide how English language should be used,” he said. “I mean, it’s good for my book sales, I guess.” He does see the rhetorical argument for a new term: It’s harder to argue against super intelligence than artificial intelligence. “If you define superintelligence as we already have superintelligence and it hasn’t caused any catastrophe yet, then what’s the big deal? And you then would need to introduce some new term to refer to this like hypothetical future capability that’s even more powerful.” Trump knows a thing or two about saying things so much that they take hold in the public. He rarely speaks in public without repeating the same talking points about “fake” news, the “radical left” Democrats, or about how wonderful his own leadership has been, regardless of what the facts are. At the UN, Trump compared his rebrand to the evolution of “global warming,” which he said was “reborn to climate change because the planet was cooling, not warming, and nobody was dead.” That’s not exactly what happened, as anyone paying attention to the warming climate in recent years can pretty easily confirm.

cnn.com.title: Saudi Arabia will have to respond to Houthi airport attack – but the choices are stark
cnn.com.text: As Saudi Arabia reckons with the deadliest attack on its soil in more than a decade, questions swirl over how Riyadh will respond as Yemen’s Iran-allied Houthis continue to wreak havoc on the kingdom. The kingdom launched a major offensive last week to support Yemeni government forces fighting the Houthis, but the rebels have so far held their ground. Instead, they have escalated their campaign against the kingdom, culminating in Saturday’s missile attack on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport that killed at least 13 people. Drawing from Iran’s playbook in its conflict with the United States, the Houthis are vowing a painful escalation, targeting critical infrastructure in Saudi Arabia and imposing a global economic cost. The Houthis have longstanding grievances against Saudi Arabia over Riyadh’s decade-long war against the group, which triggered the world’s worst humanitarian crisis. The recent Houthi escalation, however, is increasingly seen as an extension of Iran’s conflict with Washington. After eleven years of trying to contain the Houthi advance militarily and through talks, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and his brother, Defense Minister Khaled bin Salman, face limited options. Across the border, the rebels have grown more powerful, consolidating control over major cities and pushing to seize others, such as the densely populated Taiz. “This threat has to be dealt with once and for all,” Ali Shihabi, an author and commentator on Saudi politics told CNN. “A lot will depend on the performance of the Yemeni government troops on the ground and Saudi is helping them extensively with air power.” So far, Saudi Arabia has largely confined its role to providing air cover for the anti-Houthi Yemeni coalition, stopping short of any major deployment of its own troops on the ground. Whether that restraint will hold after Saturday’s strike on Riyadh remains an open question. Sending large numbers of Saudi troops into Yemen would plunge the kingdom into a an expensive and grinding ground war across rugged terrain and undercut the image Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman is carefully cultivating of a stable, investment-friendly kingdom and global tourism hub. Better missile capability Barely two decades ago, the Houthis were little more than a small religious revivalist movement. With Iranian backing, they have since grown into a formidable fighting force in possession of ballistic missiles and capable of striking as far away as Tel Aviv. “They’ve developed their warfare,” a southern Yemeni official who fought the Houthis for years told CNN. “They’ve gotten more sophisticated in their attacks, they’re persistent and they’ve enhanced their intelligence.” Yemen’s government alleges that Houthi rebels have worked with Iranian Revolutionary Guard experts to modify missiles into more effective weapons.
