Eyewitnesses said the attack began around 06:00 local time (04:00 GMT), with the aircraft firing more than five missiles directly at the miners' camps, destroying them and excavation pits with people still inside, the newspaper wrote.
The Sudan Tribune reported claims in June that Egyptian forces had used drones and artillery to target artisanal mining sites in the same region, killing several, after sporadic incidents of Egyptian border guards of burning equipment, torching temporary shelters, and firing live ammunition to disperse mine workers.
Days later, Egypt's border agency announced that it and the military had begun a sweeping security campaign along the border to foil illegal migration, drug smuggling and illegal mining.
At the same time, Sudan's de facto leader announced an investigation into the alleged strikes, which were said to have killed dozens.
Gold lies at the core of the border tensions.
Sudan's ongoing civil war has led to a surge in artisanal mining - an often risky practice conducted by civilians with rudimentary tools and without official permission - particularly in remote areas near its borders.
Gold-rich areas such as those in River Nile state lie along porous borders in terrain historically associated with cross-border smuggling routes, with artisanally mined gold potentially feeding into those channels.
Egypt's border force said in June that it had seized 86 tonnes of gold ore along with amateur prospecting equipment.
Artisanal mining has also reportedly continued in Sudan's conflict zones and smuggled gold may be a source of income for armed insurgent groups.
This has raised concerns of illicit Sudanese gold undermining the legitimate Egyptian gold market.

bbc.com.title: Watch: What's behind Trump's energy ceasefire claim?
bbc.com.text:
Watch: What's behind Trump's energy ceasefire claim?
US President Donald Trump has said Ukraine and Russia have agreed to an immediate "energy ceasefire".
Moscow is yet to comment on the announcement and Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky told US media it was "news to me".
Trump also recently announced a US deal to import Russian diesel, in an attempt to bring the fuel price down ahead of the midterm elections.
The price of diesel in the US has been high since the start of the war with Iran and the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
The BBC's Joe Inwood examines Trump's announcement and what might mean for the president ahead of the midterm election.

bbc.com.title: Poland detains man suspected of planning assassination of PM Tusk
bbc.com.text:
- Published
Poland's Prime Minister Donald Tusk said a man accused of plotting an assassination attack against him and his defence minister has been detained.
The interior ministry earlier reported that police had received credible information about possible attacks against Tusk and Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz.
Polish security services convened a special meeting on Sunday after receiving information about the planned attacks, with a spokesman saying officials were treating the threat as "deadly serious".
Tusk thanked the police for "swift and decisive action" in arresting the suspect.
The suspect was arrested in the Lower Silesia region and was a Polish national, Jacek Dobrzynski, a spokesman for the Special Services Co-ordinator told local media.
"In this case we are talking about a strong likelihood that these threats could actually be carried out," he said.
The plan was uncovered when an email with information about the potential attack was forwarded to police by the State Protection Service, which is responsible for ministers' security, Interior Ministry spokeswoman Karolina Galecka said.
Tusk has been Polish prime minister since 2023, having previously held the office from 2007 to 2014.
He served as president of the European Council from 2014 to 2019.

bbc.com.title: Riyadh airport attacks another dangerous moment in already tense conflict
bbc.com.text:
- Published
The attacks on King Khalid Airport in Riyadh mark another dangerous moment in a region that is already fraught with tension and conflict.
Saudi Arabia wasn't ready for this.
In recent weeks the Houthis have stepped up their attacks on Saudi Arabian soil, but their attacks over the past few days have hit the country's critical infrastructure in the form of the capital's main airport, apparently penetrating Saudi air defences with ease.
Saturday's attack killed 12 people and hurt more than 300. On Sunday the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said an "unknown projectile" had hit a passenger hall and a cruise missile had been intercepted nearby.
The physical damage can be quickly repaired, but the country's reputation as a safe haven of stability is taking a battering.
As well as all the airport attacks, the Houthis have sought to take control of strategically significant positions along the Red Sea coast and around the Bab al-Mandeb Strait. This further increases the risk to safe navigation along the vital maritime corridor - although the Yemeni government says it has "secured" the strait.
The civil war in Yemen between the country's government - which is internationally recognised and supported by Saudi Arabia - and the Houthis, who are backed by Iran, has been going on for more than a decade. It has left many thousands of people dead and plunged Yemen into one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.
It is a complex and often confusing geopolitical conflict, and this latest escalation needs to be seen in the broader context of the tension between Iran, the United States and Israel.
Not since the al-Qaeda insurgency of the mid-2000s has the Kingdom faced such a serious threat.
The Saudi government overcame that challenge through an effective hearts and minds campaign. Then it weathered the Arab Spring uprisings around the region which saw off leaders in Tunisia, Libya, Egypt and Yemen.
It even shrugged off – with some annoyance – an Iranian ballistic missile attack on Riyadh in March.
But this is different. Saudi Arabia may have one of the most powerful air forces in the Middle East, and it has been carrying out devastating air strikes on Houthi positions. Despite this, the opposing forces have managed to seize large portions of the country, particularly in the north and west.
But the Houthis know exactly where to hit back: at the soft underbelly of the Saudi economy.
As part of the "axis of resistance", the Houthis are a vital strategic partner for Iran. From Jizan on the Red Sea to the petrochemical complex at Khurais, the Houthis are delivering explosive drones and missiles with deadly accuracy.
The Red Sea shipping route has become increasingly important, because the Strait of Hormuz, on the other side of the Gulf, has still not fully reopened since the US and Iran have failed to reach a deal to end their war.
Targeting ships in the Red Sea is another way that the Houthis are trying to exert leverage - the attacks cause global economic damage, which is a key bargaining chip for Tehran.
In early September, the White House stated it would not directly intervene in the Yemen conflict, but could provide intelligence support to the Saudis. It later confirmed that it was supplying intelligence and had deployed military experts to Saudi Arabia.
However the situation may have taken a new turn following the latest attack on Riyadh, which killed a US citizen.
Speaking to reporters, US President Donald Trump called Saturday's attack "terrible" and indicated he may intervene militarily with the Saudis.
"We just found out about the recent attack, so we'll make a decision. We move very quickly," Trump said.
But that now seems unlikely, at least before crucial US midterm elections next month.
When he was re-elected in 2024, Trump promised to end America's role in wars around the world. Despite this, the US is currently involved in three unresolved conflicts in the Middle East - in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.
Should Trump get embroiled in another one, this time in Yemen, it is unlikely to go down well with voters.
This war now looks like it will intensify before it ends in another shaky truce - with or without US involvement.
Additional analysis from Abdelbassir Hassan, BBC Arabic

bbc.com.title: Children among 139 dead after boat capsizes off Djibouti, UN says
bbc.com.text:
- Published
At least 139 migrants including 15 children have died and dozens more are still missing after a boat sank off the coast of Djibouti, the UN's migration office has said.
The boat had been travelling from Djibouti to Yemen with 305 people aboard when it capsized near the port town of Obock on Thursday night. Around 82 people were rescued, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said.
IOM's Djibouti mission chief Alexandre Coissac called the tragedy a "stark reminder" of the dangers migrants face when seeking a new life elsewhere.
Tens of thousands of migrants from the Horn of Africa make the perilous journey each year hoping to reach Gulf countries for safety and work, the agency says.
The organisation revised its toll from 109 on Sunday after 30 more bodies were recovered.
"This is a devastating loss of life," Coissac said. "Our thoughts are with the survivors and the families who have lost loved ones or remain without news of their relatives."
Local authorities are also arranging burials for those who have died, while the survivors - all Ethiopian nationals - have medical care readily available to them.
Yemen remains engulfed in a devastating civil war that has lasted more than a decade. Despite this conflict - and growing instability across the wider region - migrants still cross the Bab el-Mandeb Strait to Yemen driven by poverty, insecurity and the growing impacts of climate change.
Since 10 September, the IOM said its Displacement Tracking Matrix had observed more than 20,000 "movements" from Ethiopia to Djibouti.
IOM said it was providing assistance to 64 of the survivors at its response centre in Obock, including healthcare and support to "restore contact with their families".
The UN agency was working in "close collaboration" with local authorities to help migrants and "prevent deaths at sea and on land", it added.
More than 900 migrants died or went missing taking the same route in 2025, during an 18% increase in the number of people attempting the journey, according to IOM statistics.
In March 2026, nine people were killed and 45 went missing following a similar incident as Thursday's.
The conflict in Yemen has also displaced more than 130,000 people across the country, the UN refugee agency said last month.
Thousands of Yemenis have fled to Djibouti to escape the civil war between Houthi fighters and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government.
Djibouti is a tiny former French colony that sits just across the Gulf of Aden from Yemen.

bbc.com.title: Poland stabbings driven by online glorification of violence, Tusk says
bbc.com.text:
- Published
Three violent attacks at Polish schools this week were driven by the "glorification of violence" online, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said.
The attacks have left one woman dead and others injured, including children.
"These are very often spontaneous actions inspired by online activity," Tusk said on Sunday, during a crisis meeting with security services.
Police have arrested 117 people across the country for possession knives or other weapons, or for threatening to attack schools or fellow students, after searching tens of thousands of schools.
A woman was arrested on Saturday after injuring three people while attacking a 17-year-old girl at an educational institution in the capital, Warsaw.
It came a day after thousands of police visited schools across Poland, following two stabbing attacks earlier in the week, one of which led to the killing of a female caretaker.
"We are not dealing with any group organized on a big scale," Tusk said on Sunday.
"In the past years and months, we have noted - globally and in Poland - a rise in the fascination with violence," he added.
The prime minister said the attacks were acts of "nihilistic violence" associated with the extreme right.
"Some of the people detained are active in the ultraright environment," he said, adding that police had noticed a rise in online searches of Nazi content as well as of "mass killers who have become idols online".
On Wednesday, a 19-year-old student attacked and injured nine people at a vocational school in the central Polish province of Mazovian.
A day later, the 37-year-old caretaker was killed after a 15-year-old entered a primary school in Leszczydół-Nowiny, north of Warsaw.
Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński also said a 17-year-old was detained in the town of Sierpc, north-west of Warsaw, after allegedly stating "on school grounds that he planned to do something... dangerous - that he intended to harm someone".
Thousands of Polish police officers visited schools nationwide to try to reassure pupils after the stabbings sparked rumours of a "Bloody Friday" of more attacks stemming from a supposed online challenge.
Meanwhile, Polish security services convened a special meeting on Sunday after receiving information about a potential attack on Tusk and Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz, a spokesperson said.
A special services spokesman said officials were treating the threat as "deadly serious".

bbc.com.title: Ukraine strikes Yandex data centre in third attack on Russian tech giant
bbc.com.text:
- Published
Yandex has been forced to pause its operations at a data centre near Moscow after the facility was damaged in a Ukrainian drone strike - the third attack on the Russian tech giant's sites this week.
The company - dubbed "Russia's Google" - said no one was injured at the centre in Vladimir, east of the capital, but some of its services were unavailable to users.
Earlier this week, Yandex said it was struggling to maintain its services after two of its five data centres were hit in Ukrainian strikes.
Both Russia and Ukraine have stepped up attacks on infrastructure in recent months as the war between them continues in its fifth year following Russia's full-scale invasion.
Kyiv said it was targeting places that provide revenue streams for Moscow's war machine, and that the attacks could force Russia to divert its resources to repair the damage at Yandex.
Sunday's attack came hours after US President Donald Trump warned that Ukraine should "damn well stop" attacking Russia's oil refineries so Moscow could release more diesel to the global market - a deal that has drawn criticism from Europe and sparked a diplomatic row with Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky.
Yandex confirmed on Telegram that its data centre in Vladimir had been damaged and that operations had been "completely suspended", although it said it was working to restore connectivity.
The other strikes against Yandex facilities were on Thursday in Sasovo and Friday in Kaluga, south-west of Moscow, causing problems for some of its services, such as its AI chatbot and smart home devices.
The tech company - which also runs a food-ordering and taxi app used by tens of millions of people - said at the time that its data centres were critical for the normal operation of its services, and that it was "very difficult to predict" when they would be back online.
Meanwhile, Russian strikes on Ukraine have continued through the weekend.
The State Emergency Service of Ukraine said six people were injured in Russian attacks overnight on four districts in its south-eastern Dnipropetrovsk region.
On Saturday, at least 20 people including four children were killed in Russian attacks on Zaporizhzhia, local officials confirmed.
Russia has previously also struck Ukrainian data centres, causing internet outages and prompting some firms to move their servers abroad.

bbc.com.title: Pope Leo to have surgery after lump found on lung
bbc.com.text:
- Published
Pope Leo XIV has announced he will be operated on "in the coming days" after a nodule was found on his lung during a medical check-up.
"The doctors found an early, well-localised nodule on my lung," he told the public during his weekly Sunday prayers in St Peter's Square in Rome.
The 71-year-old said his medical team "believe it would be right to intervene" and he had agreed to the operation, while reassuring pilgrims that the mass was "well-contained" and caught "at an early stage".
The pontiff's admission that he would need surgery comes nearly a year-and-a-half after he succeeded the late Pope Francis, who also experienced issues with his lungs that required hospital treatment.
Leo concluded his Angelus prayer by thanking everyone for their "spiritual closeness" and said he entrusted himself to their prayers.
Holy See Press Office spokesman Matteo Bruni told the media that "the operation is scheduled for the first days of next week".
He added that the Pope is expected to take about a week to recover.
Vatican News, the Holy See's news portal, said the operation will take place at Gemelli Hospital in Rome.
The hospital set up a special Papal suite following the failed assassination attempt on Pope John Paul II's life in May 1981, which is still in use today.
Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni expressed her "personal solidarity" with the Pope as he "faces the ordeal ahead in the coming days".
Her sentiments were echoed by Italian President Sergio Mattarella, who offered his "sincerest wishes for a peaceful recovery and a speedy and full return to health".
Isaac Herzog, the president of Israel, also wished the pontiff "a full and speedy recovery".
The Pope, born Robert Francis Prevost, is the 267th occupant of the throne of St Peter – the first US citizen to do so.
He was ordained in 1982 and spent years as a missionary in Peru, where he is remembered as a figure who worked with marginalised communities.
During Sunday's service, the Pope confirmed his upcoming visit to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru in November will still go ahead.
The Archbishop of Montevideo, Daniel Sturla, said preparations for his tour will continue with "greater enthusiasm" as he called for prayers for his recovery.
A lung nodule is a small lump of tissue that is usually detected following an X-ray or CT scan of the chest, according to the NHS.
Most nodules do not cause other symptoms.

bbc.com.title: Buildings swept away as flash floods hit central Nepal
bbc.com.text:
Buildings swept away as flash floods hit central Nepal
A flash flood has washed away houses, bridges and damaged a hydropower project along a river in central Nepal.
The army said on Sunday that it had rescued 49 people from flood affected areas, but five are still missing, the district's top official confirmed.
It is believed that the flood was caused by a landslide upstream of the Budhi Gandaki River in the Gorkha district.
Four bridges and nearly two dozen houses have been swept away, as well as a camp at a hydropower project along the river.
Nepal is still trying to recover from catastrophic floods and landslides that swept through its border towns with Tibet two months ago, wiping out thousands of houses, destroying critical energy infrastructure and leaving thousands dead and missing.

aljazeera.com.title: India opposition plans New Delhi protest to demand election chief resign
aljazeera.com.text:
Authorities have closed half a dozen Delhi Metro stations and warned of traffic disruptions in New Delhi as opposition parties prepare to march to the Supreme Court to protest against a controversial revision of voter lists that has led to disruptions in the Indian capital.
Thousands of police officers and security personnel were deployed across central New Delhi on Monday for a third straight day, erecting heavy metal barricades and closing key metro rail stations in advance of a march called by Rahul Gandhi, the leader of the opposition in Lok Sabha, the lower house of Parliament.
Opposition parties and supporters of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) youth movement have taken to the streets almost daily this month to demand Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation over revisions to voter lists that critics say benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
Police detained thousands of protesters over the weekend as supporters of the youth-led movement attempted to hold a protest march but were stopped by security personnel, with thousands of people detained.
The Election Commission of India (ECI), which oversees the voting process in the world’s most populous nation, has denied wrongdoing.
Opposition figures have accused authorities of trying to suppress dissent through mass detentions.
Parliamentarian John Brittas of the Communist Party of India (Marxist) alleged he was “manhandled, dragged, assaulted” by police during the demonstrations on Sunday.
“This is not merely an assault on an MP. It is an assault on democratic freedoms and the rule of law,” he said.
Police did not respond to questions about the detentions or their actions during a news conference on Sunday.
Several journalists covering the protest said they were also detained despite prominently displaying their press cards.
International NGO Reporters Without Borders said at least 16 journalists were “brutally” detained while covering the protests over the weekend.
“Covering events of public interest is not a crime. It is their job. The police’s actions against the press are unacceptable,” it said in a statement.
Gandhi, a Congress party leader, urged supporters to join Monday’s march to the Supreme Court to press for Kumar’s resignation.
“Bring as much police as you want — 10 thousand, 20 thousand, 40 thousand, go ahead. Call as many BJP-RSS goons as you need,” he said in a post on X directed at Home Minister Amit Shah.
“We are not the ones to get scared. We are not the ones to back down. This fight is not going to stop now!”
The leaders of the youth-led CJP movement, which has millions of social media followers, have also pledged to continue their protests until Kumar steps down.
The protests have become one of the most significant political challenges for Modi in his 12 years in power, bringing together opposition parties, student groups and activists angered by the voter roll revisions.
The revisions resulted in more than 133 million names being removed from electoral lists, according to media reports. Critics say minorities, particularly Muslims, were disproportionately affected.
The ECI says the move was intended to eliminate duplicate, deceased and fraudulent entries.

aljazeera.com.title: Alvarez vs M’billi boxing bout to go ahead in Saudi Arabia despite attacks
aljazeera.com.text:
The world title fight featuring Saul “Canelo” Alvarez and Christian M’billi will go ahead this month in Saudi Arabia despite attacks on the country’s airports, which have killed at least 14 people in Riyadh in two days, Saudi sports promoter Turki Al-Sheikh confirms.
Alvarez vs M’billi is scheduled for October 31 in the Saudi capital, which has repeatedly come under attack from Yemen’s Houthis, but Al-Sheikh sought to allay the doubts over the bout on Sunday.
One person was killed and 11 were injured on Sunday when a projectile struck King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, according to Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA).
A Houthi strike on the same airport on Saturday killed 13 people and injured more than 300, making it the deadliest attack on Saudi Arabia in more than a decade.
The Houthis claimed responsibility for all four strikes on Saudi airports before Sunday’s attack, which has yet to be claimed by any group.
Alvarez, who has held multiple world titles across several weight classes, will face WBC super-middleweight champion M’billi in a highly anticipated bout.
“Canelo reached out and told me he’ll still fight in Riyadh this October, no matter what happens,” Al-Sheikh, chairman of Saudi Arabia’s General Entertainment Authority, wrote in a social media post. “He [Alvarez] fears nothing.”
The Mexican boxer, a former two-time undisputed super-middleweight champion, has not fought since he was beaten by American Terence Crawford in September 2025.

aljazeera.com.title: If Netanyahu goes, does anything really change for Palestinians?
aljazeera.com.text:
Four rival Israeli political movements have agreed to work together in a bid to unseat Israel’s longest serving prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu.
The factions – the Yashar party, the Democrats, the Yisrael Beytenu party and the Together alliance – span different parts of Israel’s political spectrum but say they are united in their goal to “preserve and strengthen Israel as a Jewish and democratic state”.
The opposition grouping is in a close battle with a pro-Netanyahu coalition heading into the October 27 elections, recent polling indicated, although neither side appeared on track to win a parliamentary majority.
The election comes as Israel faces a series of domestic crises that are tearing at its social fabric, including questions over political accountability for alleged corruption and security failures, disputes over ultra-Orthodox military service and efforts to exclude Arab parties from political life. The country also faces growing backlash abroad, including from allies, over its continuing attacks on Gaza and Lebanon as well as settlements, which are illegal under international law, and settler pogroms in the occupied West Bank.
Analysts said the combination makes the upcoming elections among the most consequential in Israel’s history but even an opposition victory may bring only marginal change for Palestinians suffering record levels of settler violence and mass displacement. While the opposition alliance has taken Netanyahu to task personally, there is little daylight between them when it comes to Israel’s foundational policies in Gaza and the West Bank.
“Palestinians should not expect a fundamental change in Israeli policy if the Netanyahu bloc loses power,” said analyst Samer Jaber, a doctoral researcher specialising in political economy at Royal Holloway, University of London.
“The major political blocs share core positions on the Palestinian question, including support for the existing settlement structure, while the state institutions that formulate and implement policy would remain unchanged,” he added.
What is the anti-Netanyahu coalition?
The leaders of the four major Jewish-led opposition movements gathered on September 26 and signed a declaration promising not to attack each other in the run-up to the elections and to collaborate in forming a government after the vote.
In addition to Yair Lapid, who leads the official opposition in Israel’s Knesset, the meeting included Gadi Eisenkot, who heads the Yashar party; Naftali Bennett, who leads the Together alliance, cofounded by Lapid; Avigdor Lieberman, who heads Yisrael Beiteinu; and Yair Golan, who leads the Democrats. The declaration does not set out an official leader although Eisenkot is viewed as the opposition’s most likely candidate for prime minister. In a joint statement, the figures said defeating the current government was their “shared highest objective”.
Of the four opposition parties, Yashar is projected to be the strongest. A recent poll by Israel’s Channel 12 suggested Yashar would win 23 seats in parliament, the most of any party and more than the 21 seats projected for Netanyahu’s Likud.
Trailing is the Together alliance, projected to win 13 seats, followed by Yisrael Beiteinu and the Democrats, each projected to win nine.
That would give the opposition a combined 54 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, seven short of a majority. Netanyahu’s alliance, which includes several ultra-Orthodox and far-right parties, is projected to win 49 seats.
Arab-led parties, representing the Palestinian citizens of Israel, who make up about 20 percent of the population, are projected to win 13 seats, but most leaders of the Jewish-led opposition bloc have ruled out joining forces with them.
Roi Zur, an assistant professor at the University of Essex who leads a research project on Israeli parties’ political ideology and policy, said the anti-Netanyahu coalition has a chance to win if turnout is on its side, noting that several parties that do not “strictly oppose” the prime minister could fall below the 3.25 percent threshold to enter the Knesset, shaking up the balance.
“If these parties waste enough right-wing votes, the opposition might translate their support into power,” Zur told Al Jazeera. “But this might not be enough.”
Even if the opposition alliance manages to find a way to oust Netanyahu, it would likely be weak and incapable – or unwilling – to overhaul Israeli policy in the West Bank and Gaza, analysts said.
“An anti-Netanyahu government will most likely be a very disparate coalition with a very thin majority, if any, in the Knesset. That would make it difficult for such a government to agree on any substantial perceived concessions, such as withdrawing completely from Gaza,” Anders Persson, a political scientist specialising in the Israel-Palestine conflict, told Al Jazeera.
“It would also make it difficult for the international community to meaningfully pressure such a government because there will always be a fear that an anti-Netanyahu government could quickly collapse.”
‘Mostly right-wing’
While their positions vary, most leaders of the anti-Netanyahu alliance have taken hardline positions on Gaza and the West Bank that give Palestinians little reason for optimism.
Yashar’s Eisenkot, a former Israeli military chief, has called the idea of a Palestinian state “delusional”, and he supports “strengthening” Israeli settlements. However, he opposes full Israeli annexation of the West Bank and has said he would dismantle smaller Israeli outposts not approved by the Israeli government. He also opposes the current government’s E1 settlement plan, which in effect would cut the West Bank in two. On Gaza, Eisenkot supports pursuing a United States-backed peace plan but only from a place of “strength” and only after “Hamas’s total disarmament”.
Israeli attacks across Gaza since the start of a “ceasefire” in October last year have killed nearly 1,500 Palestinians, bringing the overall death toll since the start of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023 to more than 74,000, according to the enclave’s health officials.
Bennett, a former Likud member who served in multiple Netanyahu-led governments, has described himself as “more right-wing” than Netanyahu and advocated exceptionally draconian policies in Gaza, including once calling for a “shoot-to-kill” policy against Palestinians trying to cross into Israel. Bennett staunchly opposes a Palestinian state and supports settlement expansion although he has criticised Israeli settler pogroms against Palestinians. With respect to the future of Gaza, he wants Israeli forces to stay in the enclave until Hamas is disarmed and proposes that Egypt, rather than Turkiye or Qatar, should play a future security role.
Lieberman’s Yisrael Beytenu party also supports settlement expansion, including the E1 plan. He backs annexing all of Area C of the West Bank – which constitutes 60 percent of the territory and is already under full Israeli control – while transferring control of other parts of the territory to Jordan. On Gaza, his party wants Israel to retain “freedom of action”, cut off water and electricity and eventually transfer governance to “an agreed-upon international entity”.
Golan’s Democrats party is the only one to support a form of two-state solution although it frames it as “responsible separation” that includes the “full demilitarisation” of the Palestinian state and complete Israeli security control of the Jordan Valley and other key areas. His party also supports complete demilitarisation for Gaza and a reconstruction process that involves regional states.
Palestinian lawyer and analyst Diana Buttu said each of the opposition leaders “has supported Israel’s genocide in Gaza” while backing settlements or not believing in full “equality for Palestinians”.
This orientation reflects hardening views within Israeli society itself.
According to a September Pew Research Center poll, only 17 percent of Israeli respondents said peaceful coexistence alongside an independent Palestinian state is possible. And according to an August survey by the Jewish People Policy Institute, 38 percent of Jewish Israeli participants favoured annexing the entire West Bank and more than half supported retaining the settlements as part of any future agreement on a Palestinian state.
‘Lessen the harms’
Nevertheless, some analysts said a new government could roll back or slow down some of the most “controversial and radical steps” of Israel’s current government, which includes far-right settlement proponents Itamar Ben-Gvir, the minister of national security, and Bezalel Smotrich, the minister of finance. Smotrich last month said Israel should “go to war” in the West Bank and repeat what it “did in Gaza”.
Changes enacted by a new government would likely include suspending the E1 settlement project and cracking down “on extremist settler violence/terrorism in the West Bank”, said Dov Waxman, a professor of political science at the University of California, Los Angeles, who specialises in Israeli politics and the Israel-Palestine conflict.
A new government would also be expected to “allow more humanitarian aid to enter Gaza in a more predictable, consistent manner and for reconstruction to finally begin there”, he added.
Ehab Jabareen, a Palestinian political analyst and researcher in Israel, told Al Jazeera that a new government led by Netanyahu’s opponents would likely be “more receptive to US and international pressure”, giving more space for potential reconstruction in Gaza.
But overall, Jabareen said, such a government is unlikely to alter Israel’s overarching “paradigm” towards Palestinians. “I would expect the difference to be less about whether Israel maintains control over the Palestinians and more about how the control is exercised, legitimised and managed,” he said.
Amjad Iraqi, senior analyst for Israel and Palestine at the International Crisis Group, said any “shades of difference” would be meaningful for Palestinians who are currently “suffering nearly uninhibited brutality”.
“We’re at a point of mitigation,” Iraqi told Al Jazeera. “It is about trying to lessen the harms. Palestinians are not in a position to expect any kind of radical shift, but every life saved, every piece of land saved matters a lot for people on the ground.”

aljazeera.com.title: India protest live: Opposition to march to Supreme Court over ‘vote theft’
aljazeera.com.text:
India’s main opposition party, the Indian National Congress, has announced a march to the Supreme Court to meet Chief Justice Surya Kant and submit a memorandum demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged vote fraud.
Kant, however, has refused to meet the opposition leaders, saying cases related to a revision of electoral rolls that removed 130 million people from voter lists are already pending before the top court.

aljazeera.com.title: Countries warn against travel to Saudi Arabia following Houthi attacks
aljazeera.com.text:
Several countries have warned their citizens against travel to Saudi Arabia following a series of Houthi attacks on airports in the kingdom.
On Monday, Australia and New Zealand became the latest to issue advisories against travelling to the kingdom, following similar warnings from the United States, Canada, the UK, South Korea, and Japan.
Australia’s Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade said Australians should avoid King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and “reconsider” travel to other Saudi airports.
New Zealand’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade urged citizens not to travel to the Saudi capital’s main gateway and the provinces of Najran, Jazan and Asir for any reason, and to avoid “non-essential” travel to Saudi Arabia as a whole.
The US embassy in Riyadh on Sunday advised US citizens to reconsider travel to the kingdom, citing the threat of attacks by Iran and the Iranian-backed Houthis.
Global Affairs Canada issued an advisory against non-essential travel to any part of Saudi Arabia.
South Korea’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs recommended that its citizens in Saudi Arabia leave unless they are on essential business and advised anyone planning to travel to the kingdom to cancel their trip.
The UK’s Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office urged citizens to avoid travel to Jeddah and Dammam, and to all airports apart from Medina International Airport, except for essential reasons.
The warnings come as Saudi Arabia reels from five attacks on its airports in less than a week.
One person was killed and 11 others were injured on Sunday when a projectile struck King Khalid International Airport, according to Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA).
A Houthi strike on the same airport on Saturday killed 13 people and injured more than 300 others, marking the deadliest attack on Saudi Arabia in more than a decade.
The Houthis claimed responsibility for all four strikes on Saudi airports before Sunday’s attack, which has yet to be claimed by any group.
King Khalid international airport and King Fahd international airport in Dammam remain closed following the attacks, causing significant disruption to aviation across the Middle East.
The attacks have also disrupted flights to and from King Abdulaziz International Airport in Jeddah.
More than 150 flights were cancelled and 374 flights were delayed at the Jeddah airport on Sunday, according to the flight tracking website Flightradar24.
Brendan Sobie, an independent analyst and consultant in Singapore, said it was too early to predict the ramifications of the attacks for aviation across the region and beyond.
“As has been the case with the Iran war and the impact from that crisis on the UAE, Kuwait and Bahrain, the impact of this latest crisis really depends on how long it lasts, how long Riyadh airport remains closed, and how long and to what extent are the restrictions once it reopens,” Sobie told Al Jazeera.

aljazeera.com.title: Clashes reported in Yemen as Houthis advance towards Taiz
aljazeera.com.text:
Clashes reported in Yemen as Houthis advance towards Taiz
Heavy clashes have been reported between Houthi fighters and Yemeni- forces near the strategic southern city of Taiz, Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry reports from Sanaa on what losing the city could mean for Yemen’s internationally recognised government.

aljazeera.com.title: China sanctions Paraguay, Belize ministers over Taiwan ties
aljazeera.com.text:
China has sanctioned Paraguay’s communications minister and Belize’s foreign minister over ties to Taiwan.
The Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs made the announcement on Monday, citing the safeguarding of China’s national sovereignty and opposition to Taiwan separatist activities as the reasons behind the measures, which went into effect the same day.
The measures against Paraguay’s Communications Minister Gustavo Villate and Belize’s Foreign Minister Francis Fonseca include the freezing of their assets in China and the denial of entry visas to Hong Kong and Macau.
The sanctions also prohibit Chinese organisations and individuals from engaging in transactions, cooperation or other activities with the ministers.
The Foreign Ministry said that “certain anti-China politicians” who are “driven by self-interest” have pushed their nations to maintain diplomatic relations with Taiwan.
Beijing said the ministers had “taken a series of egregious actions and statements”, which are “damaging China’s core interests”.
Paraguay and Belize are two of 12 countries that maintain formal diplomatic relations with Taiwan.
China views Taiwan as its territory, a view the island’s government strongly rejects.
The measures come two days after Taiwan’s National Day celebration.
In a National Day speech outside the Presidential Office on Saturday, Taiwan President William Lai Ching-te said the island “cherishes peace” and will “not give up our freedom”.
China’s Taiwan Affairs Office condemned Lai’s speech, saying it “disregards facts, distorts the truth, misleads the public, and reveals ulterior motives”.
In January, Chinese President Xi Jinping pledged to achieve the “reunification” of China and Taiwan, calling the goal “unstoppable”.
Diplomatic relations
Paraguay’s Communications Minister Villate marked Taiwan’s National Day with a social media post, saying: “Paraguay reaffirms its relationship of friendship and cooperation, based on shared values and principles: the self-determination of peoples, human rights and democracy.”
The Belize embassy in Taiwan also posted a message on its Facebook celebrating the 37th anniversary of their diplomatic relations.
“Together, we look forward to a future of growth, opportunity, and lasting friendship,” the embassy wrote.
Last month, Taiwan’s Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung visited Belize. His ministry said the two sides had agreed to deepen ties.
Taiwan’s other allies in the Americas include Guatemala and Haiti. It also has formal diplomatic ties with three Caribbean islands.
The United States does not have formal diplomatic ties with Taiwan, but Washington is bound by law to provide the island with the means to defend itself.
Earlier this month, the US delivered two fighter jets to Taiwan as the island seeks to build its defence capabilities to deter a feared attack from China.

aljazeera.com.title: Netanyahu demands probe into sources for award-winning Gaza film NAZA
aljazeera.com.text:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has called for an investigation into the anonymous sources featured in a documentary alleging that Israel’s military killed civilians in Gaza using AI-powered targeting systems.
The award-winning film, NAZA, draws on testimony from 24 unnamed Israeli military whistleblowers accusing the army of using the systems to kill numerous civilians in the besieged territory.
“I demand that the chief of general staff, the head of the Shin Bet, and the attorney general launch a comprehensive investigation into the participants in the film ‘Naza’ and prosecute them for serious information security violations, criminal libel, and harm to Israel’s diplomatic and security interests,” Netanyahu said on X on Saturday evening.
“The film presents a false, misleading, and biased narrative that defames the State of Israel and the [Israeli military] internationally, severely damaging Israel’s standing,” he added.
In a statement last month, the Israeli military said it “categorically” rejected the whistleblowers’ allegations, calling some of their assertions “absurd’ and contradictory.
It insisted that the selection and approval of strikes “are made by human personnel only”, in line with the military’s guidelines.
Israeli army Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir has called for legal action against the participants to be considered and ordered an investigation into suspected leaks of classified military information used in the film’s production.
NAZA takes its name from the Israeli military term for civilian casualties expected in air strikes, an abbreviated form of the Hebrew phrase for “collateral damage”.
The film was awarded a special jury prize at the Venice International Film Festival and received a historic 25-minute standing ovation.
It has also triggered a political storm in Israel.
The film’s directors, Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, have been accused of “treason”. Netanyahu and Culture Minister Miki Zohar have threatened to revoke their Israeli citizenship.
Last week, the head of Israel’s National Public Diplomacy Directorate, Tzipi Hotovely, awarded the creators of another film, NAZA: The Real Story, certificates of recognition for countering the “blood libels” made in the original NAZA film.
According to a statement from the Prime Minister’s Office, NAZA: The Real Story features testimony from soldiers refuting the original claims.
In contrast, 43 Israeli rights groups defended the filmmakers of NAZA and denounced the threats being directed at them, according to Israel’s Channel 12 news.
Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began on October 7, 2023, after Hamas’s armed wing, the Qassam Brigades, and other Palestinian groups attacked southern Israel, killing 1,139 people and taking about 240 captive.
Since then, Israel has killed at least 74,000 Palestinians, including at least 21,000 children, according to Gaza’s Ministry of Health.

aljazeera.com.title: Ethiopian troops enter Adigrat in Tigray, near the Eritrean border
aljazeera.com.text:
Ethiopian troops enter Adigrat in Tigray, near the Eritrean border
Ethiopian government forces entered Adigrat in northern Tigray after rebel fighters withdrew, heightening tensions with neighbouring Eritrea. The two neighbours cut off diplomatic ties last week. Al Jazeera’s Hamza Mohamed reports.

aljazeera.com.title: North Korea fires multiple ballistic missiles towards the sea
aljazeera.com.text:
North Korea has fired multiple ballistic missiles towards the sea off its east coast, South Korea’s military says.
South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) said one of the missiles launched from the Pyongyang area flew more than 900km (559 miles) on Monday. The joint chiefs did not specify how many missiles were detected.
Japan’s Deputy Defence Minister Takashi Koyari said at least two missiles were launched 17 minutes apart and landed in waters outside of its exclusive economic zone.
Koyari said the first missile flew about 220 kilometres (137 miles) and the second more than 910 kilometres (565 miles), following an “irregular” flight path and suggested it may have been a hypersonic weapon.
South Korea’s presidential office said that Pyongyang’s repeated missile launches violate United Nations Security Council resolutions, urging an immediate stop.
Monday’s launches add to heightened tensions on the Korean Peninsula, as both countries have been conducting weapons tests.
Escalating tensions
JCS spokesperson Jang Do-young said the latest missile launch appears to be a show of force, days after South Korea tested its own hypersonic weapon.
On Thursday, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung oversaw the country’s first test-firing of a hypersonic missile, a rare public showcasing of a missile test by a South Korean president.
Lee’s office said the hypersonic weapon, once fully developed, would enhance South Korea’s ability to strike key targets by surprise in the “Korean Peninsula theatre of operations”.
On October 3, North Korea also tested a hypersonic intermediate-range missile designed to evade missile defences in South Korea and Japan.
Last week, Seoul demanded an apology after a landmine blast wounded three soldiers in the Demilitarized Zone between South and North Korea. A joint South Korean-UN investigation concluded that two landmines were planted by North Korean forces about a year ago. Pyongyang dismissed the claim and accused South Korea of provocation.
Prior to the border mine blast, Seoul said it was conducting “preliminary coordination efforts” to facilitate dialogue between Pyongyang and Washington.
Lee pledged to reopen dialogue with North Korea in his first speech after taking office in 2025.
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un continues to flaunt his nuclear weapons programme, while rejecting US and South Korean offers to resume stalled diplomacy.
Talks between Kim and United States President Donald Trump abruptly ended in 2019. Kim Jong Un’s government continues to demand that Washington abandon its “hostile” policy towards Pyongyang and drop demands for North Korea’s denuclearisation as a condition for talks.

aljazeera.com.title: At least 139 dead as migrant boat from Djibouti to Yemen capsizes
aljazeera.com.text:
At least 139 dead as migrant boat from Djibouti to Yemen capsizes
At least 139 migrants, including 15 children, have died and 84 remain missing after a boat carrying more than 300 people capsized off Djibouti en route to Yemen. The disaster highlights the dangers of the Eastern Route, where more than 900 people died or went missing in 2025.

aljazeera.com.title: Saudi Arabia says 1 dead, 11 injured in latest attack on Riyadh airport
aljazeera.com.text:
A projectile has struck Saudi Arabia’s King Khalid International airport, killing one person and injuring 11, according to the country’s civil aviation authority.
The General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) identified the deceased in Sunday’s attack as a Pakistani resident and said the injured were transferred to several hospitals for medical care.
The strike on terminals 3 and 4, which serve domestic flights, occurred a day after a Houthi missile hit the airport, killing 12 people and wounding more than 300, according to the Saudi-led coalition fighting Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen.
India’s embassy in Saudi Arabia said one of its citizens died on Sunday due to injuries sustained in Saturday’s attack, bringing the death toll to 13.
Following Sunday’s attack, GACA said damage assessments and safety inspections of the airport were under way.
A witness on board a taxiing aircraft at the airport told the Reuters news agency that a projectile struck the tarmac next to several parked planes at about 8:30pm (17:30 GMT) on Sunday, causing a fire.
The witness said the aircraft returned to the gate, where the passengers disembarked and were told to leave.
The Riyadh airport has been struck four times in the past five days. Houthi attacks on King Khalid airport on Thursday killed at least three Saudi citizens, including a pilot, according to GACA.
The airport has been closed since Saturday’s attack, which was the deadliest in the country since the US-Israel war on Iran began in late February.
The Houthis claimed responsibility for the strikes before Sunday’s.
The airport attacks have escalated the war in Yemen and threaten to draw in the US military. US President Donald Trump says he is weighing whether to join the fight against the Houthis.
The escalation puts further pressure on global oil supplies and prices, as well as on commercial shipping through the Bab al-Mandeb strait off the Yemeni coast, a crucial alternative waterway to the Strait of Hormuz.
Trump had said he intends to speak with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who is seeking help against the Houthis, but there were no signs on Sunday that the US president had followed up on his claim.
There are fears that US intervention could prompt the Houthis to halt shipping through Bab al-Mandeb, further restricting the flow of oil out of the Gulf.
The rebels seized key areas along the strait last month. The Saudi-led coalition, backing forces loyal to Yemen’s internationally recognised government, has been trying to seize them back.

aljazeera.com.title: Bridge washed away by torrent of water in Nepal
aljazeera.com.text:
Bridge washed away by torrent of water in Nepal
Flash floods along Nepal’s Budhi Gandaki River swept away homes and bridges, forcing residents to flee to higher ground. Five people are missing, and six have been rescued, authorities said.
Published On 12 Oct 2026

aljazeera.com.title: UK PM Andy Burnham says it is ‘clear’ Russia interfered in 2016 Brexit vote
aljazeera.com.text:
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said it is “clear” that Russia interfered in the country’s 2016 Brexit vote, warning French and German voters of the same threat.
“I asked the question coming to Downing Street: Was there interference in the 2016 referendum from Russia? And I’ve had the clear answer that yes, there was,” Burnham said in an interview with The Rest Is Politics podcast released on Sunday.
Burnham’s comments mark the first time a UK prime minister has publicly acknowledged that Russia interfered in the UK’s vote to leave the European Union. Burnham did not provide evidence for or details on the claim.
He said that “these things are important now to put clearly on the record, and, I believe, help voters in Germany and France understand that some of this politics is instigated via our enemies, namely Russia.”
Burnham said he spoke with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz about possible links between Russia and the far-right Alternative for Germany party when the two leaders met last week in Berlin.
In his address to the United Nations General Assembly in September, Burnham also condemned Russia’s attempt to interfere in the UK’s 2019 general election.
According to a 2020 report by Parliament’s Intelligence and Security Committee, the UK government had failed to ask for a deep assessment of Russia’s interference in the 2016 referendum. The report did confirm that Russia had meddled in the 2014 Scottish independence referendum, however.
Russia has repeatedly denied meddling in Western democracies or interfering in another country’s elections or referendums, casting the UK as being gripped by “anti-Russian hysteria”.
UK reconsiders Brexit
Last month, Burnham argued that the UK should reconsider options for a future relationship with the EU, including rejoining the bloc, reigniting the decisive debate more than a decade after the historic vote.
He said that the UK’s departure from the bloc had failed to fulfil Brexit supporters’ pledge of “taking back control”, and instead has made the UK weaker economically and on immigration.

aljazeera.com.title: Iran’s FM urges diplomacy in call with Saudi counterpart
aljazeera.com.text:
Saudi Arabian Minister of Foreign Affairs Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud has received a phone call from his Iranian counterpart, Abbas Araghchi, the Saudi state news agency reported.
The two ministers discussed the recent escalations in the region after the Houthis, backed by Iran, attacked Saudi airports.
In a post on Telegram on Sunday, Araghchi emphasised that insisting on a military approach while disregarding political solutions would further complicate the situation. The Iranian minister said the region’s crises have no military solutions. Last week, Araghchi said “there is no military solution” to the US war, adding, “only negotiations based on justice and fairness” could end the conflict.
Araghchi said Iran is ready to provide any assistance necessary to facilitate the start of dialogue between Saudi Arabia and Yemen and to help achieve a political solution.
Following the deadly attack on the Riyadh airport that killed 12 people and wounded 300, US President Donald Trump said he would reconsider the US role in Yemen, adding that he is weighing resuming strikes on Iran.
These remarks represent a departure from the president’s comments on Thursday that Washington will not resume strikes on Iran until after the US midterm elections.
Iranian and Saudi diplomatic ties have endured despite longstanding friction, with embassies restored under a 2023 Chinese-brokered agreement remaining operational. Before that breakthrough, a seven-year diplomatic rupture had fuelled regional proxy conflicts.
Riyadh’s relationship with Tehran has deteriorated since the start of the US-Israel war on Iran in late February. Following the attacks, Tehran and its aligned forces have struck US military assets and energy infrastructure across the Gulf region, including oil fields in Saudi Arabia.
In March 2026, Prince Faisal warned Iran that tolerance of its attacks on Saudi Arabia and those of neighbouring Gulf states is limited, calling on Tehran to “recalculate” its strategy.

aljazeera.com.title: Hurricane Isaias leaves trail of destruction across the US Gulf Coast
aljazeera.com.text:
In Pictures
Residents across the southeastern United States have begun cleanup efforts after Hurricane Isaias, the first Atlantic tropical cyclone of the 2026 season, slammed ashore near Destin, Florida, on Friday.
As of midafternoon Sunday, roughly 356,000 customers remain without power in southern Alabama and the northwestern region of Florida, according to data from PowerOutage.com, an independent tracking website.
At its peak, the storm knocked out power to nearly 800,000 homes and businesses across the Gulf Coast.
Sarah Gatewood, a spokesperson for the utility company Florida Power and Light (FPL), announced that workers from across Florida and more than two dozen other states had mobilised to restore power.
At least four deaths have been linked to Isais after it made landfall as a Category 2 storm on the five-tier Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale.
The tempest churned northward into Alabama on Saturday with fierce tropical-storm-force winds before weakening into a post-tropical cyclone and tracking further north towards the Appalachians.
Though its power is waning, the storm continues to endanger the mid-Atlantic region with the potential for flash flooding.
According to the National Weather Service (NWS), surface observations indicate that Isaias now has maximum sustained winds of 160 km/h (100 mph) and an estimated minimum central pressure of 28.88 inches, or 978 millibars.
Across Florida and Alabama, residents have reported damage from the storm’s high-velocity winds.
A Rest and Relax Inn in the resort city of Pensacola, Florida, saw its roof sheared off during the hurricane, and a boathouse was flattened in Destin.
The immediate struggle for basic necessities was most stark in Pensacola, the westernmost part of the Florida Panhandle, where the storm downed power grids and caused widespread structural damage.
Hundreds of cars lined the block around a United Cajun Navy distribution site, a volunteer disaster relief organisation, on Saturday morning.
Pensacola’s Mayor DC Reeves warned of critical drinking water shortages following the storm, which affected drinking wells and water infrastructure. Residents, he said, remain under an advisory to boil tap water before use.
“We are winding down day three of storm response and recovery operations, and we remain focused on public safety, clearing debris, and restoring critical infrastructure and services,” Reeves said on social media.
Isaias also forced the indefinite closure of Pensacola International airport, Florida’s 10th-largest airfield, due to severe damage.
Fallen trees and power lines continue to make travel hazardous in Houston County, Alabama, which remains under an emergency flash flood warning, according to state emergency officials.
“Due to the impacts of Hurricane Isaias, all Houston County roads are closed until further notice,” the agency posted on X.

aljazeera.com.title: Ceuta or Sebta? Why one city has two names and a disputed status
aljazeera.com.text:
Spain’s King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia are due to visit Ceuta on October 13 and Melilla the following day, in Felipe’s first visit to either city as king since he ascended the throne in 2014.
The trip comes after a major migration crisis at the Ceuta border in July and as the long-running dispute between Spain and Morocco over the two cities on the North African coast remains unresolved.
Spain considers Ceuta and Melilla part of its territory, while Morocco regards both cities and several smaller Spanish-held territories in North Africa as part of its own territory.
The city that sits on the southern side of the Strait of Gibraltar also has different names in Spanish and Arabic.
In Spain, it is Ceuta. In Arabic, it is Sabta, commonly written as Sebta in Latin script.
So why does the same city have two names? And how did a city on the North African coast come under Spanish sovereignty?
Where does the name Ceuta come from?
The name is much older than either modern Spain or Morocco.
The city was known as Sabta in Arabic. Spain’s Ministry of Culture identifies Sabta with present-day Ceuta and traces its history through successive periods of Idrisid, Umayyad, Taifa, Almoravid, Almohad and Marinid rule.
The Spanish form, Ceuta, developed from earlier forms of the name. Sabta and Ceuta are different linguistic forms of the same city.
Who controlled Ceuta before Spain?
Ceuta passed through several political and dynastic systems in the Maghreb and al-Andalus.
Under the Idrisid dynasty, the city was in the hands of the Banu Isam before being taken by the Umayyad Caliph Abd al-Rahman III in 931, bringing it into the political sphere of al-Andalus.
In the 11th century, Ceuta became linked to the Taifa of Malaga. It later came under the Almoravids and Almohads. From the beginning of the 14th century, it became part of the Marinid sphere with periods when other local dynasties held power.
By the early 15th century, Ceuta was under Muslim rule.
That changed in 1415.
How did Ceuta become Portuguese?
On August 21, 1415, Portuguese forces led by King John I captured Ceuta.
The Portuguese conquest brought an end to more than seven centuries of Muslim rule in Ceuta. Ceuta’s own cultural heritage authority dates Muslim rule from 709 to the Portuguese conquest in 1415.
Ceuta remained Portuguese for more than two centuries.
Portugal and Spain were then ruled by the same monarchy from 1580 to 1640. When Portugal restored its independence in 1640, Ceuta remained under the Spanish monarchy rather than returning to Portuguese rule.
The 1668 Treaty of Lisbon, which formally recognised Portuguese independence, left Ceuta in Spanish hands.
That is how Ceuta came under Spanish sovereignty.
Why does Morocco claim Ceuta?
Morocco’s argument is rooted in the city’s history and geography.
Ceuta lies on the North African coast, surrounded by Morocco on its landward side. Morocco has claimed Ceuta and Melilla since gaining independence in 1956 and regards the two cities as occupied Moroccan territories.
Spain takes the opposite position.
Under Spanish law, Ceuta is an autonomous city. Its Statute of Autonomy describes Ceuta as an integral part of the Spanish nation and gives the city its own system of self-government.
The dispute, therefore, is not about who administers Ceuta. Spain does. It is about sovereignty.
Morocco says Ceuta should form part of Moroccan territory. Spain says its sovereignty over the city is established and Ceuta is part of Spain.
Neither side has accepted the other’s position.
Why doesn’t history settle the dispute?
Because the two sides interpret that history differently.
Morocco points to Ceuta’s long history within Muslim political systems in the Maghreb and its location on the North African coast. Spain points to centuries of Portuguese and Spanish control and to Ceuta’s present constitutional status as part of Spain.
The historical record does not provide a simple answer to a modern sovereignty dispute. The political systems that ruled Ceuta before 1415 were not nation-states with today’s borders, and the city’s current status is based on centuries of subsequent Portuguese and Spanish rule.
Morocco’s territorial claim dates from the period after independence in 1956, but Spain has continued to exercise sovereignty over Ceuta.
Why does Morocco call it Sebta?
Sebta, or Sabta, is the Arabic name for Ceuta and predates the modern sovereignty dispute.
In Morocco, Sebta is the Arabic name used for the city while Ceuta is the established Spanish form.
The choice of name can have political resonance because Morocco disputes Spanish sovereignty over the city. But using Sebta is not automatically a political statement. It is also simply the Arabic name.
What about Melilla?
Melilla’s history is different from Ceuta’s.
Spanish forces took control of Melilla in 1497 when it was incorporated into the Crown of Castile.
Ceuta, by contrast, was first Portuguese before remaining under the Spanish monarchy after Portugal regained its independence.
Today, both cities are Spanish autonomous cities, and Morocco claims sovereignty over both.
Why does Ceuta still matter?
Ceuta’s importance today goes beyond its size.
Ceuta is considered part of Spain, but it is not included in the European Union customs territory. Its border with Morocco is also an external border of the Schengen area.
That has made Ceuta a focal point for migration and border policy as well as a recurring issue in relations between Madrid and Rabat.
The issue returned sharply to the headlines on July 30 when more than 72,000 migrants entered Ceuta from Morocco, according to the Reuters news agency.
Now Felipe’s planned visits to Ceuta and Melilla are putting the two disputed cities back in the spotlight.

aljazeera.com.title: Iran war live: Riyadh airport hit again; Tehran says US reply ‘inadequate’
aljazeera.com.text:
Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, says the US has accepted some of Tehran’s seven conditions for a deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, but described the response as “inadequate”.
One person has been killed and 11 others wounded in a new attack on Saudi Arabia’s King Khalid International airport, hours after Houthi-affiliated media reported an air strike on the rebel-held airport in Yemen’s capital, Sanaa.

aljazeera.com.title: Pakistani national killed in second Houthi strike on Riyadh airport
aljazeera.com.text:
Pakistani national killed in second Houthi strike on Riyadh airport
Saudi authorities say a Pakistani national was killed and several people injured in a second strike on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport. Sunday’s strike followed an attack on Saturday that killed 12 people and injured more than 300. Al Jazeera’s Malik Traina reports.

aljazeera.com.title: US Homeland Security secretary sees no ‘risk’ from livestreamed execution
aljazeera.com.text:
United States Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has defended the planned livestreaming of Nidal Hasan’s execution, playing down warnings that images of his death by firing squad might be used as a propaganda tool for violent groups.
In an interview on Sunday with the CBS News show Face the Nation, Mullin framed the decision as part of President Donald Trump’s hardline approach to crime.
“I follow President Trump. He’s a commander-in chief of the country,” Mullin said, crediting the Republican leader with “restoring America values”.
Mullin also brushed aside concerns that the images of Hasan’s execution could be leveraged against the US.
“I don’t see an elevated risk at this point at all because of this,” Mullin said. “I think people need to understand, if you attack America, we will come after you, and we will make sure that the punishment fits the crime.”
Hasan, a former US Army major, was sentenced to death in August 2013 after being convicted of shooting and killing 12 unarmed active-duty soldiers and a retired serviceman at the Fort Hood military base in Texas.
The attack took place on November 5, 2009, when Hasan opened fire in a medical facility on the base where service members receive routine check-ups before deployment. The incident is considered one of the deadliest mass shootings to take place on a US military base.
Another 32 people were injured in the shooting. In the process of responding to the attack, police on the military base shot Hasan, leaving him paralysed from the waist down.
Critics have questioned the optics of broadcasting a firing squad killing of a man in a wheelchair. The livestreamed execution is scheduled for December 3.
But Mullin dismissed those concerns, arguing that viewership is optional. “Once again, no one has to watch it if they don’t choose to,” Mullin said.
Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth had announced plans last week to livestream the upcoming execution, triggering a wave of criticism. But Trump on Saturday suggested he may reconsider the decision.
“There are two thoughts: Don’t show it and show it. Because, you know, by showing it, maybe other people won’t be doing what he did,” Trump told reporters outside the White House.
“So I’ll make a decision, ultimately. I know what the military would like to do, but we’ll make a decision.”
Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle, however, have denounced the idea of a public execution.
In a Sunday morning appearance on NBC’s Meet the Press, Republican Senator Thom Tillis warned that broadcasting Hasan’s death would “put at risk” US lives.
“Terrorist organisations will use this as a recruiting tool. It will radicalise other people, and this is not who we are,” Tillis said.
“Look, the Fort Hood shooter should be put to death, but there’s a way to deal with this that’s proper, and there’s a way to deal with this that’s more improper than I have ever observed in my life.”
Tillis, whose term as senator ends in January, also directed criticism at Hegseth for what he suggested was reckless leadership.
“It’s another example of why Pete Hegseth and all of his bravado needs to get the hell out of the Department of Defense, because he is a failed leader,” Tillis said.
The senator was considered one of the deciding votes in Hegseth’s January 2025 confirmation vote, and he has since called his support for Hegseth’s cabinet nomination “the biggest regret” of his tenure.
Other Republicans echoed Tillis’s concerns about the livestream. Senator Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, for instance, compared the public execution with something she would expect “from terrorists and dictators”.
She also argued that Hasan has sought public attention, something he would receive in a broadcast execution.
“It would give this individual, who deserves no further notoriety, the martyrdom he seeks,” Murkowski added.
Republican Representative Tom Barrett of Michigan, a former military member, issued a statement on Friday explaining that he had trained at Fort Hood a year before the attack.
He also said he opposed the public execution, despite considering Hasan “evil”.
“Secretary Hegseth should seriously reconsider this decision,” Barrett wrote on X.
“Making a public spectacle out of an already tragic situation is unnecessary and does not serve a public interest.”
Military executions are extremely rare in the US and can only be approved by the president under the Uniform Code of Military Justice.
If the order against Hasan is carried out, he will be the first member of the US military to be executed since 1961.

aljazeera.com.title: Footage shows moment Russian strike hits Ukrainian grocery store
aljazeera.com.text:
Footage shows moment Russian strike hits Ukrainian grocery store
CCTV footage shows the moment of a Russian strike on a residential street in Kharkiv, Ukraine, followed by fires and debris. The attack hit a grocery store, killing three people and injuring 20, including two children, officials said.

aljazeera.com.title: CCTV shows moment of deadly Houthi strike on Riyadh airport
aljazeera.com.text:
CCTV shows moment of deadly Houthi strike on Riyadh airport
CCTV footage released by Al Arabiya shows the moment of a Houthi strike on Riyadh’s international airport on Saturday. The attack killed at least 12 people and injured more than 300. A warning this video contains distressing images.

aljazeera.com.title: At least 72 Sudanese miners killed in air strike: Rights monitor
aljazeera.com.text:
An air raid at a gold mine near the disputed Sudan-Egypt border has killed at least 72 workers, according to a Sudanese rights group, after survivors described scenes of chaos in the mountainous region.
Emergency Lawyers, which documents atrocities in Sudan’s war, accused the Egyptian military of carrying out the attack.
“Egyptian fighter jets targeted civilian miners in the northern Wadi area inside Sudanese territory, resulting, according to preliminary information, in the killing of 72 civilians,” the Khartoum-based rights organisation wrote on X on Sunday.
The reported attack on Saturday cannot be independently verified, and Egypt has issued no official comment.
It was this year’s second attack on the mountainous border region of Jabal al-Uqaydat, a gold mining area. Similar strikes, also reportedly carried out by Egypt, killed 23 workers at the gold mining site in June.
The Egyptian military said at the time that it had conducted a “large-scale operation” against illegal gold mining within its borders.
The border between Sudan and Egypt is disputed, with both countries claiming the resource-rich Halaib Triangle.
Images shared on social media and by local rights groups, which could not be verified, showed dozens of bodies strewn in rubble and others wrapped in funeral shrouds. Miners described an air strike on the area.
Gold rush
Since April 2023, the war in Sudan between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) has killed more than 200,000 people and created a humanitarian crisis that has pushed many into the dangerous gold mining industry, which fuels both sides’ war efforts.
The rugged mountainous area, home to bountiful mineral deposits, stretches for hundreds of kilometres and includes the disputed Halaib Triangle.
Emergency Lawyers said the attack occurred within Sudanese territory.
“The repeated attacks on the gold and mineral-rich border regions reflect a desire by Egyptian authorities to expand and assert control over Sudan’s natural resources,” it said.
The Egyptian army said in June that it carried out its operation “within Egyptian territory”.
It said 223 people were detained, including 136 foreign nationals, and announced a campaign to counter “illegal gold mining and arms smuggling” in the area.
Despite backing Sudan’s army chief, Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, Egypt considers the war at its border – which stretches 1,200km (745 miles) from the Red Sea to Libya – a significant threat to its security.
East of the Nile River, the porous border has for years been a thriving conduit for gold, illicit trade and human trafficking, which Egypt has tried to stem, including by using mass deportations.

aljazeera.com.title: Waves crash into homes as excavators try to protect California properties
aljazeera.com.text:
Waves crash into homes as excavators try to protect California properties
Waves crash into homes as excavators try to protect California properties Construction crews were seen trying to block waves entering homes along California’s coast, after Tropical Storm Rachel brought flooding and power outages to the region.

aljazeera.com.title: UK Greens leader seeks rule change after party declares Zionism is racism
aljazeera.com.text:
Zack Polanski, the leader of the United Kingdom’s Green Party, has proposed a potential overhaul of his party’s democratic mechanisms, calling for the leader to have larger control over strategic direction.
The appeal came in an article published in The Guardian on Sunday after party members passed a motion declaring that Zionism is racism at their annual conference on October 4 in a divisive vote.
Polanski also failed to grab a parliamentary seat in the wake of the row with Israel in a by-election.
The Labour Party won the election for the parliamentary seat vacated by former leader Keir Starmer in Holborn and St Pancras on Friday, fending off a strong challenge from the left-wing Green Party in a boost for British Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
“Our party democracy must now evolve to meet that – creating wider engagement for members, giving leaders more responsibility to set the party’s strategic direction, and making our processes as robust and accessible as possible,” he wrote.
“Above all, that unity must be deployed in the service of changing this country for the better,” the Green Party leader added.
Criticism over vote on motion
Polanski also replied to the criticisms of him for not participating in the vote on the motion on Zionism.
“I have been asked why I was not present for the vote. The answer is that my priority was fighting a hugely consequential by-election for our party,” he said, adding that he put all his “energy into the race in Holborn and St Pancras”.
He admitted that some members feel “let down” by his decision not to make an appearance there.
The Green Party’s motion, which called for “Palestinian liberation, the right of return, Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS), and a full arms embargo against Israel” was criticised by Jewish groups, other parties and most Green Party MPs.
After conceding defeat in the fiercely contested by-election, Polanski answered his critics, saying he would stay on as leader.
He was barred from entering Israel after his party backed a motion to define Zionism as racism.

npr.org.title: Trump says Russia and Ukraine agree to an 'energy ceasefire'
npr.org.text:
Trump says Russia and Ukraine agree to an 'energy ceasefire'
WASHINGTON — U.S. President Donald Trump said Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an "energy ceasefire" in the 4 1/2-year-old war, but he offered no details on it and Kyiv reported attacks by Moscow on energy sites after his statement.
Trump's brief social media post said only that the ceasefire took effect immediately, adding: "Do not break it!"
Moscow did not immediately comment. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that while his country "welcomed" the announcement by Trump as "good news for everyone," Russia was still hitting energy infrastructure in Kyiv and in the city of Kharkiv.
"Unfortunately, Ukrainian skies have been infested with Russian 'shaheds' all day today," he said in an evening address, referring to drones launched by Moscow . "There have been glide bomb strikes and strikes on our energy infrastructure too. A power plant in Kharkiv was attacked this evening."
The presidential office confirmed the Kharkiv attack came after Trump's ceasefire post.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine was "ready to refrain from striking Russian energy infrastructure — and we count on the same readiness from Russia."
Russia has sought to deny Ukrainian civilians power, heat and running water during the war, hoping to wear down public resistance to Moscow's full-scale invasion. Ukrainian officials describe the strategy as "weaponizing winter."
Zelenskyy said Ukraine has proposed many de-escalatory steps but Russian President Vladimir Putin "had one answer to all of them — 'nyet.' We do hope that he will finally say something different to America, Ukraine, and the entire world."
He said Kyiv is maintaining contact with the U.S., and he thanked Americans for their support. He said on X that he had spoken about the development with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte.
In an interview broadcast earlier Sunday, Zelenskyy said Kyiv was ready to stop striking Russian refineries if Moscow halted attacks on Ukraine's energy system, and he asked Trump to press the Kremlin to agree.
"We are asking President Trump, (to) give them (a) signal, not (to) attack energy infrastructure of Ukraine," he told ABC's "This Week ."
On Sept. 14, Trump claimed on social media that both countries had agreed "not to hit" each other's energy infrastructure but offered no details on that proposal either. While Zelenskyy had said Ukraine was ready to comply if Russia did, nothing came of the proposal.
Trump spars with Zelenskyy
Trump said Saturday it was time for Ukraine to get a new president, suggesting Zelenskyy has not done enough to end the war and blaming him for high diesel prices in the U.S.
Zelenskyy said in response to Trump's comments that Ukraine could hold elections if Russia agreed to a 60-day ceasefire.
"Give us two months, 60 days off. Total ceasefire, 60 days, and we will organize elections," he said, adding that Ukraine would be ready to accept whatever choice its people made.
"With all respect to President Trump, it's up to our society, up to our people to choose one or another leader," he said. Holding an election during the war would be unlawful and that Ukraine would need security guarantees to allow for safe voting, Zelenskyy added.
Ukraine has been under martial law since Putin launched the full-scale invasion in February 2022, and the Ukrainian Constitution bars elections while it remains in force.
