Staff, often known by kinship titles like “uncle”, regularly crossed conversational boundaries, Hughes said.
“Often, personal things were discussed in very public matters,” she said.
“The nature of boundaries is really something which is not particularly, I believe, understood by staff at Redeemer in the way we understand it in most school contexts.”
The school also had an emphasis on surveillance and “dobbing”, public humiliations and punishment, she said.
A boy and girl were made to stand on chairs in front of a year 7 class after teachers intercepted a love note, Hughes said of her time at the school.
Noel Cannon read the note to a collection of students before they were “dressed-down in front of four year groups and many teachers”, she said.
The parliamentary committee is investigating the management of the Parramatta-based school and oversight from government bodies.
The Communities and Justice Department received 15 risks of significant harm notifications since 2004 but they had not triggered a field assessment, an earlier response to questions on notice revealed.
Cannon and other school representatives were invited to appear at the inquiry and state the school’s case.
Committee chair Abigail Boyd said she was disappointed an attempted summons to appear went begging.
AAP has contacted the school for comment on the students’ allegations.

theguardian.com.title: Doctor warned Elizabeth Struhs would not be safe at home years before religious sect killed her by withdrawing medicine
theguardian.com.text:
A medical specialist at the Queensland Children’s hospital warned that Elizabeth Struhs would not be safe at home with her mother years before her parents allowed her to die by withdrawing lifesaving medicine, a coronial inquest has heard.
Elizabeth, a type 1 diabetic, died at the age of eight from diabetic ketoacidosis on 7 January 2022, at her family home in Toowoomba, west of Brisbane, after her parents and other members of a religious sect withdrew the insulin she needed to survive and sat around singing and praying while she slowly died over the course of several days.
All 14 adult members of the sect, known as the Saints, were convicted of her manslaughter last year, including her father, Jason Struhs, mother, Kerrie Struhs, and brother, Zachary Struhs, and the leader of their sect, Brendan Stevens.
The group, which some have referred to as “a cult”, did not believe in medicine, and believed Elizabeth would be miraculously healed of her incurable illness and be resurrected after she died.
Elizabeth had been hospitalised in 2019 in a similar incident. Her mother, Kerrie, openly refused to provide her medical care and was charged and convicted with failing to provide her the necessaries of life as a result of the incident in 2021.
A coronial inquest, which sat for its first day on Monday, heard that doctors had attempted to warn the child safety department that Elizabeth could not be safely returned to Kerrie.
Coroner Ainslie Kirkegaard heard from an experienced medical specialist who helped care for Elizabeth after her admission to the Queensland children’s hospital’s intensive care unit on 17 July 2019. The doctor cannot be identified for legal reasons.
The doctor wrote a professional report about the child one day later raising concerns about her safety, the inquest heard.
The doctor said she was concerned partly due to Elizabeth’s condition at presentation, describing her as “extremely unwell” and requiring intubation and a ventilator.
But she was also concerned about the religious beliefs of Elizabeth’s mother, Kerrie, she said.
Kerrie refused to even attend the hospital to see her child, and denied that she was sick or would ever require medication in a phone conversation, the doctor told the court.
Kerrie also had no questions about her daughter’s condition, the doctor said.
Counsel assisting Simon Hamlyn-Harris read from the doctor’s nine-page report, which was sent to child safety and the police.
“‘Type 1 diabetes is a life-threatening condition that requires complicated care by the parents, the report reads,” he said.
“If her mother continues to deny the requirement for insulin and the related treatments Elizabeth could not be in Kerrie’s care’.
“With ‘not’ in bold,” Hamlyn-Harris added.
The doctor consulted the hospital’s child protection and forensic medical service before writing the report.
“My concerns were so strong that if [a nurse at the service] had said not to I was still planning to submit a report,” the doctor said.
Elizabeth was ultimately returned home to live with her family, with an intervention parental agreement: a short-term, voluntary, intensive arrangement which allows child safety authorities to aid a child in danger without a child protection order, the inquest heard.
The court heard this was done without the knowledge of the hospital team.
“There is still significant risk in that context,” the doctor said, on Monday.
“I would not be supportive of that treatment if I was the clinician involved in that discharge home plan.”
The doctor said she raised concerns at the time that diabetes required lifelong treatment, and that the risk posed by the illness can change over time, due to physical or social changes.
Elizabeth’s father, Jason, agreed to care for Elizabeth after her discharge from hospital, which he did for three years.
At the time, Jason was a longtime sceptic of his wife’s religion, and had saved Elizabeth’s life by taking her to hospital against the wishes of his wife in 2019 and then testified against her at a criminal trial.
Both Jason and Kerrie were found guilty in 2021 of failing to supply the necessaries of life for their daughter, relating to the incident in 2019 which was so serious Elizabeth was taken to hospital in a coma.
Jason was sentenced to six months in prison, wholly suspended for a period of 12 months, while Kerrie was sentenced to 18 months’ imprisonment with a specified parole release date of 15 December 2021.
But Kerrie helped convert Jason to her religious beliefs while serving her prison sentence. He was then convinced to give up treating Elizabeth’s diabetes with insulin, leading to her death.
The inquest continues.

theguardian.com.title: Mystery of 1950s wedding photo album found dumped in Wakefield solved
theguardian.com.text:
When Andrew Bedford discovered an old wedding album dumped outside his city centre cafe in Wakefield, West Yorkshire, he considered chucking it into a nearby wheelie bin.
But when he opened the album, the vintage photographs of the happy couple on their wedding day in 1957 seemed too precious to throw away.
Unable to work out the identity of the bride and groom – their handwritten names had become too faded to read – he rescued the album and brought it back to his cafe, Eva’s Kitchen, for safekeeping.
His partner, Éva Lemperger, put out a plea on social media to help identify the couple.
Now the mystery has been solved after a local family historian took up the case and tracked down the couple’s 65-year-old son, Michael Dawson.
He revealed the album had been stolen from a storage unit near the cafe, along with other cherished family heirlooms, after his parents died.
It contains some of his only surviving photographs of his mother and father, Maxwell Dawson and Barbara Parr, and he now plans to “protect it with [his] life”.
Bedford said: “I was just so happy he got it back. I thought, if it had been mine, and I’d lost pictures of my family – and they were only pictures I had of them – I’d have been elated if somebody had found them and given them back to me.”
When the case of the mysterious wedding album was picked up by his local newspaper, the Wakefield Express, it caught the attention of a local historian and amateur sleuth, Anne-Marie Fawcett. “I run a local history group on Facebook with over 15,000 members, and I’m really interested in local history, particularly family history,” she said.
“I love researching. I love uncovering stories and finding connections. And I like getting to the bottom of mysteries … When I saw that nobody knew who the album belonged to, I thought, that’s something to get my teeth into.”
A clue in the birth certificate of another guest helped her to identify the church the couple were married in: Wadsley Parish Church in Sheffield. She then used a photo enhancing tool to decipher the name of the bride. “But there was more than one Barbara Parr in the records, so I had to follow them all.”
When she came across an electoral roll entry suggesting Parr’s husband, Maxwell, had lived near Wakefield, she guessed she had found the right couple and appealed for information about the family on social media.
An old school friend of Michael Dawson’s remembered him and helped Fawcett to find a photograph of him, enabling her to track him down on Facebook.
“I sent him a message, and he rang me,” said Fawcett. “He was absolutely made up.”
Dawson told her the album had been stolen from the storage unit where he and his brother had stored the cherished contents of his parents’ home after they died. “Someone had broken in and taken all the family treasure. He said he’d lost everything. So you can imagine how I felt to be able to reunite him with this [album] … I’ve got goose pimples talking about it. Everybody loves a happy ending, don’t they?”
Dawson told the BBC: “I’m absolutely elated because I am sentimental and it’s important for me to have these photos.
“I will protect it with my life now, based on the fact that it’s all I’ve got.”
Asked how he felt about Fawcett’s detective efforts, he joked: “I think she probably knows more about me than I do, which is a worry.”
But he added: “I thought I’d lost everything. I can’t thank her enough.”

theguardian.com.title: UK van drivers face extra £2.5bn in diesel costs this year, figures show
theguardian.com.text:
Millions of British van drivers face a combined £2.5bn cost to cover the rising price of diesel this year, according to figures, fuelling calls for the government to scrap its planned fuel duty rise.
The owners of diesel vans and pickups can expect to collectively spend almost £8.5bn at the pump this year, according to analysis for the Guardian, after diesel prices climbed to record highs due to a global fuel shortage caused by disruption to refineries in the Middle East and Russia.
The estimated fuel costs, calculated by analysts at Moneysupermarket, is significantly above the £5.95bn spent last year, raising concerns that the price of food and goods transported by road could rise sharply as retailers pass on increased logistics costs.
The comparison site warned last week that the average fuel bill for a van driver could reach £1,965 this year, up from £1,294 for the average van in 2025 based on typical mileage and fuel consumption.
The number of vans on British roads has grown significantly in recent years fuelled by the boom in online shopping, home deliveries and the rising number of self-employed people working in trades.
Although the adoption of electric vans has begun to increase, about 95% of light commercial vehicles are still powered by diesel. The average pump price climbed to a above £2 a litre for the first time this month, up over 40% since late February, when the US-Israel war on Iran began disrupting supplies of crude and refined oil products from the Gulf, leading to cost increases across the economy.
The rising cost burden has led to calls for government help in the upcoming budget, including abandoning plans to raise fuel duty from next year. The planned increase – postponed from September – will add 3p a litre in duty from 1 January, and another 2p from 1 March, in “a hammer blow” for costs, according to the Road Haulage Association (RHA).
Richard Smith, the RHA’s managing director, said: “Many of our members run on margins of around 2%. Surging diesel prices are impacting firms across the country, with some spending many thousands extra every week on fuel.
“Adding [fuel duty rises] on top of today’s fuel prices would be a hammer blow for many firms that move goods and the households that buy them. A fuel duty hike is a food price hike.”
Data from the motoring group RAC showed that, despite a recent dip in the cost of diesel, the price remains about 57p a litre higher than before the US-Iran conflict while petrol remains 42p higher. This means households are paying £31 and £23 more respectively every time they fill up a family sized car, according to the group.
The fuel duty rise “will only make prices at the pump even more expensive,” according to Simon Williams, the head of policy at the RAC.
“As things stand, this year is still set to be the second most expensive year on record for drivers,” Williams said. “The government has the power to take some of the sting out of higher fuel costs, either by extending and increasing the fuel duty cut or reducing VAT as they’ve done with domestic electricity.”
Smith added that the RHA was calling on the chancellor to bring in a 15p a litre rebate for British van, coach and haulage operators after Spain, France and Italy offered similar help for commercial vehicle businesses. “It’s time we caught up,” he said.
On Friday, the US president, Donald Trump, attempted to ease pressure at the pump for US drivers by announcing a deal for Russian deal, in a move which infuriated the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
The government was contact for comment.

theguardian.com.title: Drivers forced to use parking apps can pay up to 40% more
theguardian.com.text:
Drivers are unwittingly paying up to 40% more to park as more councils switch to app-only payments and force customers to pick up the tab.
Many councils across England have removed pay and display machines and replaced them with app payments, including a number in London. Most local authorities encourage drivers to pay by app to beat queues, while apps are often the only way to pay when ticket machines are out of order. However, many car park signs fail to mention that app payments may incur an additional service fee.
Parking apps save councils money by removing the cost of installing and maintaining ticket machines, but while a few pay the app providers directly for their services, many leave drivers to foot some or all of the bill through “convenience fees” or “service fees”.
These typically range from 10p to 30p, but they are not included in the advertised parking tariffs in car parks, even when an app is the only payment option, and they are often not strongly flagged within the apps.
Of the parking apps tested by the Guardian, none clearly displayed the service fee until the payment stage, and even then, some required customers to click on an information symbol to find out why the price had increased.
These surcharges can push up the cost of an hour’s parking slot dramatically. In Harrogate, North Yorkshire, drivers who park in the town centre and pay by app are hit with a mandatory 30p service charge – a 38% rise on an 80p tariff.
Meanwhile, the price of two hours at the council’s Christleton Road car park in Chester soars by 40% when the 20p convenience fee is added to the 50p tariff.
Extra fees are added if drivers agree to receive booking confirmation and expiry alerts. They are typically between 10 and 30p per text.
According to the Advertising Standards Authority, quoted prices must include all mandatory fees for a contract to be valid. Drivers enter a contract with a council as soon as they accept the car park’s terms and conditions and park their vehicle.
However, few realise that they enter a separate contract with the app provider if they choose to pay online. App fees, therefore, may not legally have to be displayed on parking council signs.
Because service fees are agreed between local authorities and individual app providers, and since they can vary depending on location, drivers have no way of predicting what they will be charged.
The Guardian tested the apps by booking an hour’s parking at car parks around the country.
RingGo’s convenience fee added an extra 20p to the £2 tariff at Kings Yard in Lancaster. Drivers have to click on a small “see prices” link above the prominent “Next” button when they have chosen their location to see the charge. It is mentioned again on the payment page, but only when the “i” symbol beside the final price is clicked.
PayByPhone charged a 15p service fee on top of the £5.10 parking tariff at Dudley Street car park in Birmingham. The existence of the charge was not explained until the payment page and was hidden behind the Apple Pay button. Customers have to scroll down to the end of the page to see it.
Customers using JustPark have to click on a tiny pale grey “i” symbol beside the final price at the end of the booking process to discover its transaction fee. This added 12p to a £3.50 parking charge at Charmouth Road car park in Lyme Regis, Dorset.
MiPermit listed its 10p convenience fee above the final price at the end of the booking. This was levied on top of the £1.90 parking charge in Littlehampton, West Sussex.
RingGo said the fee funded the service it provided and that it was up to the councils it worked with whether or not to display it on car park signs. “In line with existing regulations, wherever pricing information is shown in the RingGo app, we also display any additional fees,” said Adam Dolphin at its parent company Arrive.
JustPark said mandatory fees were included in the price quoted during payment. “Nothing is added at the payment stage,” said a spokesperson. “The ‘i’ icon simply shows how that all-in price is made up, for drivers who want the detail.”
PayByPhone said its pricing was transparent. “The pricing elements related to parking, SMS options and service fees are presented before payment confirmation,” said a spokesperson. “Applicable pricing information – whether fees, parking rates or options – is available on the website and in the app.”
MiPermit was contacted for a comment.
The Local Government Association, which represents councils, said it was up to app providers to ensure their fees were clear and upfront.
The Department for Transport said parking tariffs and surcharges were a matter for councils. “Drivers should be able to see clearly what they will be charged before they pay for parking,” a spokesperson said.
A spokesperson for the AA said: “When a driver walks to the signs in the car park and sees £1 per hour, that’s what they should be charged, not £1 plus a 25p service charge.”

theguardian.com.title: Delhi police shut metro stations ahead of election protest march
theguardian.com.text:
Authorities in India’s capital closed six metro stations and warned of traffic disruptions on Monday, as opposition parties planned to march to the supreme court in protest against a controversial revision of voter lists that has sparked days of unrest in Delhi.
Opposition parties and supporters of the “cockroach” youth movement have taken to the streets almost daily this month to demand the resignation of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over the revision that critics say benefits prime minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP).
The revision that started last year saw over 130 million names – more than the population of Japan – deleted from voter lists during a verification exercise, including 30 million who could not be traced. Others included 28 million people who had died, and 63 million who had relocated.
Opposition parties allege Muslim voters and other minorities, who are unlikely to support the Hindu nationalist ruling party, are disproportionately affected by the deletions – charges both the poll panel and BJP reject.
Police detained thousands of protesters in Delhi over the weekend, including leaders of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP), as supporters of the youth movement sought to march in protest and were stopped by thousands of security personnel who locked down central Delhi.
The Election Commission has denied favouring any party and said wrongly deleted voters could re-enrol, while the BJP has accused its rivals of trying to undermine the country’s democracy by questioning legitimate electoral processes.
Police said the six metro stations were closed on Monday for “security reasons” and traffic restrictions and diversions would be imposed in 20 locations.
The main opposition Congress party has announced a march to the supreme court to submit a memorandum to the Chief Justice demanding an end to what it calls “vote theft” and Kumar’s resignation.
“Youth, all opposition parties, civil society groups, all those who believe in democracy and stand by the Constitution of India, will walk with us,” Congress leader Rahul Gandhi said on X.
Chief Justice Surya Kant, however, declined a meeting request in an email, saying Gandhi and the Congress delegation should instead approach the court legally since the issue was already being heard by the court and should be addressed through judicial proceedings, a Congress source said.
Separately, the CJP said its leaders would meet Delhi police to “demand” a date for a peaceful protest. It has threatened to announce a new call to protest if a date is not given within 24 hours.
The youth movement, which has mobilised protests in recent months against issues ranging from government school infrastructure to jobs, is one of the biggest political challenges to Modi and his BJP in his 12 years in power.
The protests erupted after the Indian Express newspaper reported last month that Kumar’s two deputies raised several concerns internally about voter list revisions, registration procedures and digital systems.

theguardian.com.title: Lawyers who helped detained Australian Robert Pether leave Iraq criticise Wong for announcing news
theguardian.com.text:
Advisers to Australian Robert Pether have expressed concern about the timing of a statement from the foreign minister announcing his departure from Iraq, saying it was issued at a sensitive period while the engineer was still transiting through Turkey.
Penny Wong’s office issued a statement on Monday announcing that Pether had been allowed to leave Iraq after five years trapped in the country, including a four-year stint in jail that his family feared would kill him.
The news was welcomed by his family, who said they had been “living in hell” since Pether was arrested without charge in April 2021 in connection to a business dispute between his firm – which was building a new headquarters for the central bank – and the Iraqi government.
Pether was released from jail last year due to his deteriorating health, but was banned from leaving the country until last week, when an Iraqi court dismissed proceedings against him and lifted the travel ban, citing a lack of evidence.
He was allowed to board a flight on Monday to Ireland, via Turkey, after painstaking negotiations involving officials in Ireland, Australia, Egypt and Iraq – and Pether’s international pro bono team at Slaney Advisors, a consultancy specialising in international arbitration.
The managing director, Peter Griffin, said he was shocked by the timing of Wong’s statement.
He said it was issued while Pether was transiting through Turkey and still at risk, particularly if there was premature and negative media reporting concerning the Iraqi government’s handling of the case.
“We were aware for some time that minister Wong was keen to be the first to break this fantastic news,” Griffin said. “But Robert’s safety was paramount.”
Wong’s office declined to respond to the criticism. Earlier, the foreign minister said: “The Australian government welcomes the Iraqi government’s decision to allow Mr Robert Pether to leave Iraq today.
“I spoke to Mr Pether shortly before his departure from Baghdad and am pleased he is now free to move forward with his life and be reunited with his family.
“Today’s outcome follows many years of persistent advocacy by the Australian government, including at the highest levels of government, and sustained consular assistance to Mr Pether and his family.”
Pether’s wife, Desree, said she was “hugely relieved”.
“It’s been an absolute nightmare, especially these last few months,” she said. “So many obstacles and plot twists right up to the last minute.”
Pether and his Egyptian colleague Khalid Radwan were detained in Baghdad in 2021 after flying in for a meeting with bank officials to resolve a dispute they were having with his engineering firm, CME Consulting.
Pether was later sentenced and fined over allegations that his firm spent money that should have gone to an architect and a subcontractor.
In a report in March 2022, the UN working group on arbitrary detention found Pether had been arbitrarily detained in breach of international law.
The UN body also found the arrest constituted an “enforced disappearance” and may have involved forms of torture. The working group said it had received complaints that Pether “was exposed to extreme cold, threats of death, humiliation and various forms of psychological abuse”.
“Mr Pether was detained in a [2x2 metre] cell with the lights permanently on,” the working group said in its report. “He was reportedly blindfolded, interrogated, screamed at, threatened, insulted and shown torture rooms.”
Pether’s family described the arrest and ongoing detention as a living nightmare. His health dramatically deteriorated.
In 2022, the Guardian obtained an emotional letter from Pether to his family, penned from behind bars. The letter warned his prognosis was “bleak” and he was facing a potential “death sentence”.
Pether wrote about potentially telling his family he might not come home.
“How do you tell a little girl who loves unicorns and cats that her daddy will not be coming home? How do you tell your children that you are proud of them but will not be sharing the accolades (and pitfalls) of their lives with them?” Pether wrote.
“And toughest of all, how do you tell your wife, who is very much the other half of you, that you will not be keeping the promise you made to grow old together?”
Desree had previously been critical of the efforts of Australian officials to secure Pether’s release. The Australian government said it had raised the case with Iraqi authorities more than 200 times.
Following her husband’s release from jail in 2025, Desree said from Ireland she was “grateful to everyone who contributed to this happening”.
The UN working group posed serious questions about the conduct of Pether’s trial.
The 2022 report aired allegations that Pether’s evidence was mistranslated to indicate guilt and said that even during the trial “Pether and Radwan did not have clarity around their charges”. Charges were dropped during the hearing and replaced with others.
“In the light of the above, the working group concludes that the violations of the right to a fair trial and due process are of such gravity as to give the deprivation of liberty of Messrs Pether and Radwan is arbitrary,” the report stated.

theguardian.com.title: IFS: budget will be ‘work of fiction’ without clear plan to cover UK’s £35bn spending pressures
theguardian.com.text:
John Healey has been warned by Britain’s leading tax and spending experts that his budget risks being a “work of fiction” unless he sets out plans to cover £35bn in spending pressures.
As the war in the Middle East rattles the public finances, the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said the damage from higher inflation meant the chancellor would need to either top up funds for his current government spending plans or impose deep real-terms cuts by the end of the decade.
Against a febrile backdrop in the bond market, the thinktank warned Healey that failure to address the issue at his 28 October budget risked leaving the impression that Labour was setting unrealistic spending plans.
Helen Miller, the director of the IFS, said: “Simply pencilling in implicit cuts that he has no intention of delivering would make the budget a work of fiction.”
Her comment echoes a criticism levelled at Jeremy Hunt, the former Conservative chancellor, who before the 2024 general election was accused by the then head of the Office for Budget Responsibility of setting unrealistic spending plans.
Publishing its influential “green budget” report, which analyses the public finances before Healey’s speech to the Commons, it called on the chancellor to avoid announcing a “steady as she goes” budget that delayed decisions until next year’s spending review.
“If John Healey sets out spending envelopes for public services that he would not be willing to live within, his plan for meeting the fiscal rules will not be credible,” it said.
Last week, the governor of the Bank of England, Andrew Bailey, said fiscal policy “must be credible and be seen as such by financial markets”. The following day, the Times quoted a government source as saying: “Andrew Bailey needs to focus on doing his job.”
Miller said the Treasury adopting an assumption that “everything can be kicked forward” to next year’s spending review risked undermining the chancellor’s credibility.
“We would be better served by a chancellor who hopes for the best, but plans for the worst, rather than sets out plans that either say, ‘I hope it’ll be fine and some money will come in’, or ‘I’ll get a plan in a year’s time’.”
Attention before the budget has largely focused on the hit to the chancellor’s headroom against Labour’s main fiscal rule to balance day-to-day public spending with revenues in 2029-30.
With the war in the Middle East fuelling a dramatic sell-off in the market for government debt, higher borrowing costs are expected to erase a significant chunk of the £24bn buffer left by the former chancellor Rachel Reeves at the spring statement.
Leading economists have predicted the market moves since the start of the war in February could wipe out about half of the headroom, adding to nerves in the Treasury over the risk of a market backlash.
The IFS said that although the surge in debt interest costs could add £10bn to borrowing in 2029-30, the exchequer would benefit from higher inflation boosting tax revenue – meaning Healey could see headroom cut by only £4bn.
However, it warned against focusing on this buffer because the inflation shock rippling from the Middle East would also dramatically hit the government’s plan for funding public services.
Higher inflation squeezes public spending power, forcing the government to choose between accepting real-term cuts and finding efficiency savings or topping up departmental budgets either by raising taxes or allowing an increase in borrowing.
The IFS said a choice to leave spending totals unchanged at the budget would implicitly mean allowing the quality or quantity of public services to fall. However, it said compensating for the inflation shock, and funding Healey’s pledge to raise defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030, would require tax rises or benefit cuts of about £35bn.
“Choosing to stay the course with the inherited tax and spending plans would mean allowing inflation to blow departments’ spending plans off course,” Miller said.
“It would be a choice to tolerate chunky cuts to the quantity or quality of some public services – cuts that would be larger if defence spending was increased within existing totals.”
She said Healey would not need to make detailed plans for the next spending review period at the budget but merely set out overall spending envelopes that he would be prepared to live within.
A spokesperson for the Treasury said: “The chancellor is fully focused on his priorities to boost business, help with the cost of living and support people in every postcode, underpinned by fiscal discipline and a commitment to meet the fiscal rules with a buffer against uncertainty.
“The Office for Budget Responsibility will publish its updated forecast alongside the budget in October and we will not comment on rumour, speculation or proposals about its contents ahead of then.”

theguardian.com.title: Burnham to urge MPs to embrace closer ties with EU
theguardian.com.text:
Andy Burnham will put Brexit back on the Commons agenda as MPs return from recess, warning that failing to pursue a better deal with the EU would be a “major dereliction of duty”.
The prime minister will use a statement to the Commons on the first day back after the party conference break to urge MPs to face up to the damage caused by Brexit, and embrace closer ties with the EU to increase economic growth and tackle illegal immigration.
In a stern warning ahead of the upcoming UK-EU summit, Burnham will argue that Britain cannot afford to turn its back on opportunities for greater cooperation with Europe and that maintaining the status quo is no longer good enough.
He will call for a calm, clear-eyed assessment of Britain’s relationship with Europe and urge MPs from across the Commons to back a pragmatic approach.
Burnham is expected to argue that most of the public would expect the government to seize the opportunity if closer cooperation could strengthen immigration controls while reviving the economy.
A No 10 source said: “Andy understands why some politicians don’t want to face up to the reality that Brexit has not delivered what they once promised. But it is time for a different conversation about what our long-term relationship should be.
“Sticking with the status quo and not working relentlessly to secure a good deal that boosts growth would be a major dereliction of duty.”
The prime minister’s statement comes on the same day MPs are due to debate a petition in Westminster Hall, calling for Britain to apply to rejoin the EU, which got more than 111,000 signatures.
The intervention comes amid renewed divisions over Britain’s relationship with Europe, with senior Conservatives vowing to reverse Labour’s moves towards closer EU ties, including a proposed agreement designed to ease post-Brexit barriers on food and agricultural trade. It has prompted warnings from businesses that abandoning such arrangements could prolong costs and uncertainty caused by checks and paperwork at the border.
But the idea of Britain having a closer relationship with the EU has also prompted unease within Burnham’s own ranks. Some MPs representing leave-voting constituencies fear renewing the Brexit debate could reopen old divisions, with senior ministers warning of the political and economic risks of pursuing EU membership.
Burnham’s statement also follows his declaration on Sunday that Russia interfered in the 2016 Brexit referendum. The prime minister has said he sought clarification on foreign interference after entering Downing Street and received confirmation of Russian involvement, although he did not reveal the evidence or suggest it had changed the referendum result.
The prime minister has already signalled a significant change in tone from his predecessor Keir Starmer, who ruled out rejoining the single market or customs union.
At Labour’s conference in Liverpool last month, Burnham said Brexit had done more harm than good and promised to examine Britain’s longterm relationship with the EU. He opened the door to options including fully rejoining the bloc.
Monday’s statement will turn the focus towards the immediate negotiations, with ministers seeking progress on removing trade barriers, including bureaucracy affecting food imports and exports, and closer cooperation on migration.

theguardian.com.title: Imran Khan’s party decries ‘coup’ after Pakistan suspends provincial government
theguardian.com.text:
Pakistan has declared a state of emergency in a province led by Imran Khan’s PTI party and suspended its government, a move a party spokesperson described as “more of a coup disguised as emergency”.
President Asif Ali Zardari declared the emergency in the north-western Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province on Sunday, after the federal government said authorities there had failed to tackle Islamist militancy in the province bordering Afghanistan.
The state of emergency and imposition of a new governor in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa sharply escalates a standoff between Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party and the government, and comes a week after PTI supporters gathered in the province intending to march on Islamabad to demand Khan’s release.
Hundreds of activists and three of Khan’s sisters were detained before the planned march, in what the PTI called one of the strongest crackdowns in years.
Khan’s aide and PTI spokesperson Zulfikar Bukhari called the government’s move “more of a coup disguised as emergency,” adding that it risked inciting more bloodshed and instability and was intended to stop the protest.
Pakistan’s constitution allows the government to take over from provincial authorities during an emergency, and the law minister, Azam Nazeer Tarar, said a provincial governor would take charge in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, which has suffered an increasing number of militant attacks in recent months.
Tarar told a news conference in Islamabad that the governor will initially be in place for six months, but could stay for as long as needed. The interior ministry said it would be deploying troops in the province.
The federal government and the military accuse PTI of failing to curb militants. The party rejects the charge and says Islamabad has not provided the funding and equipment it needs.
Restrictions have been placed on the movements of Sohail Afridi, who had previously been in charge of the province, one of his close aides told Reuters.
Maulana Fazlur Rehman, leader of the JUI-F political party and engaged by the government to mediate with PTI, also condemned the move. “Imposition of emergency is an ambush on democracy,” he told a news conference in Islamabad.
In Islamabad, the government has deployed tens of thousands of security forces and lined roads with containers ready to block roads, to bar protesters from reaching parliament.
Candidates backed by Khan’s party won the most seats in the 2024 election but formed a government only in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Supporters of the 74-year-old former cricket star say the military rigged the vote against him, which the military denies.
Cases against Khan range from concerns over state gifts to instigating violence and an accusation of an unlawful marriage. All but one conviction have been suspended or overturned, with appeals pending. He denies wrongdoing.
President Zardari declared the emergency on the advice of the prime minister, Shehbaz Sharif, after a cabinet decision, the president’s office said.
Sharif told the cabinet that security forces and citizens had been under attack for two years. “We can’t just act as a silent spectator.”
Islamabad also accuses Afghanistan of harboring militants who launch attacks inside Pakistan, and says PTI has sympathised with the Taliban in Kabul and its domestic affiliates. Both deny the charge.

theguardian.com.title: Pennsylvania shooter who killed eight was a grandfather, says slain child’s dad
theguardian.com.text:
The man who killed eight people, before turning the gun on himself, in a mass shooting in a home in Erie, Pennsylvania, on Friday was a grandfather who had not shown signs that he was capable of such violence, according to people who knew the shooter.
A man whose toddler was among those killed said on Sunday that the man never seemed distressed or out of the ordinary, the Associated Press reports.
“I think that was a front for him,” said Julius Windham during a memorial to victims of Friday’s shooting. Windham’s one-year-old daughter, Amarianna; her pregnant mother; and the woman’s five-year-old son and unborn baby were among the victims.
“Him every day, him smiling and being just – you would think of nothing like that would happen,” Windham said.
The 45-year-old gunman took his own life. Authorities have not released his name, but the Erie police chief, Rick Lorah, said he was related to seven of the victims. The eighth was a friend of the pregnant woman, he said. Police have not made their names public, either.
Mourners on Sunday placed candles, flowers and stuffed animals outside the home where the man opened fire shortly before 5 pm on Friday. Windham wore a T-shirt with pictures of the slain woman and children and the words “Forever in my heart”.
“Words can’t even explain what I’m going through right now,” Windham said. “But I gotta be strong for my community, you know what I’m saying? My family, my daughters, my sons, everybody.”
“We don’t want that dark memory to be what defines their lives in this world,” a family friend told Cleveland 19 News. “How do you even fathom something like this? How will you go home and tell your kids: ‘Hey, your mom, your siblings, your uncles and everybody else just got murdered by your grandpa?’”
Video and audio evidence recovered by investigators included muffled gunshot sounds coming from inside the home just before two “distressed” women arrived and began pounding on the door, Lorah said. The gunman then came out and shot them before returning inside.
Responding officers found the two women dead outside. After deploying a drone and robot, they went inside and found the bodies of the five-year-old boy and one-year-old girl on the first floor; two more women and two young men in a stairwell; and the shooter on the second floor.
“Out of respect for the victims and the families, I will not discuss the details of what our officers encountered inside that home,” the chief said at a news conference.
“But I want our community to understand the gravity of what happened and the profound impact this tragedy has had on those involved and on our community as a whole,” he said.
Erie is about 120 miles (190km) north of Pittsburgh.
Lorah declined to discuss motive but suggested mental health could be a factor. He said investigators would talk to relatives and examine the cellphones of the women who were killed outside the home.
“They knew something was going on at that house,” Lorah said. “We have to figure out what that is.”
Nicole and Debra Eller, whose best friend was among the victims, told the Associated Press they have known the family for more than 30 years. Nicole Eller said the shooter “was a good guy, and then he started going downhill with everything”.
“They were a lovely family. Who would have thought this would ever happen?” Debra Eller said. “Oh my gosh, this is so upsetting. This should have never happened to her or the kids or anybody. His grandchildren, his kids, how can you do that?”
The Erie shooting was reminiscent of a 1982 massacre in Wilkes-Barre, Pennsylvania, in which a man killed 13 people, including five of his own children.
At a news conference on Saturday, Erie’s mayor, Daria Devlin, addressed a portion of her remarks directly to the victims’ families.
“I am so deeply sorry,” Devlin said. What happened to you was horrific, and there is nothing that any of us can say today that will make this any easier ... Our entire community is with you, we’re grieving with you. And we are here to support you.”
“My heart breaks for this family. Lori and I are praying for their loved ones and the entire Erie community,” said Pennsylvania’s governor, Josh Shapiro, in a post on X on Saturday.

theguardian.com.title: Riyadh airport hit again after deadly Houthi missile attack, Saudi authorities say
theguardian.com.text:
A projectile hit a passenger terminal at the airport in Riyadh on Sunday, the day after a deadly missile attack on the facility carried out by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebel group killed 13 people.
An unidentified projectile hit terminal 4 at King Khalid international airport, starting a fire, killing one person and injuring 11, according to Saudi civil aviation authorities. Air defences also intercepted a cruise missile in the vicinity of the airport. It was the latest of several attacks on the airport in the past week.
The escalating attacks threatened to draw more countries into the Yemen conflict and further widen the regional fallout of the US-Iran war, which has already spread to Lebanon and Iraq.
In a post on X, the British embassy in Saudi Arabia advised against all but essential travel to the cities of Jeddah and Dammam and to avoid almost all airports.
After Saturday’s strike on Riyadh airport, the US president, Donald Trump, said he was weighing whether to join the Saudi military campaign in Yemen, telling reporters: “We’re going to look into it.”
The Iran-allied Houthis claimed to have launched several attacks on the airport, including the attack on Saturday, which killed 13 people and injured more than 300 – the deadliest attack on a Gulf country since the war with Iran started in March and an apparent escalation in the Houthis’ war with Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government that Riyadh sponsors.
In response to the attack, Saudi authorities extended the closure of the airport and said schools would be moved online until Thursday.
The Houthis claimed that Saudi Arabia struck the airport in Yemen’s rebel-held capital, Sana’a, on Sunday, without providing more information on damage or casualties.
Videos circulated on social media showing travellers walking through debris-strewn ground in the Riyadh airport as sirens blared. Four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a US citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese were killed in the missile strike.
On Sunday evening, Saudi authorities also confirmed King Fahd international airport in the eastern city of Dammam had been attacked, with the country’s civil aviation authority saying on X: “The assessment of the damage and verification of the safety of airport facilities were still under way, in coordination with the relevant authorities.”
On Saturday night, the spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen, Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki, said the coalition would “respond firmly” to the attack, offering few other details.
The Houthis said a Saudi airstrike on Sana’a on Sunday hit a home and killed a child, as well as injuring six others.
The Houthis doubled down on their threats on Sunday, warning airlines, passengers and staff to stay away from Saudi airports. The group said “the worst is yet to come” if Saudi military action in Yemen continued.
“We renew our warning to all airlines, experts, employees, workers and travellers against using Saudi airports and airspace, as they are vulnerable to attack and have become a theatre of operations for our forces,” the Houthis said on X.
Trump said on Saturday night that he would speak to the Saudi crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, after the previous attack on the airport.
The US has already been assisting with intelligence cooperation and targeting, with about 200 US military advisers stationed in Saudi Arabia to help with the campaign. Until now, the US has not directly taken part in fighting against the Houthis.
Direct US involvement could lead the group to resume its targeting of ships passing through the Bab al-Mandab strait, through which about 10% of global maritime goods transit.
It would also further entangle the US in Middle East wars as the American public grows increasingly frustrated with the continuing Iran conflict. Trump is facing the midterm elections in November with an unpopular war and soaring prices at home threatening his party’s performance at the polls.
Saudi Arabia is already carrying out airstrikes against the Houthis in Yemen. The Houthi government’s health ministry said coalition airstrikes over the last six weeks had killed 91 Yemenis and wounded 168, 60% of whom it said were women and children.
Saudi-backed government forces in Yemen launched a campaign to push the Houthis back from the areas the group conquered over the past month. Despite claiming initial successes, the government forces have not been able to loosen the Houthis’ grip over areas closest to the Bab al-Mandab strait such as Perim Island.
The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia said one of its citizens died on Sunday after being wounded in the Riyadh airport attack a day earlier.
The Egyptian woman killed in the attack on the airport was a flight attendant identified as Azza Ramzy, 28, who worked for the Saudi airline Flynas, according to Egyptian state-run TV.
The Syrian woman was a widowed mother of four who had been living in Saudi Arabia for five years, a relative told the Associated Press. The Syrian embassy in Riyadh identified her as Buthaina Ahmad Oweida.
Her niece, Nisreen Oweida, said her aunt was 56, from Syria’s northern Idlib province, and had left during the country’s civil war. She was living in Mecca and had been returning from a visit to her sister in Riyadh when she was killed, the niece said.
The airport attack was met with a wave of international condemnation, including from the UN secretary general, António Guterres, and the president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen.
“Attacks by Iran’s proxies are pushing the region into a spiral of violence,” von der Leyen wrote on X. “They are destabilising crucial global transport and energy nodes.”
The increasing intensity of Houthi attacks against Riyadh and its energy infrastructure has brought more foreign involvement in the Yemen war. Governments are facing pressure over oil prices, already high from the US-Iran war since March.
On Monday, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey issued a joint statement saying they would move quickly to implement their mutual defence pact, including by speeding up the deployment of military forces in the kingdom.
The UK said it would assist with defensive military support of Riyadh, providing refuelling for aircraft working to intercept Houthi missiles.
Saudi Arabia has asked for further assistance from France, Egypt, the UK and Pakistan as its stock of interceptor missiles are running low.
The Houthis launched a military campaign to take Yemen’s Red Sea coast in early September after months of escalating tensions with the Yemeni government and its Saudi patron. The campaign interrupted years of relative calm in the country after a 2022 UN-brokered ceasefire froze frontlines between the Houthis and the government.
Despite the Saudi-supported counteroffensive, the group seems to have held on to its recent gains. It is unclear what further Saudi military action would look like against the Houthis, who resisted years of strikes by an international coalition, as well as by the US.
Saudi Arabia led an international coalition that intervened against the Houthis in Yemen in 2015 after the group took over Sana’a and toppled the Yemeni government. Recent Houthi attacks against Saudi energy infrastructure, as well as Houthi military advances, have pulled Saudi Arabia back into the Yemen war.

theguardian.com.title: Zelenskyy signals surprise at Trump claim of Russia-Ukraine ‘energy ceasefire’ but would back it if Moscow does – as it happened
theguardian.com.text:
Zelenskyy says Ukraine awaits details of ceasefire but signals support
Volodymyr Zelenskyy says he has discussed an energy ceasefire with the leaders of Canada, Finland and Nato and is awaiting details from the US.
Writing on X shortly after saying such a deal was “news to me”, the Ukrainian leader said:
“Ukraine supports the ceasefire, and it’s important for Russia to support it as well. We are awaiting details from the American side. From our Ukrainian side, there is always FULL support for de-escalation steps, protection of lives, and the necessary decisions to end the war and ensure lasting peace.”
Donald Trump has claimed Russia and Ukraine have agreed to an “energy ceasefire”, though the US president gave no details of the purported agreement. “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” he wrote on his Truth Social network.
Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said the “energy ceasefire” was news to him. He told the news outlet Axios that he was not aware of an “energy ceasefire” between Ukraine and Russia announced by Trump, but added that if Moscow agreed to such a ceasefire, Kyiv would accept it.
Russia has yet to comment on Trump’s claim that Kyiv and Moscow had reached an energy ceasefire.
Zelenskyy said he has discussed an energy ceasefire with the leaders of Canada, Finland and Nato and is awaiting details from the US. The president of the EU Commission later said she had spoken to the Ukrainian leader. Ursula von der Leyen posted on X that she “fully supported the call of President Zelenskyy for a ceasefire that would protect global food supplies and energy infrastructure in Ukraine and Russia”.
Russia’s military said on Sunday it had struck a logistics centre in southern Ukraine’s Mykolaiv region and a cargo vessel in the Black Sea. A Russian defence ministry statement posted on Telegram said the logistics centre in the town of Ternivka was used to store military and dual-use cargoes for the Ukrainian military.
The US is threatening to stop the procurement system that provides Ukraine with weapons in order to press Kyiv to halt its deep strikes on Russian energy infrastructure, the Financial Times reported on Sunday, citing officials in Europe.
A Russian strike near a grocery store in Kharkiv, Ukraine’s second largest city and a frequent target of Moscow’s attacks, killed three people and injured nine, Regional Governor Oleh Syniehubov said on Telegram.
In western Ukraine, the mayor of the city of Ivano-Frankivsk said a Russian attack killed two people.
Volodymyr Zelenskyy says Russia hit power plant ‘after’ Trump’s energy ceasefire statement.
The Ukrainian leader said he had briefed EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen “on the brutal Russian strikes that continue unabated”.
“Just before our conversation, the Russians struck a power plant in Kyiv with a ‘shahed’ drone, and many districts experienced power outages. Later, there were strikes on energy facilities in the Kharkiv region.
“And all of this happened AFTER the President of the United States made his statement about an energy ceasefire”, he posted on X.
US threat to stop procurement system that provides Ukraine weapons, FT
The US is threatening to stop the procurement system that provides Ukraine with weapons in order to press Kyiv to halt its deep strikes on Russian energy infrastructure, the Financial Times reported on Sunday, citing officials in Europe.
The US had made threats to cut off intelligence sharing and the Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) mechanism for procuring US weapons for Ukraine, the officials added.
“They are calling Kyiv . . . they are calling everyone [in Europe],” said an official who received a call from a US defence official.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Sunday in response to critical comments from US President Donald Trump that he will organize elections in Ukraine if Russian President Vladimir Putin agrees to a 60-day ceasefire.
“Please tell Putin, give us two months, 60 days of total ceasefire, 60 days, and we will organize elections,” Zelenskyy told ABC’s This Week programme.
Trump on Saturday criticized Zelenskyy for attacking Russian oil refineries a day after the US temporarily lifted sanctions on Russian fuel that were designed to deprive Moscow of revenues to fund its war in Ukraine.
“I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president,” Trump had told reporters at the White House.
In response, Zelenskyy said “it’s up to Ukrainians” to choose their leader and noted that Putin would also like to change who is leading Ukraine.
He said it is easy for Ukraine to be blamed for higher fuel prices “when everybody in the world understands because of the war in (the) Middle East, the prices are rising.“
Earlier on Sunday, Zelenskyy said Ukraine was ready to halt attacks on Russian oil refineries if Moscow ceases its own strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
Under terms of the deal as described by Trump on Friday, Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel to US and global markets, equal to about 2.25 million barrels of fuel. The US exports about 1.5 million barrels of diesel per day.
Trump is under pressure to bring down rising fuel prices ahead of November midterm elections that will determine whether his Republican Party will retain control of the US Congress for his final two years in office.
Many lawmakers, including Republicans, have criticized the diesel deal as rewarding Putin.
Russia strikes logistics centre in Ukraine and cargo vessel
Russia’s military said on Sunday it had struck a logistics centre in southern Ukraine’s Mykolaiv region and a cargo vessel in the Black Sea.
A Russian Defence Ministry statement posted on Telegram said the logistics centre in the town of Ternivka was used to store military and dual-use cargoes for the Ukrainian military.
It said the vessel was carrying a military cargo to the Black Sea port of Chernomorsk.
France backs a “real energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine, President Emmanuel Macron said on Sunday, after his US counterpart Donald Trump announced a truce along those lines without giving details.
“Currently, Russia continues to refuse that, by lately intensifying further its strikes on Ukrainian infrastructure,” Macron said, adding: “France will continue to stay by the side of Ukraine and President Zelensky.”
The president of the EU Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, has expressed her “full support for President Zelenskyy” amid calls for a ceasefire.
In a telephone call with the Ukrainian leader, von der Leyen posted on X that she “fully supported the call of President Zelenskyy for a ceasefire that would protect global food supplies and energy infrastructure in Ukraine and Russia.
“The war has entered a new, grimmer phase”, von der Leyen said. “Russia is stalling on the battlefield and striking civilians far behind the front lines.
“I conveyed our solidarity with the Ukrainian people. And my full support for President Zelenskyy as he leads the fight for his people’s freedom.”
Zelenskyy says Ukraine awaits details of ceasefire but signals support
Volodymyr Zelenskyy says he has discussed an energy ceasefire with the leaders of Canada, Finland and Nato and is awaiting details from the US.
Writing on X shortly after saying such a deal was “news to me”, the Ukrainian leader said:
“Ukraine supports the ceasefire, and it’s important for Russia to support it as well. We are awaiting details from the American side. From our Ukrainian side, there is always FULL support for de-escalation steps, protection of lives, and the necessary decisions to end the war and ensure lasting peace.”
Russia has yet to react to Trump's ceasefire claim
Russia has yet to comment on Donald Trump’s claim that Kyiv and Moscow had reached an energy ceasefire.
On Friday, Trump had warm words for the Russian president after the country struck a deal to sell diesel fuel to the US in return for sanctions relief.
Speaking to reporters outside the White House on Friday, Trump said: “That is massive amounts of oil coming into our country. And I want to thank President Putin, to be honest with you. We have massive amounts of oil coming into our country, and it’s diesel which is what we want, so: thank you.”
A senior Ukrainian official has also reportedly told the FT that Ukraine had no information about Trump’s proclaimed ceasefire deal.
The official was quoted as saying: “Just now our repair teams are restoring electricity and water supplies in Kyiv” following Russian strikes. “Nobody has heard [of the ceasefire].”
Donald Trump’s call for Zelenskyy to make way for a new Ukrainian leader drew criticism from his own party.
Don Bacon, a Republican Nebraska congressman and former military officer, suggested Trump was not fit to lead.
Reacting to Trump’s statement that “it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president’”, Bacon wrote on: “We need a president who is up to the task of leading the free world.”
The latest acrimonious row between Washington and Kyiv began on Friday when Trump announced he was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel exports. He said the move would reduce global and domestic fuel prices before next month’s US midterm elections.
A furious Zelenskyy called the decision “weak” and said it would generate “billions” in extra revenue for Putin, enabling him to wage war “even more intensely”. An equally irate Trump warned that Zelenskyy should “damn well stop” hitting Russian refineries. Ukraine needed a “new leader”, he said on Saturday.
Responding to Trump, Zelenskyy said it was up to Ukraine’s society to chose “one or another leader”. He told ABC News he was willing to bow down to US demands and to organise elections, but only if Putin agreed to a “total” sixty-day ceasefire.
Zelenskyy says ceasefire 'was news for me' but Kyiv would accept it if Moscow does
Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskiy has said the “energy ceasefire” was news to him.
He told the news outlet Axios that he was not aware of an “energy ceasefire” between Ukraine and Russia announced by  Donald Trump, but added that if Moscow agreed to such a ceasefire, Kyiv would accept it.
“The ceasefire announcement was news for me. But if Russians agree to an energy ceasefire Ukraine will agree. If president Trump negotiated it with Putin — please tell us when the ceasefire begins — we are ready and we will accept it,” Zelenskiy was quoted as saying by Axios.
Just hours before Donald Trump claimed the two sides had agreed a ceasefire on energy strikes, Volodymyr Zelenskyy rebuffed his demand that Ukraine stop bombing Russian oil refineries.
Zelenskyy demanded Moscow has to first halt its own “brutal” attacks on Ukraine and its energy infrastructure.
Ukraine’s president said any deal to end his country’s long-range drone strikes on targets inside Russia would have to be “reciprocal”. It should be backed by “real guarantees” – meaning punitive measures against Moscow from Ukraine’s allies, including the US.
Trump claims Russia and Ukraine agree to stop attacks on energy infrastructure
Donald Trump has claimed Russia and Ukraine have agreed to an ”energy ceasefire”, though the US president gave no details of the purported agreement.
“Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” he wrote on his Truth Social network.
Trump made the announcement on his Truth Social account shortly after Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, told ABC on Sunday that Ukraine was ready for a ceasefire, including on energy infrastructure.
This announcement follows Trump’s criticism of Zelenskyy for attacks on Russian diesel facilities, which he blames for global shortages.
Stick with us as we bring you the latest developments as we get them.

theguardian.com.title: Trump and Rubio weigh firing Kimberly Guilfoyle after reports of improper conduct
theguardian.com.text:
Donald Trump and Marco Rubio, the secretary of state, are considering firing US ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle after a series of reports alleging she has engaged in improper and possibly illegal conduct before and during her tenure in Athens.
A senior US official said Sunday that Trump and Rubio are “extremely pissed off” by Guilfoyle’s reported conduct and would likely decide on what action to take this week after Monday’s federal holiday.
The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal deliberations, said Rubio had been particularly angry, not least because he visited Athens just last week and Guilfoyle attended most, if not all, of his events and greeted him on his arrival with a bear hug as the allegations swirled.
In a series of stories, the Wall Street Journal has reported questionable conduct by Guilfoyle, including an alleged threat to a host country official, accepting improper gifts and services and offering to use her influence inside the administration in return for the payment of a large credit card bill.
Guilfoyle has not addressed the reports directly, although her lawyer has said she did nothing wrong and the US embassy in Athens has tacitly expressed support for her.
After defending Guilfoyle following the first report, Rubio has declined to comment publicly on the growing allegations. On Wednesday, Rubio said: “Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here.”
But after another report appeared late Wednesday, Rubio on Thursday before leaving Athens berated journalists for asking about the allegations saying he didn’t know if they were true and that he would not respond if he could not confirm.
“You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something and you reported it, it’s the gospel. It’s not the gospel. It’s not the gospel for me. That’s not the way we do things,” Rubio said at the foot of his plane as Guilfoyle, who was there to see him depart, looked on.
The official said that Rubio had grown increasingly frustrated as the reports multiplied.
A second US official, who also spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss personnel matters, said the state department’s inspector general is looking into the allegations, which first began surfacing in the Journal late last month and have since multiplied.
The second official could not say if a formal IG investigation had begun. Inspectors general often conduct informal inquiries into complaints against staffers and many times those inquiries do not result in a full-on investigation, which can result in disciplinary action up to and including dismissal.
The state department has declined to comment on a potential IG investigation.
The top two Democrats on the House foreign affairs and Senate foreign relations committees, Representative Gregory Meeks of New York and Senator Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, as well as the ranking member on the House committee for oversight and government reform, Robert Garcia, Democrat of California, have already called for an investigation into Guilfoyle.
Since late September, the Journal has detailed numerous accounts of questionable conduct by Guilfoyle. Its first report said that she had told guests at a reception that the US could undermine the Greek government if it chose to, promoted the business interests of one particular Greek construction and energy company, and allowed its lobbyist into private diplomatic meetings.
While Rubio was in Athens, the Journal reported – citing text messages – that Guilfoyle had asked a Trump donor and supporter to pay a $100,000 credit card bill just before her confirmation hearing, promising him access to administration officials if he did.
The Journal then reported that Guilfoyle had been enraged about not being invited to a Greek-themed event at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, earlier this year and demanded to attend while boasting about luxury travel to France with energy company executives.
Another report, from the British tabloid The Daily Mail, said that Guilfoyle had alienated staff at the US embassy in Athens and had pushed the bounds of behavior appropriate for the top representative of the US government to Greece.
Guilfoyle is a former Fox News Channel host and California prosecutor who was once engaged to Trump’s son Donald Jr.

theguardian.com.title: Middle East crisis: Riyadh airport hit again as Houthis claim attacks, including strike that killed 12 – as it happened
theguardian.com.text:
Following yesterday’s attack on Riyadh international airport that killed 12 people and injured hundreds, the site was hit again on Sunday. Authorities said an “unidentified projectile” struck Terminal 4 at King Khalid International Airport. Air defenses also “intercepted and destroyed a cruise missile” in the vicinity of the airport.
An Egyptian flight attendant, a Syrian woman, and an Indian national were among the 12 killed in yesterday’s Saudi airport attack. The Egyptian woman killed was identified as Azza Ramzy, 28. The Syrian woman was identified as Buthaina Ahmad Oweida.
The Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation said in a statement that today’s attack on King Khalid international airport in Riyadh “resulted in injuries” but did not specify how many.
Yemen’s Houthis have claimed responsibility for both Saturday and Sunday’s attacks on Riyadh Airport. The group said on Sunday they had targeted Riyadh’s airport several times as well as Saudi energy facilities, a day after Saturday’s deadly attack.
The United Arab Emirates issued a statement in solidarity with Saudi Arabia, expressing support for “all measures aimed at safeguarding the kingdom’s security and stability”. The UAE message is significant given the major rupture in relations this year.
The Houthis this morning issued a warning to travelers and airlines to stay away from Saudi airports following yesterday’s attack. A Houthi military spokesman warned the public to “take our warning seriously” and also claimed that “Saudi Arabia bears responsibility for any failed interceptions”.
The attacks on Riyadh airport came just before a major oil summit, the World Petroleum Congress, scheduled for this week. The repeated attacks have temporarily halted oil flows and driven up global oil prices. The CEOs of major companies Shell, ExxonMobil, BP, TotalEnergies had been due to attend the summit but given the attacks, it’s unclear if executives will take the risk.
Indian national dies from injuries following Riyadh airport attack
An Indian national wounded in yesterday’s Houthi airport attack in Riyadh has died from his injuries, the Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia said in a statement.
“It is learnt that one Indian national injured in the Riyadh attack has unfortunately lost his life today,” the embassy said. “We convey our heartfelt condolences to the family of the deceased. We are in touch with the family and will provide all support for ensuring the early repatriation of mortal remains.”
In an earlier statement, the embassy said that 11 Indians were among those injured in yesterday’s attack.
Yemen’s Houthis are claiming responsibility for both Saturday and Sunday’s attacks on Riyadh Airport. The group said on Sunday they had targeted Riyadh’s airport several times as well as Saudi energy facilities, a day after Saturday’s deadly attack.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the Iran-backed group “carried out four qualitative operations in the past 24 hours using ballistic and cruise missiles and drones,” AFP reported.
Saree said the group targeted the Riyadh airport multiple times, as well as the Dammam airport and two facilities belonging to the Saudi state oil company Aramco.
Saudi authorities say latest airport attack 'resulted in injuries'
The Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation said in a statement that today’s attack on King Khalid international airport in Riyadh “resulted in injuries” but did not specify how many.
The statement said that an “assessment of the damage and verification of the safety of the facilities is ongoing”.
Earlier on Sunday, an “unidentified projectile” hit Riyadh’s international airport, the same site targeted in Saturday’s strike which injured hundreds of people and killed 12. Minutes earlier, Yemen’s Houthis claimed responsibility for the attack.
Israeli prime minister condemns attack on Riyadh airport
Benjamin Netanyahu, the Israeli prime minister, condemned on Sunday the “horrific terrorist attack” on Riyadh airport in Saudi Arabia.
“I condemn in the strongest possible terms the horrific terrorist attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh,” Netanyahu wrote in a social media post, adding that he extended Israel’s “deepest condolences” to the families of the victims.
Yemen’s Houthis claim responsibility for Riyadh airport attack that killed 12 people
Yemen’s Houthis have claimed responsibility for the attack targeting Riyadh airport, according to a statement released by the group.
The Houthis claimed to have launched strikes against Dammam airport and Saudi Aramco facilities located in Saudi Arabia’s Eastern Province. It is not immediately clear whether the group is claiming just yesterday’s attack or the strike from earlier today as well. Saudi authorities have not yet issued a confirmation.
SriLankan Airlines announced that it has suspended all flights to Riyadh, Saudi Arabia until October 18 “in view of the recent security incident affecting Riyadh Airport and ongoing safety and operational assessments.”
“The safety and security of our passengers and crew remain our highest priority and services will resume once the prevailing conditions are assessed to be suitable for commercial flight operations,” the statement said.
Attacks on Riyadh airport and capital come on eve of major oil summit
Saudi Arabia of course is the world’s top oil exporter and its oil refineries and facilities have been repeatedly targeted by the Houthis this past month.
It was forced to temporarly close its key East-West pipeline last month after a drone attack on the 1,200km Saudi Aramco pipeline which spans the Arabian peninsula.
That temporarily halted oil flows; the kingdom had been diverting much of its oil that used to go out through the Strait of Hormuz through the pipeline to be shipped out through the Red Sea, however that trade route has now also been targeted by the Iran-allied Houthis.
That has driven up global oil prices and spooked the market. The kingdom was in fact due to host a major oil summit – the World Petroleum Congress - this week in Riyadh.
The CEOs of major companies Shell, ExxonMobil, BP, TotalEnergies had been due to attend but given the attacks, it’s unclear if exceutives will take the risk. Saudi authorities were saying this morning that the summit would still proceed.
If confirmed as a strike, this marks the fourth attack on the Saudi capital’s airport just this week alone.
The Houthis haven’t claimed responsibility for Saturday’s attack on King Khalid International in Riyadh, but earlier this morning issued a threat warning travellers and airlines and trade operators to stay away from all Saudi airports and airspaces – barring those of Islamic holy cities Mecca and Medina.
The Houthis have declared that all Saudi airspace is a theatre of their military operations.
They’ve escalated their attacks as Saudi Arabia has launched hundreds of airstrikes on Houthi areas in Yemen this week, as part of the Yemeni government force’s counter-offensive this week to repel the Houthis from a critical Red Sea strait.
Riyadh international airport reportedly hit again in second strike
The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen says an “unidentified projectile” hit Riyadh’s international airport on Sunday – the same site targeted in Saturday’s strike which injured hundreds of people and killed 12.
Coalition spokesman Major General Turki al-Malki said the projectile struck Terminal 4 at King Khalid International Airport, causing a fire, AFP reported.
Al-Malki said air defences also “intercepted and destroyed a cruise missile” in the vicinity of the airport.
The airport has been closed today following yesterday’s deadly attack.
Houthi airport attack forces swift rethink of Trump’s new 'Blame Ukraine' strategy
Patrick Wintour
The reckless missile attack on King Khalid international airport in Riyadh on Saturday did not just export the death and misery inside Yemen to Saudi Arabia, it also left Donald Trump forced to reconsider his diplomatic and political strategy designed to take him into the midterm elections next month.
The US president’s plan had only been unveiled on Saturday.
It was to blame what he described as “a world problem” – spiralling diesel prices – on the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, saying his attacks on Russian oil refineries were the cause. He was going to keep the political temperature down on his war of choice in Iran and its spillover in Yemen until after the midterms.
In pursuit of this strategy, he claimed the Iranian blockade in the strait of Hormuz was in effect broken, producing figures on daily oil barrel exports to assuage the markets. As a further insurance he also claimed it was impossible to negotiate with the Iranians since there was no single leadership in Tehran.
Saudi Arabia, in conjunction with Turkey, and Pakistan, were largely to be left to sort out the Houthis along the Red Sea. The fate of Yemen, the poorest country in the world according to the International Monetary Fund, was not going to shift votes in Kansas or Alaska.
Now, after the Riyadh airport attack, it is doubtful, for a basket of reasons, that this anyway threadbare strategy, largely born of desperation, can hold.
For all the talk of the Gulf becoming responsible for its own security, it is doubtful that Saudi Arabia can be left to fend for itself after the carnage in Riyadh. One of the the 12 dead is an American and there may be more among the severely injured. Something is clearly wrong with Saudi defences since the Houthis are firing rockets from 500 miles away, and they are reaching their target too often.
The US has had a unilateral ceasefire with the Houthis since 2025, and once the hostilities between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis recommenced in the summer, the pact was quietly renewed.
Trump has twice rejected Saudi appeals for help. Can he spurn them three times? The pressure to act as allies are expected to may prove overwhelming.
Egyptian flight attendant and Syrian woman among 12 killed at Saudi airport
We have some more detail on the 12 people killed in the Houthi missile strike on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airporton Saturday.
The attack on a civilian space – the airport had no military facility- has drew widespread condemnation from Arab and Western leaders and the UN.
Saudi authorities said the dead included four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a U.S. citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese.
The Egyptian woman killed has been identified as Azza Ramzy, 28, a flight attendant who worked for the Saudi airline Flynas, according to the Egyptian state-run TV.
The Syrian woman has been identified as Buthaina Ahmad Oweida by the Syrian embassy in Riyadh.
She was a widowed mother of four who had been living in Saudi Arabia for the past five years after fleeing the Syrian civil war, her niece told AP. She had been visiting her sister in Riyadh and was on her way home to Mecca, where she lived, when she was killed in the attack.
There is attention too on the still yet to be identified American citizen who was killed at the airport because that will add to Saudi pressure on Donald Trump for the U.S. to join in the fight.
As we await more detail on this reported blast in the Saudi capital, it’s worth noting that there’s been a distinct lack of information coming from Saudi authorities on the Houthi attacks and other dangers.
Officials have announced that schooling will move online until the end of the week, meaning schools and campuses are closed.
But they have otherwise been largely quiet on the major attack on the country’s largest airport yesterday which killed 12 people and injured 300 more.
They have not issued a wider emergency alert, nor given a national address or offered any assurance to residents on why and how the kingdom’s air defences failed. We know that Saudi Arabia has been requesting more missile interceptors from the US and other European allies – but the US is also facing its own shortage due to the Iran fighting.
The Houthis have targeted Riyadh’s airport for the past few weeks – including two attacks earlier in the week, which killed four people. But Saudi authorities have not publicly announced a closure of King Khalid International Airport, with the suspension of flights detected through air traffic monitoring sites instead.
This withholding of information the public is in line with a pattern of communication from not just Saudi but other Gulf state authorities these past seven months since they’ve come under attack from Iranian missiles and drones.
