Gulf authorities have tended to suppress the flow of information – ostensibly for national security purposes and to maintain public confidence in the countr'y’s defences.
However, the lack of information is also leading to confusion and speculation online, particularly as the Houthis continue to threaten new strikes against the kingdom.
Houthi state media says capital's airport hit by Saudi strike
Houthi-run state TV is reporting that Saudia Arabia has carried out a strike on the main airport in Sana’a, the Yemeni capital currently controlled by the Houthis.
Al Masirah TV said the strike had hit Sana’a International Airport.
No comment yet from Saudi authorities or the Saudi-backed government forces in Yemen.
Earlier however, the coalition had issued a issued a statement saying they would “respond decisively” to the Houthis’ “terrorist attack” on Riyadh’s airport on Saturday which killed 12 people and injured 309.
The Saudis have launched hundreds of air strikes on Houthi positions in Yemen since fighting recommenced last month.
UK advises against travel to parts of Saudi Arabia
The UK Foreign Office has updated guidance for British nationals following the deadly Houthi attack on Saturday.
It has advised against:
All travel to within 10km of the border with Yemen
All but essential travel to Aseer province, Riyadh province, Najran province, Jizan province and Taif city and Taif International Airport
There are an estimated 20,000- 30,000 British nationals living in Saudi Arabia, although those numbers have presumably fluctuated since the war began and Iran and its allies fought back against US and Israeli strikes by targeting cities like Dubai and Doha, in Gulf states allied with the US.
In the first fortnight of the war earlier this year in March, more than 102,000 Britons across the Middle East registered with the Foreign Office for help.

theguardian.com.title: Abdul El-Sayed: Democrats must ‘win by massive numbers’ to fend off Trump election denial
theguardian.com.text:
Democrats must “win by massive numbers” during November’s federal midterm elections because Donald Trump and his Republican allies are bound to try to sow doubt about the integrity of the results, Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan said on Sunday.
El-Sayed’s comments on NBC’s Meet the Press came with the Democrats favored to win control of the House of Representatives during the 3 November midterms – and polls show that the party could also win Senate seats in states that traditionally elect Republicans and gain a majority there, too.
Meanwhile, Trump has long baselessly maintained that the 2020 presidential election which he lost as an incumbent to Joe Biden was stolen by fraudsters.
He also gave a primetime speech in July in which he made unverified claims about Chinese interference in the election, and he fired members of an independent federal election commission.
When asked later by a rightwing broadcaster whether the president might declare a national security emergency pertaining to elections for the midterms, Trump ignited alarm among some observers by replying: “Let me just say, stranger things have happened, OK?”
The New York Times, meanwhile, reported that Trump had cast doubt on elections on 440 days of his second presidency, which began in early 2025.
As such, on NBC’s Meet the Press Sunday, El-Sayed was asked whether Democrats needed to turn out in such numbers in November that the election would be “too big to rig” – as it had recently been put by former vice-president Kamala Harris, who lost the 2024 White House election to Trump.
“Donald Trump has already threatened to do what he did in 2020, which is deny the outcomes of an election,” El-Sayed said. “So, yes, we have to win by massive numbers.”
The Cook Political Report revised its predictions on Tuesday and declared that “A Senate Majority is Squarely in Democrats’ Sights”.
A recent New York Times and Siena University poll found Democratic Senate candidates leading in Alaska, Ohio and Texas, states that Trump won by double digits in 2024.
The poll showed El-Sayed leading Republican candidate Mike Rogers by five points.
El-Sayed on Sunday’s Meet the Press alluded to how Rogers had also claimed that a 2024 US Senate election which he lost to Elissa Slotkin, a Democrat, was stolen from him – after first having conceded the race.
Rogers in November 2025 was reported to have said at events that a single van carrying fraudulent ballots in Detroit cost him the race against Slotkin.
“The guy … I’m running against insinuates that he didn’t actually lose,” El-Sayed said to Kristen Welker. “That’s the guy I’m running against right now.”

theguardian.com.title: Trump announces partial ceasefire in Ukraine war as Zelenskyy says deal is ‘news to me’
theguardian.com.text:
Donald Trump has announced an energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia, apparently without consulting Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who said the deal to stop long-range attacks was “news to me”.
In a social media post, the US president claimed the two sides had reached an agreement. “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” he wrote on Truth Social.
He offered no further details. Zelenskyy said he was surprised by the announcement but would agree to it if Vladimir Putin did the same. “If President Trump negotiated it with Putin – please tell us when the ceasefire begins. We are ready and we will accept it,” the Ukrainian president told the Axios website.
Earlier, Zelenskyy rebuffed Trump’s demand made on Saturday that Kyiv stop bombing Russian oil refineries. Zelenskyy said Moscow had to first halt its own “brutal” attacks on his country’s energy infrastructure.
Any deal to end long-range drone strikes by Ukraine on targets inside Russia would have to be “reciprocal”, he said. It should be backed by “real guarantees” – meaning punitive measures against Moscow from Ukraine’s allies, including the US.
There was no sign that the Kremlin was observing Trump’s ceasefire. According to Zelenskyy, Russian drones took to the sky “throughout the day” on Sunday. There were also “unfortunately” several airstrikes, he said, including on energy infrastructure.
The Ukrainian president said the Russians hit thermal power station No 5 in the eastern city of Kharkiv – the latest of more than 200 strikes this week against electricity generation and transmission facilities in Ukraine. There were another 17 hits on gas and oil facilities, he added.
The fast-moving row between Washington and Kyiv began on Friday when Trump announced he was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel exports. He said the move would reduce global and domestic fuel prices before next month’s US midterm elections.
A furious Zelenskyy called the decision “weak” and said it would generate “billions” in extra revenue for Putin, enabling him to wage war “even more intensely”. An equally irate Trump said Zelenskyy should “damn well stop” hitting Russian refineries. Ukraine needed a “new leader”, he said on Saturday.
Responding to Trump, Zelenskyy said it was up to Ukrainians to choose “one or another leader”. He told ABC News he was willing to accept Trump’s demands and to organise elections, but only if Putin agreed to a “total” 60-day ceasefire.
The bitter public feud is the most serious between the US and Ukraine since last year, when Trump berated Zelenskyy in the Oval Office.
The Financial Times, citing officials in Europe, reported on Sunday that the US is threatening to stop the procurement system that provides Ukraine with weapons to press Kyiv to halt its deep strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.
The New York Times has reported that US officials have offered the Kremlin lucrative economic incentives in exchange for a ceasefire. They reportedly include releasing billions in Russian sovereign assets that are frozen. The Trump administration also revisited a plan to sell parts of Russia’s energy company, Lukoil. The multibillion deal would benefit Middle Eastern investors, the paper reported, some with “business ties” to US negotiators.
On Saturday, Trump criticised Zelenskyy and said he had refused to make a deal to end the fighting. In response, Ukraine’s president laid the blame for Europe’s biggest war since 1945 on “Russia and Russia alone”. “It is possible to stop strikes on energy infrastructure as early as today, but Putin does not want to do so,” he said.
Ukrainian officials point out that the White House is demanding Kyiv give up its most effective weapon, without demanding any corresponding concessions from Russia. In recent weeks, Kyiv has dealt a major blow to Russia’s economy, striking oil complexes, warehouses and datacentres.
Russia’s own bombing campaign has been relentless. On Saturday it killed 23 people in the city of Zaporizhzhia, including four children, and hit a five-storey apartment block in the frontline town of Sloviansk. Zelenskyy said Moscow’s aerial campaign involved thousands of aerial bombs and jet-powered drones. It continued “unabated”, he said.
The head of Ukraine’s foreign affairs committee, Oleksandr Merezhko, said Trump’s “bullying” demand for Zelenskyy to quit had strengthened him at home “paradoxically”, after recent damaging corruption scandals. “Putin’s plan is to decapitate Zelenskyy and remove him as a wartime leader. Trump is siding with Putin,” Merezhko said.
He added: “I’m afraid that behind this situation is Trump’s worldview. He wants to do business with Putin. For him, Ukraine seems like an obstacle to be removed. Both Trump and Putin wish to pressure us into capitulation.”
Referring to the notorious 1939 agreement between Nazi Germany and the USSR, Merezhko said: “We are moving to a new Molotov-Ribbentrop pact and to a world of strongmen and spheres of influence.”
Merezhko said Ukraine would continue to destroy enemy oil refineries, against US wishes, because they funded Russia’s war machine and acknowledged that a cutoff of US intelligence sharing with Kyiv – threatened by the Trump administration – would “blind” Ukraine’s air defence systems. “This would be an act of complicity with Putin’s genocide. It would mean more dead civilians and dead children,” he said.
Ukrainian negotiators had been meeting in Florida with their American counterparts, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, when Trump announced the US was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel. Blindsided, the Ukrainians went home early. “It felt like a trap,” one stunned Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent newspaper.
On Sunday, Zelenskyy shored up support in a series of conversations with key allies including Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, the Polish leader, Donald Tusk, and the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen.
Earlier Zelenskyy spoke with the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, France’s president, Emmanuel Macron, and the Finnish president, Alexander Stubb. Downing Street said Burnham recognised the last 24 hours had been “difficult” for Ukraine and “reiterated his complete solidarity”.
Downing Street said the two leaders agreed “to maintain pressure on Russia” and to strengthen the sanctions regime, despite Trump’s efforts to the contrary. “Russia should agree to an immediate energy ceasefire, ending its brutal strikes on Ukrainian infrastructure and its attacks on shipping in the Black Sea,” a statement added.
Speaking over the weekend, Zelenskyy said Trump’s decision empowered Putin and gave him “extra money for the war”, running into millions and “perhaps billions”. “It is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should act. And, in my view, it is a weak decision,” he said.
- Luke Harding’s Betrayal: Trump, Putin and the New Age of Conquest is published by Guardian Faber

theguardian.com.title: Volkswagen boss backs EU plan to bolster domestic European industry
theguardian.com.text:
The boss of Volkswagen has backed EU proposals to boost its domestic industry, arguing European carmakers need to be able to “compete under comparable conditions” with Chinese rivals.
Oliver Blume said “Made in Europe” rules from the EU “must reward real value creation in Europe”, speaking in Paris before the motor show this week.
The rules are aimed at countering the rapid rise of Chinese brands in Europe in the automotive sector and other important manufacturing industries. Lower-priced Chinese manufacturers have prompted a crisis in several industries.
Volkswagen is among the most-affected European companies. Germany’s biggest carmaker has launched a brutal plan to cut as many as 100,000 jobs. Blume said it was the “largest transformation programme in its history”.
The proposals for the Made in Europe rules, formally known as the Industrial Accelerator Act, would limit subsidies and public procurement to products with a large proportion of their materials and manufacturing coming from within the EU.
Blume listed a litany of challenges facing European carmakers, saying: “Europe is under enormous competitive pressure.” These included: high energy costs; lower demand as consumers struggle with high inflation; the need to be quicker to develop cars; and intense competition from China.
On Friday, the EU said it had reached a landmark deal with China to “halve” its sales of hybrid cars in the bloc amid fears surging sales could kill off parts of the European car industry.
Blume said Germany’s carmakers were happy to compete with Chinese rivals, but said the EU should try to reward businesses with significant European footprints.
“Companies that invest and develop in Europe must see a clear benefit,” he said.
Referring to Chinese companies, he added: “Those who sell here should compete under comparable conditions and create jobs and value here in Europe, too.
Blume added: “We believe in open markets, but openness also means standing up for our own interests in Europe. Because a strong industrial base means more than economic success. It protects technological independence.”
Volkswagen is exhibiting at the Paris show for the first time in 20 years. Blume emphasised the “close ties between France and Germany”, while hosting the French industry minister, Sébastian Martin.
Arno Antlitz, VW’s chief financial officer, said the job cuts were necessary to “increase our economic power” by increasing profitability and allowing it to defend its “home turf”.
The company is cutting the number of models it offers worldwide from 150 to 75 across brands including Audi and Škoda. It hopes the move will reduce complexity in its factories and for dealers, cutting the cost of each vehicle it makes.
On Sunday, it revealed the production version of its ID Tiguan, an electric edition of its bestselling family SUV.

theguardian.com.title: Donald Tusk says man accused of plotting to kill him detained
theguardian.com.text:
The Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, said on Sunday that a man accused of plotting to assassinate him and his defence minister had been detained.
“The man threatening an attack has been detained,” Tusk wrote on X, praising the police for their “swift and decisive action”.
The arrest was also confirmed by the country’s interior minister, Marcin Kierwiński.
The interior ministry had earlier said that Tusk and the defence minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz may have been targeted.
It ordered authorities to take action “in connection with the information received by the police concerning a possible assassination attempt on the prime minister... as well as the deputy prime minister”, who is also defence minister, spokesperson Karolina Gałecka wrote on X.
Members of the police, state protection service (SOP) and internal security agency were present at Sunday’s meeting.
“We are treating this matter as deadly serious,” a spokesperson for the minister-coordinator of special services, Jacek Dobrzyński, told journalists afterwards.
“Month by month, year by year, more and more various threats and menacing messages reach the police, SOP, and the services concerning Poland and Poles,” he said. In this case we are talking about a strong likelihood that these threats could actually be carried out.”
Poland, a Nato and EU member, has been on high alert after a series of stabbings in the last week, which Tusk on Thursday denounced as a “cult of violence”.

theguardian.com.title: Trump’s deal with Putin will have little impact on US diesel prices, experts say
theguardian.com.text:
Donald Trump’s deal with Vladimir Putin to temporarily lift sanctions on US imports of Russian diesel will have little “meaningful” effect on motorists and businesses in the US and overseas, energy and foreign policy analysts have predicted.
The US president infuriated Volodymyr Zelenskyy when he announced the deal on Friday, writing on Truth Social that the agreement with his Russia counterpart to supply millions of tonnes of diesel was essential to reduce fuel prices in the US, which have soared after his decision to go to war against Iran.
The package announced by Trump involves 300,000 tonnes of diesel released immediately “to the American and global marketplace” followed by 500,000 tonnes in November and a further 1m tonnes after that. The 300,000 figure equates to about three-quarters of what the US would use in a day, according to calculations using figures from the US Energy Information Administration.
“Diesel prices for Americans and, indeed, the world, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST! Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my greatest priority,” Trump posted.
However, experts suggested that the quantities involved – and the time it will take for the supplies to arrive in the US – is “too little, too late” to affect current high diesel prices, which observers have linked to challenging Republican party polling numbers before next month’s midterm elections.
US prices have surged by almost 70% since the start of the Iran war, to about $6.30 a gallon, according to American Automobile Association. In the UK, the average price of diesel climbed to a record £2 a litre earlier in October, and sat just below that mark on Friday.
Ashley Kelty, an energy analyst with the investment bank Panmure Liberum, said: “It is not going to have any impact on prices. The first amount [due to be shipped to the US] is so small.
“They are going to have to charter vessels, load them and transport the cargo to the US. That will take about three weeks – so we are pretty much at the end of the month and about a week before the midterms.”
The US Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, said on Sunday: “This is good for the American people … bringing these diesel prices down.”
However, Kelty said the diesel shipments would also cause complications in a global supply chain, including multinational companies having to work out which of its supplies originated from Russia and therefore might breach sanctions in other jurisdictions, including Europe.
The US Treasury suspended sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April as part of the deal, while keeping in place other sanctions on Russian products.
Zelenskyy described Trump’s deal as a “weak decision”, saying it would encourage Russia to keep attacking Ukraine, but Trump then blamed Kyiv’s strikes on Russian energy infrastructure for rising fuel prices. Trump said Ukraine neeeded “a new leader”.
On Sunday, Zelenskyy said he would be ready to stop hitting Russian oil refineries if Russia curbed its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
Trump later posted on Truth Social: “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it! Thank you for your attention to this matter.”
Maximilian Hess, the founder of the political risk consultancy Enmetena Advisory and a fellow at the Foreign Policy Research Institute, said: “It will not have any meaningful domestic US effect or international effect given its full terms are highly unlikely to be met as a result of the impact of Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian refining which have limited its diesel output.
“The whole point of the deal for Putin is that it fails, which he can blame on Ukraine and thus stoke tensions between Trump and Zelenskyy. Indeed, it’s already working.”

theguardian.com.title: ICE agent strikes man with vehicle during pursuit in Texas, officials say
theguardian.com.text:
An Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent driving a vehicle struck a man on Saturday while trying to pursue him and someone else in the Houston area, according to authorities.
The federal agency had been trying to pull over and arrest Jose Mendoza-Cervantes in north-west Harris county, Texas, when he and the victim, Miguel Parra-Hernandez, exited the vehicle, officials said.
Surveillance footage showed the officer chase Parra-Hernandez and then hit him with his car. Parra-Hernandez suffered a broken leg and was taken to a hospital, the Harris county sheriff’s office said.
In a statement, the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) that oversees ICE said the agency had been trying to arrest Mendoza-Cervantes after a judge had issued him a final order of removal from the United States.
Mendoza-Cervantes had been arrested four times for driving under the influence and arrested for unlawful possession of a firearm, the DHS statement added. He remained at large as of Saturday morning.
DHS did not address questions from the Guardian seeking the name of the officer who struck Parra-Hernandez and whether he was equipped with a body-worn camera, which ICE policy requires.
Parra-Hernandez’s hospitalization came with ICE facing criticism throughout Donald Trump’s second presidency for the agency’s aggressive arrest, detention and deportation tactics.
More than 30 people have died in 2026 during interactions with immigration officials, the Guardian reported in late September.
On Friday morning, a 72-year-old man shot an off-duty ICE official who was “intoxicated and agitated” and was accused of attacking the man and his daughter on their property in Fresno, California.
On Thursday, in New York City, an ICE agent shot a man who was in his vehicle with a five-year-old child, mayor Zohran Mamdani said in a statement.
Markwayne Mullin, the Trump administration’s homeland security secretary, later said on CBS’s Face the Nation that ICE took the time to learn the “pattern of life” of the man shot in New York on Thursday – but “we didn’t know the five-year-old was in the vehicle”.
The Harris county precinct 4 commissioner, Lesley Briones, alluded to those various other cases in a statement on Saturday, saying: “Under the Trump administration, ICE has brought chaos and destruction to communities across our country.”
Briones described herself as “horrified” after Parra-Hernandez’s case on Saturday and called for ICE to release any relevant video to the sheriff’s office.
DHS did not immediately respond to the Guardian when asked for comment on Sunday.

theguardian.com.title: Thousands without power in Florida and Alabama as Isaias moves north
theguardian.com.text:
As what was left of Hurricane Isaias moved north on Sunday, bringing moderate to heavy rainfall across the central Appalachians and the mid-Atlantic region, nearly 396,000 customers across the Florida Panhandle and southern Alabama remained without power.
Heavy rainfall associated with the storm could bring isolated flash flooding and strong wind gusts and remain a threat across the south-eastern US, especially near the southern Appalachians, according to the National Weather Service (NWS). That could bring scattered power outages and downed trees and power lines. Life-threatening surf and rip current conditions were expected to continue along the Gulf and south-eastern Atlantic coasts.
According to the National Weather Service, parts of the Carolinas and Virginia, including Raleigh, Richmond and Washington DC were under threat of tornadoes on Sunday.
At least four deaths were linked to the storm, including two people killed when trees fell on to homes in Florida and Alabama. Forecasters warned that flooding could stretch into the Appalachians.
Isaias came ashore as a category 2 hurricane on Friday near Destin, Florida, a Gulf Coast vacation spot filled with high-rises and tourist shops. This has been the first hurricane to make landfall in the continental US in two years, since Milton struck western Florida in October 2024.
Despite warnings of storm surges ahead of the storm, several major routes along the coast were open by daybreak on Saturday and free of downed trees and power lines typically seen after major hurricanes.
Hurricane-force winds in the Florida Panhandle blew the roof off a Pensacola hotel, and the city’s mayor said the airport “took some damage”. The storm flattened a boathouse in Destin and ripped away part of the facade of a high-rise in Panama City Beach.
In Florida’s Escambia county, sheriff Chip Simmons said a woman was killed when a tree fell on her home – and a man died of carbon monoxide fumes from a generator running in his garage. Four of the man’s family members, ranging in age from four to 72, were treated but were expected to survive, the sheriff said.
The first hurricane of the Atlantic season, Isaias roared farther into Alabama with tropical-force winds.
One person died when a tree fell on a house in Birmingham, the city’s fire chief, Cory Moon, said. A second storm-related death in Alabama was attributed to a motor vehicle crash involving a downed tree in Barbour county, said Josh Johnson of the state’s emergency management agency.
Along Alabama’s Gulf coast, authorities in Mobile reported numerous downed trees and power lines.
Donald Trump approved an emergency declaration for Georgia after the president did the same for Florida and Alabama, allowing for federal aid.
The US Energy Department authorized emergency exchanges of crude oil from the nation’s strategic petroleum reserve to address disruptions in supply because of the storm.
The NWS said parts of Georgia and the Carolinas could see heavy rain capable of causing flash floods.
Meanwhile, in the Pacific, Simon strengthened to 155mph (250kph), only just below the threshold for becoming a category 5 storm, as it approached Mexico’s coast. Simon was expected to bring heavy rainfall beginning on Sunday to parts of south-western Mexico with life-threatening flooding and mudslides.
Forecasters say that conditions brought by Simon are spreading northward along a stretch of coastline that includes Puerto Vallarta. Rain could average 8-16in over sectors of south-western Mexico, with as much as 30in possible in places across Michoacán, Colima and Jalisco through Monday.
A woman, a man and their dog in Burke county, North Carolina, were rescued on the Catawba River after their camping trip was overflown by the rising water brought by remnants of Simon that caught them off guard.
Tropical storm Rachel was also expected to bring heavy winds and rain to northern Mexico and southern California. The National Weather Service has issued a flash flood warning in parts of San Diego, Riverside and Imperial counties. Officials issued mandatory evacuation orders for some residents in the Long Beach peninsula through Tuesday.
Eight buildings have been red-tagged, or deemed unsafe to enter, and one has been yellow-tagged amid conditions from Rachel. Long Beach officials have provided about 11,000 sandbags for the storm to protect homes from the rising tide.

theguardian.com.title: Houthi attack on Riyadh airport forces swift rethink of Trump’s new strategy
theguardian.com.text:
The reckless missile attack on King Khalid international airport in Riyadh on Saturday did not just export the death and misery inside Yemen to Saudi Arabia, it also left Donald Trump forced to reconsider his diplomatic and political strategy designed to take him into the midterm elections next month.
The US president’s plan had only been unveiled on Friday. He said it was the result of “a world problem” – spiralling diesel prices – which he blamed on Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s attacks on Russian oil refineries. He was going to keep the political temperature down on his war of choice in Iran and its spillover in Yemen until after the midterms.
In pursuit of this strategy, he claimed the Iranian blockade in the strait of Hormuz was in effect broken, producing figures on daily oil barrel exports to assuage the markets. As a further insurance he also claimed it was impossible to negotiate with the Iranians since there was no single leadership in Tehran.
Saudi Arabia, in conjunction with Turkey, and Pakistan, were largely to be left to sort out the Houthis along the Red Sea. The fate of Yemen, the poorest country in the world according to the International Monetary Fund, was not going to shift votes in Kansas or Alaska.
Now, after the Riyadh airport attack, it is doubtful, for a basket of reasons, that this anyway threadbare strategy, largely born of desperation, can hold.
For all the talk of the Gulf becoming responsible for its own security, it is doubtful that Saudi Arabia can be left to fend for itself after the carnage in Riyadh. One of the the 12 dead is an American and there may be more among the severely injured. Something is clearly wrong with Saudi defences since the Houthis are firing rockets from 500 miles away, and they are reaching their target too often.
The US has had a unilateral ceasefire with the Houthis since 2025, and once the hostilities between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis recommenced in the summer, the pact was quietly renewed. Trump has twice rejected Saudi appeals for help. Can he spurn them three times? The pressure to act as allies are expected to may prove overwhelming.
But “the blame Zelenskyy, trade with Russia” strategy is anyway unlikely to work. The amount of additional diesel Vladimir Putin will put on the market is not enough to bring down prices at the pump. Russia accounted for about 12% of global diesel shipped by sea. Exports have fallen by about a third, according to calculations by the Center for Research on Energy and Clean Air.
The deal has also reawakened Europe’s worst fears about Trump’s relationship with Russia only weeks after Congress had passed a sanctions package against Moscow authorising Trump to penalise buyers of Russian energy.
Europeans know full well that the inflation problem helping to drive populism is caused by the Iran war and not by Zelenskyy’s tactics. The only question is who will say so. The former UK Conservative prime minister Boris Johnson did not hold back, writing: “It is sickening that the USA is now lifting sanctions on Russian fuel, and transparently ridiculous to blame Ukraine for the spike in prices that obviously began with the closure of the strait of Hormuz. Putin is murdering innocent Ukrainian civilians every day. The Ukrainians are fighting for their lives. And yet the White House is apparently determined to force American drivers to bankroll Putin’s slaughter.”
The German education minister and a member of the CDU, Karin Prien, said: “For a few litres of diesel. What moral bankruptcy.”
Mark Rutte, the Nato secretary general and Trump ally, will this week travel to Estonia, one of the countries most supportive of Ukraine. He will have some explaining to do. Estonia’s foreign minister, Margus Tsahkna, vowed that EU foreign ministers on Monday will impose the biggest package of sanctions in its history, and he, along with Sweden, now wants to revisit using frozen Russian assets to help Ukraine.
What is worse, it looks as if the political damage to the Republicans caused by the Iran war is irrecoverable. Polls show the ship has sailed. The war has already been weaponised as a pocketbook issue by every Democratic candidate in every TV debate. Republican candidates, challenged to disown the war, are scrambling for the relative safety of identity politics.
The Iranians are also trying to maximise the damage they cause in the strait of Hormuz, countering the Trump narrative that the blockade has been broken. Scenes of tankers on fire are proliferating.
So Trump post-Riyadh needs to rethink. He can rejoin the war against the Houthis, ending the unilateral US ceasefire, but, if so, he knows from experience this will be costly. The first three weeks of the war against Iran cost $1bn a day. Many of the US president’s advisers say he may as well also attack Iran, the Houthis’ backers, as Tehran expects him to do. The Iranian military nevertheless still believes it has escalation dominance, and what happened in Riyadh can be repeated across the Gulf.
The alternative is that his team can negotiate discreetly and indirectly with Tehran as is occurring in Doha. Some Iranians are urging their leadership to seize the chance, arguing Trump is uniquely vulnerable in the run-up to the midterms.
A deal could be done, including on uranium enrichment, but it would not be palatable for the US – or for the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu’s re-election chances.
China and Russia are trying to sort out the Houthis diplomatically, but the Houthi objectives are broadening, while the south of Yemen is split about its future inside the country, a division that harms the country’s ability to be the ground component that Saudi Arabia needs to supplement its air-power dominance. Taiz, the third city of Yemen, is struggling to overcome a Houthi siege. The Saudis can deliver retribution, but retribution is not a solution to a decade-long civil war.
So for the moment the twin Trump strategy – to park the Iran and Yemen conflicts while blaming Zelenskyy – is now so transparent, so morally craven, and in its own terms so ineffective, that it looks unsustainable. The only question is whether the strategy will be jettisoned by the president or instead just rejected by the American people at the ballot box.

lemonde.fr/en.title: 'We are still in the Middle Ages': Women on sexual violence in e-sports
lemonde.fr/en.text:
In the close-knit world of e-sports, the sudden disappearance of Corentin M., known online as Chreak, did not go unnoticed. Corentin M., 28, a streamer and commentator for League of Legends (LoL) competitions was publicly accused of rape by two women at the end of June, and then suspended by his employer, the broadcaster OTP. The statement announcing his suspension cited allegations "of extreme seriousness."
Several complaints were filed against Corentin M, who was charged with rape in July, French prosecutors confirmed to Le Monde. He has been placed under conditional release and remains innocent until proven guilty. His lawyer, Benjamin Bohbot, said his client "denies the allegations against him."
The case is the latest in a long list of cases of gender-based and sexual violence that have in recent years rocked the world of competitive video gaming, a scene that is particularly young and male-dominated. Yet these scandals have not led to any genuine industry-wide reckoning on the issue.
Le Monde spoke with around 20 women professionals in the French e-sports sector who denounced – most often under the condition of anonymity for fear of retaliation in their professional lives – acts of violence committed by men: physical and psychological pressure, sexual assault, revenge porn, sexual harassment, sexist cyberbullying and more. All said they had also heard of other such incidents among their peers. "We are still in the Middle Ages when it comes to how women are treated in this industry," said one of them, Khorée, an e-sports consultant.

lemonde.fr/en.title: From farms to high schools, France is a nation on edge
lemonde.fr/en.text:
It is a country on edge, exhausted. Its people are at their wits' end, burned out and fraying. After an endless summer marked by heatwaves and wildfires, France is waking up as if from a bad dream, sweating, feverish and restless. Overwhelmed by the accumulation of crises and mounting anxieties that hint at the beginnings of a perfect storm, the country is on the brink between revolt and resignation, like a patient gripped by catatonia.
"Going on strike or joining a protest has become a luxury. You need to be able to afford to miss a day's work," said Jérémie, a 31-year-old warehouse worker, his eyes fixed on the meter at the Intermarché gas station in Caulnes, Brittany. (People cited by their first name did not want to give their full name.) He watched the pump carefully to make sure he did not go over €30, the maximum he was allowing himself at the moment. Every day, Jérémie drives about 100 kilometers. "When you live in the countryside, it's impossible to get by without a car," he said. "Every trip is an investment."
The accumulation of crises is unprecedented: heatwaves devastating agriculture, out-of-control debt, soaring interest rates, a growing cost of living, housing shortages, rising unemployment, a demoralized civil service, anger among high school students... Anywhere one looks, the future appears bleak and menacing. On top of an accelerating climate crisis for which the country is unprepared, a financial crisis and a surge in unemployment due to the rapid advances in artificial intelligence (AI) could hit in the very near future. In all these areas, France seems to be falling behind, and its government has no solutions. The country is losing its footing.

lemonde.fr/en.title: Netanyahu seeks probe into Israeli whistleblowers featured in Gaza war documentary
lemonde.fr/en.text:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu called on Sunday, October 11, for an investigation into the anonymous sources featured in the award-winning Gaza war documentary NAZA. The film is based on testimony from 24 unnamed Israeli military whistleblowers who accuse the army of killing numerous civilians in Gaza with the use of AI-powered targeting systems.
"Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu this evening asked the chief of staff of the Israeli army, the head of the Shin Bet [Israel's domestic intelligence service], and the state attorney to open a thorough investigation targeting the participants in the film NAZA and to prosecute them," Netanyahu's office said in a statement.
NAZA takes its name from the Israeli military term for civilian casualties expected in airstrikes, an abbreviated form of the Hebrew phrase for "collateral damage." Awarded a special jury prize at the Venice Film Festival, the film received a historic 25-minute standing ovation, but it has triggered a political storm in Israel.
"This film tells a false, misleading and biased story that defames the State of Israel and the army around the world," Netanyahu said, according to the statement. He has previously declared his intention to back legislation to strip citizenship from people who "defame" soldiers.
The Israeli army, for its part, has "categorically" rejected the accusations contained in the film, expressing doubts about the reliability of the anonymous contributors.

lemonde.fr/en.title: Is it ever a good idea to... wear a dark suit-shirt-tie combination?
lemonde.fr/en.text:
Some columns write themselves, buoyed by a sly, knowing laugh, a healthy dose of snobbery, and the confidence that comes from flattering the majority at the expense of a defenseless minority. Others, however, require you to dive in with courage and honesty. As we prepare to scrutinize our icon – and the people's icon – we will need all of the above.
After watching Zinédine Zidane's first matches as head coach of the French national football team, our sense of duty compels us to break with the chorus of unanimous praise and speak plainly. On the French bench, the world champion wore a midnight blue suit, a midnight blue tie and a midnight blue shirt. Suffice it to say, there was something "off" – especially when it came to the shirt.
Brutally and inelegantly, the shirt swallowed the tie and turned our hero's outfit into a strange monochromatic block, lacking in contrast or depth. With just one poorly chosen piece, the once radiant player suddenly became a rather austere, if not downright somber, coach – at least in terms of style.
This is the perfect opportunity to reiterate how perilous – if not downright impossible – it is to wear dark shirts with a suit. Beyond aesthetics, they too often signal a quest for distinction and individuality that comes across as a cry for help. Much like the infamous pairing of a suit with white sneakers, the dark suit-tie-shirt combo carries the ultimate risk of appearing "falsely cool."
As this promising new chapter at the head of the French team begins, allow us, dear Zidane, to suggest that you place your trust in your grace, charisma, natural elegance and eternal youth by quickly swapping your navy blue shirt for a garment worthy of you: a beautiful white or sky-blue poplin shirt, for example!

lemonde.fr/en.title: 'Netanyahu's diatribes against antisemitism aim above all to silence his critics'
lemonde.fr/en.text:
"Netanyahu is good for the Jews." Under this slogan in 1995-96, Benjamin Netanyahu, then leader of Likud, the main opposition party in Israel, campaigned against the governments of Labor prime minister Yitzhak Rabin (1922-1995), and then of Shimon Peres (1923-2016), who were, at that time, engaged in a peace process with the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO). No Israeli leader before him had dared claim that he was "good for the Jews" and that his rivals were not.
Yet the ambitious Netanyahu, then in his thirties, brought an unprecedented virulence to Israeli debate, stepping up the lies, false equivalencies and provocations to discredit the septuagenarians Rabin and Peres. He helped fuel a climate of hatred that, in November 1995, led to the assassination of Rabin by a fanatic supporter of settlement in the West Bank. Far from moderating his rhetoric after such a tragedy, Netanyahu intensified his attacks on Peres, narrowly winning the May 1996 elections.
Slander, slander and slander again
Since that first electoral victory, Netanyahu governed Israel for more than 19 years in total. This unmatched longevity at the helm of Israel was sustained by ever more unbridled brutality, not only against the Israeli opposition, but also against all established institutions – judiciary, police, or press – that could still put a cap on the prime minister's ambitions.
Slander, slander, and slander again became for Netanyahu not only a reflex, but a policy, both in Israel and on the international stage. In the United States, the prime minister chose to ally himself with "Christian Zionists," who support resettlement of Palestinian territories, rather than with the Jewish community, which has mostly supported compromise with the PLO. For Netanyahu, it hardly matters that major American figures among the "Christian Zionists" have caused controversy with their antisemitic outbursts; he prefers their fervent but unconditional support, even if it means alienating part of the Jewish diaspora.

lemonde.fr/en.title: Raphaël Glucksmann wins French center-left presidential primary
lemonde.fr/en.text:
MEP Raphaël Glucksmann was, on Sunday, October 11, elected the center-left candidate for next year's French presidential elections, the vote's organizers said, winning comfortably in the first round. Glucksmann, 46, who leads the center-left Place Publique party, won 66% of the 120,787 votes cast in the primary.
Socialist Party leader Olivier Faure was a distant second with 14% of the vote, and the other three candidates scored less than 10%. "This result says something powerful," Glucksmann posted on X. "A left that is faithful to its values can unite, govern and win."
Glucksmann presents himself as a break from the policies of French President Emmanuel Macron and one who can beat the far right. But he is currently polling at between nine and 14%, well behind the frontrunner, far-right candidate Marine Le Pen.
He also trails center-right contender Edouard Philippe, who served as prime minister under Macron, and hard-left veteran Jean-Luc Mélenchon, whose radical left-wing party, La France Insoumise, boycotted the primary.
Rights campaigner
When, in August, Glucksmann announced his intention to run for the presidency, he distanced himself from what he called "classical political" circles. Instead, he emphasized his past work abroad, in the aftermath of genocide in Rwanda and as a former adviser to the anti-Moscow former Georgian president Mikheil Saakashvili.
Elected to the European Parliament in 2019, Glucksmann's work there has also focused on human rights and he has been a staunch defender of Ukraine. While Glucksmann strikes a more reformist and centrist tone than the Socialist Party, he has cooperated with them in the past, presenting joint electoral lists. And now, it is in his interest to work with the venerable party and benefit from its campaign machine.
However, he has ruled out any cooperation with Melenchon, who is still the leading contender on the left.
His critics say he is "too Parisian," too detached from the realities of everyday French people to be a credible candidate. In response, he underlines his past human rights work in conflict zones such as Rwanda. "My outlook and my view of the world were not forged in Davos or Washington, but in places whose desolation I'm not sure you can even begin to fathom," he has said.
During his campaigning across France this summer, he put forward a program rooted in the left that tries to reconcile ecological transition with social progress. The first round of France's presidential election is set to take place on Sunday, April 18, with the second round set two weeks later on May 2.

lemonde.fr/en.title: Poland detains suspect in alleged assassination attempt on prime minister
lemonde.fr/en.text:
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Sunday, October 11, that a man accused of plotting an assassination attack against him and the defense minister had been detained, following an earlier announcement of suspected threats from the interior ministry. "The man threatening an attack has been detained," Tusk wrote on X, praising the police for their "swift and decisive action." The arrest was also confirmed on X by Polish Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski.
Earlier, the interior ministry said Tusk and Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz may have been targeted by assassination attempts. A "report about a potential assassination attempt on Prime Minister Donald Tusk, as well as on Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Defense Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz, was transmitted to the police via the State Protection Service (SOP)," interior ministry spokeswoman Karolina Galecka said at a press briefing.
Earlier on Sunday, the ministry ordered authorities to take action "in connection with the information received by (the police) concerning a possible assassination attempt on the prime minister (...) as well as the deputy prime minister," who is also defense minister, Galecka wrote on X. Members of the police, state protection service (SOP) and internal security agency were present at the meeting Sunday.
"We are treating this matter as deadly serious," a spokesperson for the minister-coordinator of special services, Jacek Dobrzynski, told journalists afterwards. "Month by month, year by year, more and more various threats and menacing messages reach the police, SOP, and the services concerning Poland and Poles," he said, adding that "in this case we are talking about a strong likelihood that these threats could actually be carried out."
Poland, a NATO and EU member country, has been on high alert following multiple stabbing attacks in the last week, which Tusk on Thursday denounced as a "cult of violence."

lemonde.fr/en.title: Trump announces Ukraine-Russia 'energy ceasefire,' but Kyiv reports fresh strikes
lemonde.fr/en.text:
US President Donald Trump sowed confusion on Sunday, October 11, announcing an "energy ceasefire" between Ukraine and Russia that sparked astonishment in Kyiv, silence from Moscow and support from Ukraine's Western allies.
Yet the ceasefire appeared shaky at best as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia struck multiple Ukrainian power plants on Sunday, including one in the capital and another in Kharkiv, leading to power outages and outrage.
Trump's announcement came two days after he declared a temporary easing of US sanctions on Russian diesel, prompting outrage by European allies and Kyiv, who said it would only embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin. "Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine," Trump said early Sunday on Truth Social. "Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!"
Zelensky appeared to express surprise at the announcement, saying he was seeking further details, but added that "Ukraine supports the ceasefire, and it is important that Russia support it as well." Russia has yet to confirm its agreement.
Zelensky later said that multiple Ukrainian power stations had been hit and that "Ukrainian skies have been infested with Russian 'shaheds' all day," referring to a type of drone originally designed by Iran that is now extensively used by Russia.
'Up to our people'
Ever since it launched a full-scale invasion of its neighbor in 2022, Russia has systematically hit Ukrainian energy infrastructure, leading to energy and heating shortages – prompting Ukraine to hit back at Russian oil refineries it says fund the war. More recently, Trump's war in Iran has led to oil shortages and ensuing price spikes, creating major headwinds for his Republican Party ahead of midterm elections early next month.
The ceasefire appeared to garner support on Sunday from Ukraine's key western allies, including the UK, France, Canada and the European Commission. Several leaders called on Russia to uphold the deal. However, that support was in contrast to broad criticism of the US-Russia diesel deal earlier in the week, which has led to mounting tensions between Trump and Zelensky.
Zelensky said the diesel deal was a "weak decision," while several of Ukraine's European allies expressed outrage and pledged to increase pressure on Moscow. Seven US senators – including four Republicans – released a statement Sunday blasting the diesel deal with Russia, saying it was illegal.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney added to the chorus on Sunday after a call with Zelensky, saying the diesel deal "is in direct opposition to the efforts of Ukraine, Canada and our allies to create peace and stability in Europe."
Support for Zelensky
Asked about the criticism on Saturday, Trump said it was "time for Ukraine to get a new president" who would finally settle the war.
Zelensky pushed back, telling ABC News that "it's up to our society, up to our people to choose one or another leader." He said that fuel prices were rising because of the war in the Middle East and the blocked Strait of Hormuz. "Everybody understands it," he said.
Germany's foreign minister said Sunday that Berlin continued to "fully support" Zelensky. "Europe needs stability and that means that we are very clearly continuing to stay by the side of Ukraine and its government," Johann Wadephul said in Berlin.
EU chief Ursula von der Leyen also backed the Ukrainian leader "as he leads the fight for his people's freedom." UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham also said his country "strongly supports President Trump's call today for a sustained energy ceasefire to start now."

lemonde.fr/en.title: 'The Manchester City case shows that football's worst excesses only spark a reaction once they are over'
lemonde.fr/en.text:
The wait was extremely long, but eight years after an investigation began in the wake of the "Football Leaks" revelations, the verdict delivered a shockwave that rattled two kingdoms: the Premier League and the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Owned since 2008 by Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, vice president and deputy prime minister of the UAE, Manchester City was found guilty by an independent commission of 114 out of the 115 financial regulation violations alleged by the Premier League for the 2009-2018 period, the league announced on September 29.
An arsenal of fraud, including fictitious contracts, concealed payments, and transfers via shell companies, was used to disguise the club's true finances. Heavily subsidized by Abu Dhabi, Manchester City's revenues were inflated and its expenses understated by as much as €1 billion.
The scale of this system exposes the club to penalties that are unlikely to be light: hefty fines, stripping of titles, points deductions, or even relegation. The case, still far from resolution, nevertheless raises questions beyond just City itself.
The Premier League itself contributed to the damage it must now punish – after having benefited from it. The rise of the Sky Blues – eight-time English champions since 2008 and Champions League winners in 2023 – served the Premier League's interests, while disadvantaging other clubs. Today, the reputation of the world's most prestigious and wealthiest national league is discredited, its image tarnished.
Football as a tool
The Premier League's indulgence toward the most powerful investors was already illustrated by the case of Chelsea, acquired by oligarch Roman Abramovich in 2003. It took nearly 20 years and the Russian invasion of Ukraine for the authorities – public and sporting – to finally view the source of his wealth as problematic and force him out.
Even strengthened procedures for vetting club takeover candidates were powerless to prevent the acquisition of Newcastle United by the Saudi sovereign wealth fund, the Public Investment Fund, in 2021, turning Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman into a "prince charming" in the eyes of Geordie supporters. No other national competition has lent itself so much to these image-laundering and influence operations by autocratic regimes and unsavory billionaires using football as a vehicle.

lemonde.fr/en.title: Saudi Arabia weighs response after Houthi attack on Riyadh, deadliest in a decade
lemonde.fr/en.text:
Saudi Arabia has just suffered its deadliest attack in a decade. At least 12 people were killed – Saudis and foreigners, including an American – and at least 309 others were wounded, including a French woman, after a missile fired by Yemen's Houthis struck a terminal at King Khalid Airport in Riyadh around 3 pm on Saturday, October 10. Hit in the heart of its capital, Saudi Arabia now has to choose how to respond.
Since the Saudi-led coalition's announcement on Monday, October 5, of aerial support for "Operation Dawn of Yemen," the Yemeni government forces' mission against the Iranian-backed Houthi movement, Saudi airports have been threatened or targeted by missiles and drones fired from across the kingdom's southern border almost daily.
The Houthi movement has a clear strategy: If no aircraft can land at the airport in Yemen's capital Sanaa, the same should apply in Saudi Arabia. A blockade for a bloc. Several people have been killed in recent days, including a Saudia Airlines captain, and multiple airports, such as those in Abha, Jizan and Najran, have been damaged. Air traffic has been severely disrupted.

lemonde.fr/en.title: How FIFA broke its own rules to boost the DRC's chances of World Cup qualification
lemonde.fr/en.text:
It is a sensitive issue that FIFA, the governing body of international football, buried for political reasons. According to internal documents reviewed by Le Monde, the organization's leadership concealed the ineligibility of a player on the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) national team who played in several qualifying matches for the 2026 World Cup. In disregard of its own regulations and of precedent, FIFA neglected to impose disciplinary sanctions and allowed the Congolese team to continue its campaign toward the tournament. The Leopards eventually qualified and were eliminated by England in the round of 16.
The new case exposes the interventionist approach of FIFA leadership, and particularly of its president, Gianni Infantino, at the risk of overstepping established rules and sporting integrity. In that respect, it is reminiscent of the overturning of US forward Folarin Balogun's red card against Bosnia and Herzegovina in the round of 16 of the World Cup, after US President Donald Trump put direct pressure on Infantino, in blatant disregard for fair play.
The Italian-Swiss leader, who is seeking a third term as FIFA president in an election set for March 18, 2027, has already been weakened by his ultimately abandoned plan to create a commercial company open to private investors. Since that uproar, Infantino has been fighting for his political survival and counting his supporters, particularly within the Confederation of African Football (CAF), which includes 54 of FIFA's 211 member countries. He attended a CAF "strategic conference," dedicated to the future of African football, in Cape Verde from October 7 to 9.

lemonde.fr/en.title: Pope Leo XIV says he will undergo surgery to remove nodule in lung
lemonde.fr/en.text:
Pope Leo XIV announced Sunday, October 11, he will undergo surgery in the coming days to remove a nodular lesion on his lung that was recently discovered during medical checks. The 71-year-old pope said the nodule was found at an early stage and was "circumscribed" or well-localized. The Vatican later said Leo would undergo surgery in the first days of the week, with an expected recovery time of a week.
The American pope made the announcement during his Sunday noon blessing. He thanked the crowd for their closeness and entrusted himself to their prayers.
A lung nodule is a small abnormal area measuring less than 3 centimeters that sometimes appears on a CT scan of the chest or abdomen, according to the American Cancer Society. Often, the scans are done to investigate trauma or a lung infection, unrelated to a lung cancer screening.
Leo has no previously known health problems and is considered physically active, with weekly tennis games and swimming at the papal summer retreat in Castel Gandolfo.
The pope has a major trip planned November 6-17 to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. It's unclear whether the planned surgery and recovery would affect the itinerary, but Leo said earlier in his remarks Sunday that he planned to go.
In his remarks, delivered in Italian, Leo said during a recent medical check, "doctors found a small, localized nodule in my lung. It was detected at a very early stage and is circumscribed. The doctors believe it's best to take action, so, following their advice, I've decided to have surgery to remove it."
"The surgery is already scheduled for the coming days. Thank you for your spiritual support, and I entrust myself to your prayers," he said.
Leo is expected to undergo surgery at Rome's Gemelli hospital, where Francis and popes before him were treated and where there is a special apartment for pontiffs.
Leo's predecessor, Pope Francis, died April 21, 2025, of a stroke following a long hospitalization brought on by a respiratory crisis that developed into double pneumonia. Francis suffered from chronic lung disease and had part of one lung removed as a young man.

lemonde.fr/en.title: At least 139 die off Djibouti as boat attempting to reach Yemen sinks, UN says
lemonde.fr/en.text:
At least 139 migrants died and 84 went missing when an overcrowded boat sank while heading from Djibouti to Yemen, a UN agency said Sunday, October 11. The vessel was carrying 305 people, most of them Ethiopian, when it capsized north of the Djibouti town of Obock overnight on October 8-9, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said in a statement.
"Survivors told me that the boat started to sink backwards as soon as they got in it," Alexandre Coissac, IOM chief of mission in Djibouti, told Agence France-Presse. "This is a devastating loss of life," he said earlier in the statement. "Our thoughts are with the survivors and the families who have lost loved ones or remain without news of their relatives."
The IOM gave an initial toll of 109 dead and 116 missing, and revised it to 139 dead and 84 missing in a later statement after more bodies were recovered. Among the 109 bodies earlier recovered were 52 men, 42 women and 15 children – nine girls and six boys – the initial statement said.
Eighty-two people survived the shipwreck, all Ethiopian nationals, according to the updated toll. The IOM said it was assisting 64 survivors at a migrant centre in Obock.
"This tragedy is a stark reminder of the dangers faced by migrants along this migration corridor as they seek economic opportunities" by trying to cross the Bab al-Mandeb Strait to Yemen and then reach Gulf countries, Coissac said. He said he had spoken to one survivor of the wreck who came from the Tigray region of northern Ethiopia, where rebels are battling the federal government in a recent flare-up of violence.
"Poverty, insecurity and the growing impacts of climate change drive many to undertake this journey, despite mounting instability across the Middle East," the IOM said. "Djiboutian authorities are continuing search and rescue operations as fears grow for those still missing." It called it "one of the deadliest shipwrecks recorded" on the route.
IOM spokesman Kennedy Omondi Okoth told AFP this week that 178,000 people had arrived in Djibouti from Ethiopia from January to October this year. Okoth said most of the people attempting the journey were from Ethiopia or Somalia. He said many of them were ending up "stranded" in Djibouti.
Since September 10, the IOM has detected more than 20,000 crossings to Djibouti from Ethiopia, despite a surge in conflict in Yemen. The country is stricken by fighting between the Saudi-backed government and Tehran-backed Houthi rebels, who have joined in the regional conflict involving the US and its allies against Iran.
Coissac said 150 of the people on the boat that sank off Djibouti had previously been turned back from Yemen but had attempted the crossing again.
In 2025, more than 900 migrants died or went missing along the sea route to Yemen and the number attempting the journey increased by 18%, the IOM said. A shipwreck in March 2026 left nine people dead and 45 missing.
"No one gets into a boat like that unless they believe there is no other safe way," said IOM Director General Amy Pope in a statement. "We cannot keep treating these deaths as normal. Safe and legal pathways save lives. I am asking governments and donors to act before the next boat goes down." The IOM urged "donors and partners to strengthen support for Djibouti's response, including search and rescue operations and life-saving assistance."
The African Union Commission chairman expressed his "profound sorrow over the tragic loss of life" in a statement. Mahmoud Ali Youssouf also stressed the urgent need to "address the root causes of irregular migration, combat migrant smuggling and trafficking in persons, and promote safe, orderly and regular migration."
Update on October 11 at 2:10 pm: The IMO revised the number of people on the capsized boat to 305, after initially stating that 350 people were aboard.

lemonde.fr/en.title: Indian 'cockroach' leaders released, call for more protests
lemonde.fr/en.text:
Leaders of India's online "cockroach" movement pledged on Sunday, October 11, to continue their campaign against the election commissioner, hours after they were released from detention as authorities sought to thwart a major demonstration.
The rally planned for Saturday in the capital New Delhi came after weeks of opposition mobilization following allegations of misconduct during a nationwide voter roll revision that critics say could benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling party. The Election Commission of India, which oversees the voting process in the world's most populous nation, has denied wrongdoing.
Abhijeet Dipke, founder of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) protest movement, and two other leaders were detained on Saturday before they could disembark from their flight in Delhi ahead of the planned demonstration. Thousands of protesters were also detained, according to the youth-led group and media reports.
"We will not back down," CJP co-convenor Saurav Das said at a news conference in Delhi after his release from detention. "We urge people to come out and carry out peaceful protests," he added, vowing to continue until Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar resigns.
In July, protests organised by the CJP over exam irregularities forced the resignation of the education minister, marking a rare climbdown by Modi's administration.
Ahead of Saturday's rally, authorities mounted a sweeping security operation across the capital, shutting down metro stations and more than 200 trains while imposing a ban on public gatherings in several areas. The protest leaders were released on the condition that they would maintain "peace for one year," Ratna Singh, the CJP's head lawyer, said in a social media post.
'Important to show up'
The Supreme Court, hearing petitions challenging the detentions and other security measures, directed the authorities on Sunday to ensure protesters gathering peacefully are not detained illegally. "Detention shall only be after following a legal procedure," Justice Joymalya Bagchi said in oral remarks. The court also ordered authorities to ensure there was no disruption to internet connectivity after mobile access was temporarily shut down around the Jantar Mantar protest site on Saturday.
Authorities have not commented on the detentions.
In a social media post soon after his release, Dipke took aim at Modi, who "as PM, is an embarrassment to India," he said. "Never has this country seen a bigger coward and bully."
The youth movement has emerged as one of the most significant political challenges to Modi during his third term in power, winning millions of followers on social media since it was launched in May as a satirical party.
On Sunday, an Agence France-Presse reporter saw dozens of people, including journalists, detained at three locations near Jantar Mantar, which remained fortified. "I was detained for 10 hours yesterday," said Aarti, 37, who gave only one name. "I have come again today because it is important to show up."
'Anger'
The revision of voter rolls at the center of the protest campaign resulted in more than 133 million names being removed from electoral lists, according to media reports. Critics say the revision has disproportionately affected minorities, particularly Muslims, potentially benefiting Modi's Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party. Election authorities say the revision was aimed at eliminating duplicate, deceased and fraudulent entries.
The detention of protesters on Saturday triggered sharp criticism and accusations that Modi's government was stifling dissent. The UN human rights office called for the immediate and unconditional release of all those "arbitrarily detained" in Delhi.
Rahul Gandhi of the opposition Congress party has also vowed to press ahead with protests against the election commission despite the crackdown. Gandhi said his party "and the youth of the country will once again take to the streets in large numbers" on Monday. "The more Modi and his government crack down, the more the anger of Gen Z and students will grow," he said.

spiegel.de/international.title: Three Years of the Gaza War through the Eyes of Soldiers: "The Rule Was: 'Shoot Everyone You See'"
spiegel.de/international.text:
DER SPIEGEL spoke to 10 Israelis who served in the Gaza Strip after the Hamas terror attack of October 7, 2023, remotely piloted drones or selected targets for airstrikes. The Israeli organization Breaking the Silence , which collects testimonials from soldiers about misconduct and crimes committed by the military, facilitated contact with some of them. DER SPIEGEL checked all the statements as thoroughly as possible, cross-referencing them with other accounts and with independently verifiable information, and considers them credible.
All the soldiers except one chose to remain anonymous. Their units and personal details cannot be disclosed either because of the potential negative consequences. Most refuse to serve in Gaza again, though one was recently redeployed there just a few weeks ago. A ceasefire has been in effect in Gaza for a year, but the Israeli military still occupies around two-thirds of the territory and regularly strikes targets in Gaza.
David, infantry reservist: “My unit killed many people”
David served as a reservist in an infantry unit and was deployed in central Gaza and Khan Younis for several months from October 2023 onward.
I knew from the start that this war was going to be bad. But I couldn’t imagine how bad. And I couldn’t imagine how long it would last, either. A month at most, I thought. That this war would go on for years – that seemed impossible. And then there was the scale of the destruction. From the perspective of an individual soldier, it even makes sense. Is one building the tallest in our sector? We destroy it because it could pose a threat. But then the next-tallest building becomes the tallest, and so it goes on until everything is destroyed. At first, we were told to destroy individual buildings. Later, we were assigned an entire area.
DER SPIEGEL relies on support from its readers. To enjoy the rest of this story, please consider signing up for a subscription to The German View, our English-language channel on Substack. Our Substack channel can be found here . Alternatively, you can sign up for a SPIEGEL+ subscription below.
When I returned to Gaza in 2025, there was nothing but rubble for miles. Officially, the aim was to create a "buffer zone.” But once I heard senior officers say: The Arabs have to be punished. They have to understand that we are taking more and more of their land and pushing them farther and farther back.

welt.de.title: „Bitte ‌sagen Sie Putin …“ – Selenskyj bietet unter einer Bedingung Neuwahlen in der Ukraine an
welt.de.text: Der ukrainische Präsident Wolodymyr Selenskyj hat sich offen für Neuwahlen in seinem Land gezeigt – unter der Bedingung einer 60-tägigen ‌vollständigen Waffenruhe mit Russland. „Bitte ‌sagen Sie Putin, er soll uns zwei Monate, 60 Tage völlige Feuerpause geben, 60 Tage, und wir werden Wahlen organisieren“, sagte Selenskyj an den US-Präsidenten Donald Trump gerichtet. Letztlich liege die Entscheidung über ihre Führung allein bei den ‌Ukrainern. Die Beziehungen ‌zwischen Trump und Selenskyj hatten sich zuletzt dramatisch verschlechtert. Trump forderte die Ukrainer am Samstag auf, ihren Staatschef bei Neuwahlen auszutauschen. Zudem warf er Selenskyj vor, Gelegenheiten für eine Einigung mit Russland verpasst zu haben. Wahlen sind in der Ukraine unter dem ‌geltenden Kriegsrecht aus Sicherheitsgründen verboten. Donald Trump hatte am Sonntag überraschend eine sofortige „Energie-Waffenruhe“ zwischen Russland und der Ukraine verkündet. Der ukrainische Präsident Wolodymyr Selenskyj begrüßte den Vorstoß, wartet jedoch nach eigenen Angaben noch auf Details der US-Regierung und verwies auf anhaltende russische Angriffe. Von der russischen Regierung lag zunächst keine Stellungnahme vor. Auf  seiner Online-Plattform Truth Social (verlinkt auf https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/posts/117422699218841250)  hatte Trump zuvor ohne weitere Erklärungen mitgeteilt: „Ab sofort gibt es eine ‚Energie-Waffenruhe’ im Krieg zwischen Russland und der Ukraine. Beide Parteien haben zugestimmt. Brecht sie nicht!“ Selenskyj erklärte über den Kurznachrichtendienst Telegram, die Ukraine unterstütze den Schritt und warte auf Details von US-Seite. Er habe die Ankündigung zudem mit Nato-Generalsekretär Mark Rutte, dem kanadischen Premierminister Mark Carney und dem finnischen Präsidenten Alexander Stubb besprochen. Selenskyj erklärte, eine „Energie-Waffenruhe“ wäre eine gute Nachricht für alle, müsse aber Realität werden. Die Ukraine sei bereit, ihre Angriffe auf russische Energieanlagen zu stoppen, wenn Russland im Gegenzug die Attacken auf ukrainische Infrastruktur einstelle. In seiner abendlichen Videoansprache machte der ukrainische Präsident deutlich, dass die ‌russischen Streitkräfte ihre Luftangriffe fortsetzten. So habe es einen Treffer auf ein Heizkraftwerk in Charkiw gegeben, der zweitgrößten Stadt der Ukraine. In den vergangenen sieben Tagen habe es mehr als 200 Angriffe auf ukrainische Erzeugungskapazitäten und 17 auf Öl- und Gasanlagen gegeben. In Charkiw wurden nach Angaben örtlicher Behörden durch russische Angriffe am Sonntag drei Menschen getötet und 20 verletzt. Trumps Vorstoß folgt auf tagelangen Druck der US-Regierung auf die ukrainische Führung, Angriffe auf russische Ölraffinerien zu beenden. Der US-Präsident macht diese für steigende Dieselpreise verantwortlich, die seiner Republikanischen Partei vor den US-Zwischenwahlen im kommenden Monat schaden könnten. Zuvor hatte bereits der von Trump seit Februar geführte Krieg im Iran die Treibstoffpreise weltweit in die Höhe getrieben. Den ‌Vorwurf, die Ukraine sei für die Energiepreise verantwortlich, wies Selenskyj zurück. Jeder wisse, dass der Krieg im Nahen Osten der größere Faktor sei. Um die Preise zu senken, hatte Trump am Freitag ein Diesel-Lieferabkommen mit Russland angekündigt. Demnach soll Russland sofort mehr als 300.000 Tonnen Diesel an amerikanische und globale Märkte liefern, was etwa 2,25 Millionen Barrel entspricht. Selenskyj kritisierte die Vereinbarung scharf, da sie Russland zu weiteren Angriffen ermutige. Kritik kam auch aus den Reihen der US-Republikaner: Der Abgeordnete Don Bacon erklärte, es sei an der Zeit, Sanktionen zu verschärfen, statt sie aufzuheben. Experten bezweifeln zudem, dass die Liefermenge ausreicht, um die Treibstoffpreise dauerhaft zu senken. Allein die USA exportieren ‌täglich rund 1,5 Millionen Barrel Diesel.

welt.de.title: Zur Aufrechterhaltung der „Ordnung“ – Dänemark will Lehrern körperliche Gewalt an Schülern erlauben
welt.de.text: Dänemark will Lehrkräften künftig weitergehende Eingriffsmöglichkeiten bei Gewalt und erheblichen Störungen im Schulunterricht einräumen. Ein entsprechender Gesetzentwurf sieht vor, dass Pädagogen Schüler unter bestimmten Voraussetzungen körperlich festhalten oder gegen ihren Willen aus dem Klassenzimmer bringen dürfen. Das berichtet die französische Zeitung  „Le Monde“ (verlinkt auf https://www.lemonde.fr/en/international/article/2026/10/10/denmark-set-to-allow-the-return-of-physical-force-to-maintain-order-in-schools_6758443_4.html) . Die geplanten Regelungen sollen demnach dazu beitragen, Konflikte frühzeitig zu entschärfen und die Sicherheit an Schulen zu verbessern. Lehrkräfte sollen beispielsweise eingreifen dürfen, wenn Schüler den Unterricht erheblich stören und sich weigern, den Raum zu verlassen. Auch in anderen Fällen soll körperliches Eingreifen möglich sein. Der dänische Bildungsminister Magnus Heunicke von den Sozialdemokraten erklärt: „Zum Beispiel, wenn ein Schüler eine Gefahr für sich und andere darstellt und Dinge zerstört.“ Auch wenn ein Schüler „erheblich stört“ oder „psychische Straftaten begeht“, solle das möglich sein. Durch das Gesetz solle „Ruhe, Ordnung und Sauberkeit“ in Schulen herrschen, sagte der Bildungsminister weiter. „Lehrkräfte dürfen nicht daran zweifeln, was sie machen dürfen, wenn eine Situation eskaliert. Keine Lehrkraft sollte befürchten müssen, entlassen zu werden, weil sie in einer gewalttätigen Situation bei Bedarf eingegriffen hat“, sagte er. Hintergrund der Gesetzesinitiative sind Berichte über eine Zunahme aggressiven und störenden Verhaltens im dänischen Schulalltag. Nach einer Untersuchung der dänischen Arbeitsaufsichtsbehörde gibt mehr als ein Viertel der befragten Lehrkräfte an, dass entsprechendes Verhalten zugenommen habe. In etwa jeder fünften Klasse richtet sich die Gewalt demnach auch gegen Lehrkräfte. Gesetzentwurf muss noch durchs Parlament Noch ist die Neuregelung nicht beschlossen. Zunächst muss das dänische Parlament über den Gesetzentwurf entscheiden. Sollte das Gesetz verabschiedet werden, würde sich Dänemark vom Großteil Europas abheben. Nur in England ist es bisher unter bestimmten Voraussetzungen erlaubt, körperliche Gewalt anzuwenden. In Deutschland ist körperliches Eingreifen durch Lehrkräfte grundsätzlich nur in engen Grenzen erlaubt, etwa bei Notwehr oder als letztes Mittel, um einen beharrlichen Störer am Arm aus dem Unterricht zu begleiten.
